milestones.name: Tenant foundations
milestones.text: Tenant foundations: every system has its schema, module layout, config and tenant key in place.
milestones.journey: Sign up a new tenant, create one resource and see it listed.

milestones.name: Core domain model
milestones.text: Core domain model: each system's entities and invariants are modelled and enforced.
milestones.journey: Create a resource with availability rules and see invalid rules rejected.

milestones.name: Write path
milestones.text: Write path: commands validate input and return structured error envelopes.
milestones.journey: Book an appointment, then cancel it, and see the slot released.

milestones.name: Read APIs
milestones.text: Read APIs: queries are paginated, filterable and tenant-scoped.
milestones.journey: Page through a week of bookings filtered by status.

milestones.name: Events and integration
milestones.text: Events and integration: systems exchange events through the outbox and webhooks.
milestones.journey: Book an appointment and receive the confirmation webhook and email.

milestones.name: Concurrency and retries
milestones.text: Concurrency and retries: writes are idempotent and overlapping requests are rejected safely.
milestones.journey: Submit the same booking twice and two overlapping bookings; see one succeed each time.

milestones.name: Migrations and backfills
milestones.text: Migrations and backfills: legacy data is migrated with dual reads during cutover.
milestones.journey: Import a legacy calendar export and see its bookings alongside new ones.

milestones.name: Observability
milestones.text: Observability: metrics, traces and structured diagnostics cover the booking journey.
milestones.journey: Trace one booking from hold to confirmation across services.

milestones.name: Performance and quotas
milestones.text: Performance and quotas: hot queries are indexed and per-tenant quotas apply.
milestones.journey: Exceed a tenant's booking quota and receive the documented limit response.

milestones.name: Rollout and hardening
milestones.text: Rollout and hardening: feature flags, rollback, retention and audit are in place for launch.
milestones.journey: Turn on waitlist promotion for one tenant, roll it back, and find both changes in the audit log.

identity.title: Define tenant and principal identifier types
identity.intent: Create branded TypeScript types for TenantId, UserId and SessionId so a user id can never be passed where a tenant id is expected. Put the constructors and parsers in src/identity/ids.ts and pin the wire format in contracts/identity.md. Parsers reject anything that is not a 26-character ULID.
identity.acceptance: Passing a TenantId where a UserId is expected fails to compile. Parsing a malformed string throws a typed InvalidIdError.
thinking: The first decision is whether ids are plain strings or branded. Plain strings are cheap but they let a tenant id slide into a user lookup and nothing complains until production. I will brand them.
I considered using a class per id. That buys nothing here because the values cross the JSON boundary as strings anyway, so a type brand with a parser is enough.
The ULID check needs to be strict about length and the Crockford alphabet. A regex with a length anchor is the smallest correct thing, and I will not pull in a dependency for it.

Doubt: the contract file says ids are lowercase, but the ULID spec is case-insensitive. I will normalise to uppercase at parse time and say so in the contract, otherwise two services will disagree about equality.
The test file needs one case per id kind plus the malformed-input path. I will keep the fixtures inline so a reader sees the exact inputs.
identity.approve: Branded ids close the tenant-versus-user mix-up at compile time, and the parser rejects bad input at the edge.

revise.reason: The parser accepts lowercase input but the contract says uppercase, so equality checks will drift between services.
revise.finding: Parser normalisation disagrees with the contract
revise.directive: Normalise ULIDs to uppercase in parseUserId and add a test for lowercase input.

identity.title: Scaffold the principal module boundary
identity.intent: Create the src/identity/ directory with an index that exports only the principal read model and the service interface. Other systems must import through that index and never reach into src/identity/internal. Document the public surface in contracts/identity.md so the boundary is visible to reviewers.
identity.acceptance: A lint rule fails any import from src/identity/internal outside the module. The index exports compile under tsc --noEmit.
thinking: The module boundary matters more than the files inside it. If the index leaks internals on day one, every later refactor becomes a cross-team negotiation.
I will keep the index small: one service interface, one read model type and the error classes. Anything else stays under internal.

Doubt: the repo has no existing lint rule for module boundaries, so I need to check whether the eslint config supports no-restricted-imports with a path pattern. It does, so I will use that rather than writing a custom checker.
The internal folder needs a marker file so that the empty directory survives git. I will keep that marker as a real module, not a placeholder comment.
I will run the typecheck and then try a deliberate bad import to confirm the rule actually fires.
identity.approve: The public surface is small and the lint rule makes the boundary enforceable rather than a convention.

revise.reason: The index re-exports a store type from internal, which defeats the boundary we are trying to draw.
revise.finding: Index leaks an internal store type
revise.directive: Remove the store re-export and expose only the PrincipalView type from the index.

identity.title: Load signing keys from tenant config
identity.intent: Read the per-tenant token signing keys from the config loader in src/identity/keys/config.ts, using the key ids declared in the tenant record. Refuse to start when a tenant has no active key, because a silent fallback would sign tokens with the wrong key. The contract in contracts/identity.md lists the required config shape.
identity.acceptance: Starting the service with a tenant that has no active signing key exits with a named configuration error. A tenant with two active keys signs with the newest one.
thinking: Signing keys are the one place where a silent default would be a security bug. A fallback key would quietly sign tokens for the wrong tenant, so the loader must throw.
The config shape is nested: tenants, then keys, then a status field. I want the loader to validate that shape once at startup and hand typed objects to the rest of the module.
Doubt: two active keys with the same creation timestamp would make the choice of newest key non-deterministic. I will break ties on key id so that the result is stable across restarts.
The error should name the tenant and the missing field. A message like no key is useless when the config has forty tenants.
I will write the test with a fixture where the second key is older, so the newest-wins rule is actually exercised.
identity.approve: Startup now fails loudly on a missing key, and the newest-key rule is deterministic.

revise.reason: The loader still falls back to DEFAULT_KEY in one branch, which would sign real tokens with a shared development key.
revise.finding: Fallback signing key survives in a branch
revise.directive: Delete the DEFAULT_KEY fallback and throw a MissingSigningKeyError for that tenant.

identity.title: Enforce tenant scoping on every table
identity.intent: Add a tenant_id column to the identity tables and a repository helper in src/identity/store/scope.ts that every query must pass through. Make the helper the only way to build a WHERE clause for tenant data. Record the scoping rule in contracts/identity.md so other systems copy it.
identity.acceptance: A query built without a tenant scope does not compile. An integration test shows a user from tenant A cannot read a row from tenant B.
thinking: Tenant leakage is the failure that would hurt most, so I want it structural. A helper that every query must use is better than a code review rule.
The migration adds tenant_id as not null on the existing tables. This is a fresh schema, so there is nothing to backfill and no reason to make the column nullable.
Doubt: a scoped helper can still be bypassed by raw SQL in a migration or a script. I will note that in the contract and ban raw queries outside the store folder through lint.
The compile-time check uses a branded scope type. A function that takes an unscoped query builder simply does not accept the object.
I will run the scope test against a real Postgres instance so that the SQL text and the row-level behaviour are both checked.

edit.new: export function where(scope: TenantScope, sql: Sql) {

shell.description: Dry run scope migration against test database

testOutput: NOTICE: column tenant_id added as NOT NULL
identity.approve: Scoping is enforced by the type of the query builder, so the leak path is closed by construction.

revise.reason: The helper accepts a raw string as the scope, so the compile-time guarantee does not hold for callers that build the scope by hand.
revise.finding: Scope type accepts a raw string
revise.directive: Make TenantScope an opaque branded type created only by the request context factory.

identity.title: Model users with one canonical email
identity.intent: Define the User aggregate in src/identity/domain/user.ts with a single canonical email field, normalised to lowercase and trimmed when the aggregate is constructed. Keep the display address separate so that a user can still see the casing they typed. The fields and invariants are listed in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Two users whose emails differ only by case cannot both be created in one tenant. The canonical email is stored in lowercase.
thinking: Email is the natural key people will type, so the normalisation has to happen before any uniqueness check. If it happens after, we get duplicate accounts that differ only by case.
I will keep two fields, canonicalEmail and displayEmail, because support staff still want to see what the user typed.
Doubt: some mail providers treat dots in the local part as significant and some do not. I am not going to strip dots, because that would silently merge accounts that were meant to be separate.
The aggregate constructor is the only place that normalises. A setter would let a later caller bypass it, so I am not writing one.
I will test the case-collision path explicitly, since that is the bug we are preventing.
identity.approve: The canonical email rule is in one constructor and the case-collision case is tested.

revise.reason: The aggregate stores the raw email as canonicalEmail on one code path, so the lowercase invariant is not held everywhere.
revise.finding: Canonical email skips normalisation on one path
revise.directive: Route every construction path through normaliseEmail and assert lowercase in the test.

identity.title: Model memberships linking users to tenants
identity.intent: Add a Membership entity in src/identity/domain/membership.ts that links one user to one tenant with a status of invited, active or suspended. A user can belong to many tenants, and the same user must not hold two active memberships in one tenant. The rules go into contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Creating a second active membership for the same user and tenant is rejected. A suspended membership can be reactivated without creating a new row.
thinking: The membership is where tenancy and identity meet, so I want its state transitions to be explicit. A boolean for active would not be enough to express invited.
Reactivation should reuse the existing row. Creating a new row each time would leave the history split and make audit queries harder.
Doubt: I first wrote the uniqueness rule in the aggregate only. A concurrent insert would bypass it, so the migration needs a partial unique index as well.
The status enum is closed. Any unknown status string throws during hydration rather than being mapped to a default.
I will check the migration with a dry run to be sure the partial index name matches the one the repository expects.
identity.approve: The partial unique index backs the aggregate rule, so concurrent inserts cannot create two active memberships.

revise.reason: The partial index is keyed on user and tenant but the repository reads it by the reverse order, which hides a missing index in plans.
revise.finding: Index column order does not match lookups
revise.directive: Reorder the index columns to match the repository lookup and add an explain test.

identity.title: Represent roles as a closed permission set
identity.intent: Define roles in src/identity/domain/role.ts as a closed union of owner, admin, member and viewer, each mapped to a fixed set of permission strings. A role outside that union is a compile error, and an unknown string from storage throws on load. The mapping table is written out in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Adding a role name that is not in the union breaks the typecheck. Loading an unknown role string from storage throws UnknownRoleError.
thinking: Roles look trivial but they are the source of most permission bugs. A closed union turns a typo into a failing build rather than a silent over-grant.
I considered letting tenants define custom roles. That is a real feature with its own design, so I am leaving it out and noting it as deferred.
Doubt: the permission strings might drift from the route table in the web layer. I will export the strings from this file and import them there, so there is one source.
The load path has to be strict. Mapping an unknown role to viewer would be a privilege change nobody approved.
The test iterates the union by a const array and checks each permission set has no duplicates.
identity.approve: The role set is closed and the permission map has one source that both domain and routes import.

revise.reason: The viewer permission set includes a write permission copied from member, which would let read-only users edit records.
revise.finding: Viewer role carries a write permission
revise.directive: Remove the write permission from the viewer set and add a test asserting viewers hold no write permissions.

identity.title: Encode session lifecycle as a state machine
identity.intent: Model a session as a discriminated union in src/identity/domain/session.ts with the states pending, active, expired and revoked. Transitions are functions that return the next state, so an illegal transition such as revoked to active cannot be written. The allowed transitions are listed in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Calling activate on a revoked session fails to compile. Every legal transition has a test, and every illegal one a test that expects a throw.
thinking: A session is a long-lived thing with a lot of ways to go wrong. A state machine keeps the set of legal moves in one place.
I want the states as a discriminated union so that each state carries only the fields that exist in it. A revoked session has a revokedAt and no expiresAt, for example.
Doubt: pending to expired is a real path when a sign-in link is never clicked. I almost left it out, but the expiry sweep depends on it, so it stays.
The transitions return a new value rather than mutating. That makes the test assertions straightforward and avoids shared-state bugs in the request path.
I will write the illegal-transition tests as a table, so reviewers see the whole matrix at once.
identity.approve: The transition table is explicit and the compiler rejects the moves that should never happen.

revise.reason: The expire transition is allowed from revoked, so a revoked session can reappear as merely expired and confuse the audit trail.
revise.finding: Revoked sessions can transition to expired
revise.directive: Forbid the revoked to expired transition and add a table row asserting it throws.

identity.title: Validate sign-up payloads before persistence
identity.intent: Add a validator in src/identity/commands/sign-up.ts that checks email shape, password length and tenant slug before anything touches the database. Return a list of field errors rather than throwing on the first problem, so the form can show them together. The field rules and error codes are documented in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A payload with three bad fields returns three field errors in one response. A valid payload reaches the repository exactly once.
thinking: Validation runs before the transaction opens. If it runs inside, a bad payload costs a connection and a rollback for nothing.
Returning all field errors at once is a small decision with a large effect on how many round trips a user needs to fix a form.

Doubt: the password length rule and the password strength rule are different things. I will only check length here, because strength belongs to the policy module and mixing them would make the error codes misleading.
The tenant slug check needs the lowercase-and-dashes rule to match the one used by the routing layer. I will import the regex rather than copying it.
I will test the three-error case with a real payload so the response shape is pinned.
identity.approve: Validation collects every field error before any write, which is the behaviour the form needs.

revise.reason: The email check still throws on the first failure, so a user with a bad email and a short password sees only one error at a time.
revise.finding: Validator throws instead of collecting errors
revise.directive: Replace the remaining throw with a pushed field error so all checks run.

identity.title: Create invitations with single-use tokens
identity.intent: Write the invite command in src/identity/commands/invite.ts so that an admin can invite an address to a tenant with a role. Each invitation gets a random token that is stored only as a SHA-256 hash, and the token is redeemed exactly once. The token format and expiry are recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: The raw token is returned once at creation and never stored. Redeeming the same token twice returns a typed already-used error.
thinking: The invitation is a bearer credential, so storing the raw token would be a data leak waiting to happen. I will store only its hash and show the raw value once.
The token needs enough entropy. I will take 32 bytes from crypto.randomBytes and encode them with base64url so the link is safe in a URL.
Doubt: hashing with plain SHA-256 is fine here because the token is random and long, not a human password. A slow hash would add latency with no benefit.
The invite command returns the raw token in its result. The route layer must not log that result, so I will mark the field as sensitive in the type.
I will check the test covers the replay path, because a single-use rule that is not tested tends to rot.
identity.approve: Tokens are hashed at rest, shown once, and the replay path is covered by a test.

revise.reason: The tokenHash field is assigned the raw token on one branch, which stores the bearer credential in plain text.
revise.directive: Assign the SHA-256 hash to tokenHash on every branch and add an assertion that the table holds no raw token.

identity.title: Return typed error envelopes for login failures
identity.intent: Map every login failure in src/identity/commands/login.ts to a closed error code, such as INVALID_CREDENTIALS, ACCOUNT_LOCKED or MFA_REQUIRED, inside one envelope shape. The response must not reveal whether an email exists. The envelope and code list live in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A wrong password and an unknown email return the same code and the same response body. Each code maps to exactly one HTTP status.
thinking: Login is where account enumeration happens if we are careless. Two different messages for unknown email and wrong password give an attacker a free user list.
I will centralise the envelope in errors.ts so that every identity command speaks the same shape. Ad hoc objects in each command would drift within a month.
Doubt: the lockout response has to be distinct for the UI to explain it, but it also tells an attacker that the account exists. I am accepting that trade-off and recording it in the contract.
The status mapping is a switch with no default, so adding a code without a status fails the typecheck.
The test compares the full response body of the two failure cases, not just the code, so any extra field would be caught.
identity.approve: The unknown-email and wrong-password responses are byte-identical, which closes the enumeration path.

revise.reason: The unknown-email branch returns a body with a different key order, which is enough for a timing or diff probe to tell the cases apart.
revise.finding: Unknown-email body differs from wrong-password body
revise.directive: Route the unknown-email branch through the same failure constructor so both bodies are identical.

identity.title: Accept password changes with reauthentication
identity.intent: Implement the change-password command in src/identity/commands/change-password.ts so that it requires the current password, or a fresh MFA assertion, before it accepts a new one. On success it revokes every other session for that user. The reauthentication window is set in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A change with a wrong current password is rejected and leaves the hash unchanged. A successful change revokes all sessions except the caller's.
thinking: Changing a password is a sensitive action, so a stolen session cookie alone must not be enough. The current password or a fresh MFA assertion is the gate.
The revocation of other sessions should happen in the same transaction as the hash update. Otherwise a crash between the two leaves an old session alive with a new password.
Doubt: the reauth window of five minutes is a guess. I will keep it in config so that it can be tuned without a code change.
The hash comparison must use the constant-time verifier from the password module. A string equality check here would be a small but real timing leak.
I will verify the transaction boundary by forcing a failure after the hash update and checking that the session rows are untouched.
identity.approve: The change is gated on reauthentication and the session revocation shares the transaction with the hash update.

revise.reason: The current password is compared with a plain equality check instead of the constant-time verifier, which leaks timing.
revise.finding: Password comparison is not constant time
revise.directive: Replace the equality check with verifyPassword and keep the existing test for the wrong-password path.

identity.title: List members of a tenant with cursors
identity.intent: Expose a members query in src/identity/queries/list-members.ts that pages through a tenant's active memberships using an opaque cursor built from the membership id and creation time. Page size is capped at 100, and a larger request is clamped rather than rejected. The cursor format and page limits are written in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Paging through 250 members returns each member exactly once across three pages. A limit of 500 returns at most 100 rows.
thinking: Offset pagination falls apart when members are added during a scan, so I will use keyset pagination on creation time and id.
The cursor is encoded as base64url JSON. Clients must treat it as opaque, and the contract says so explicitly.
Doubt: two members can share a creation timestamp, so the id is part of the sort key. Without it the cursor would skip rows.
Clamping rather than rejecting an oversized limit keeps the client simple, although I will log a warning so we can see callers that always ask for too much.
The test seeds 250 members with identical timestamps to force the tiebreak path.

edit.new: ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC

identity.approve: Keyset paging with an id tiebreak returns every member once, even under identical timestamps.

revise.reason: The cursor encodes only the creation time, so rows with equal timestamps at a page boundary are skipped.
revise.directive: Include the membership id in the cursor payload and compare on the pair in the WHERE clause.

identity.title: Filter sessions by status and last-seen date
identity.intent: Add a session listing query in src/identity/queries/list-sessions.ts that filters by status and by a last-seen lower bound. The filters are optional, and combined filters are ANDed. Both filter fields are documented in contracts/identity.md with their accepted values.
identity.acceptance: Filtering by status revoked and a date returns only rows matching both. An unknown status value is rejected with a validation error.
thinking: The filters are small, but a support engineer will use this query to chase a sign-in problem, so the result must match what they typed exactly.
I will build the WHERE clause from a list of predicates rather than string concatenation. That keeps the parameter numbering correct when a filter is absent.
Doubt: last-seen is stored with a timezone, and the filter is a date. I need to decide whether the bound is midnight UTC or the tenant's timezone. I am choosing UTC and writing it in the contract.
Unknown status values must fail, not be ignored. Ignoring them would return every session for a typo, which is the wrong surprise.
The test uses three sessions with boundary timestamps so the inclusive lower bound is checked.
identity.approve: The filters compose predictably and the boundary and unknown-status cases are both pinned by tests.

revise.reason: An empty status string is treated as no filter, so a client that sends an empty value silently gets every session.
revise.finding: Empty status string disables the filter silently
revise.directive: Reject an empty status string with a validation error and add a test for it.

identity.title: Look up users by normalized email address
identity.intent: Add a lookup in src/identity/queries/find-user-by-email.ts that normalises the query email the same way the aggregate does, then searches the canonical column. Use the same normaliser function, not a copy, so the two can never disagree. The lookup rule is recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Looking up User@Example.com finds the user stored as user@example.com. A miss returns null rather than throwing.
thinking: The lookup has to normalise exactly the way storage does, or case-insensitive login quietly stops working. Sharing the function is the only safe option.
A miss returning null is a deliberate choice. Callers decide whether a miss is a failure, and throwing here would force every caller into a try block.
Doubt: an input with leading whitespace from a paste could still match after trimming. I trim in the normaliser, so that case is covered, but I want a test that proves it.
The query uses the canonical column with an equality predicate and relies on the unique index from the membership work.
I will confirm the test fixture uses mixed case in the stored value, since a fixture stored in lowercase would pass without exercising the normaliser.
identity.approve: The lookup shares the aggregate's normaliser and the test fixture stores mixed case, so the path is really exercised.

revise.reason: The query still reads the raw email column, so mixed-case input now misses rows that the canonical column would match.
revise.finding: Lookup reads the raw email column
revise.directive: Point the WHERE clause at canonical_email and add a mixed-case lookup test.

identity.title: Expose a read-only session introspection query
identity.intent: Provide an introspect query in src/identity/queries/introspect.ts that answers whether a presented session token is active, and for which tenant and roles. It never returns the token hash or any credential material. The response shape is pinned in contracts/identity.md for the other systems that call it.
identity.acceptance: An active session returns its tenant and roles. A revoked or unknown token returns active false with no extra fields.
thinking: Other systems will call introspection on every request, so the response must be small and must never leak credentials.
I will return a discriminated result with active true or false, so callers cannot forget to check the flag.
Doubt: returning the roles means a role change takes effect only on the next introspection. That is acceptable, and I will document the staleness window rather than pretend it does not exist.
The query reads through the scope helper, so a token from one tenant cannot introspect against another tenant's roles.
I will test the inactive case by asserting the response has exactly one key, which keeps the shape honest.

edit.new: return { active: true, tenantId: session.tenantId, roles: session.roles };

identity.approve: The introspection response is minimal and the inactive case is pinned to a single key.

revise.reason: Spreading the session object into the response leaks the token hash field to every caller.
revise.finding: Response spreads the full session record
revise.directive: Return only the tenantId and roles fields in the active branch and assert the hash is absent.

identity.title: Publish user-created events through the outbox
identity.intent: Write a UserCreated event in src/identity/events/user-created.ts and append it to the outbox table in the same transaction as the user insert. The event payload carries the user id and tenant id, never the email. Event shape and topic name are pinned in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A failed user insert leaves no outbox row behind. A successful insert produces exactly one UserCreated row with no email field.
thinking: The outbox pattern only works if the event and the write commit together. Writing the event after the commit would lose it on a crash.
Leaving the email out of the payload is deliberate, because the event bus is read by systems that should not hold personal data.
Doubt: the event needs a version field so consumers can evolve. I am adding schemaVersion as the first field, since changing it later means every consumer breaks at once.
The outbox append uses the same client as the insert, passed explicitly, so there is no way to write the event on a different connection.
I will test the rollback path by making the insert fail on a unique violation and asserting the outbox is empty.

edit.new: await outbox.append(tx, { type: 'UserCreated', schemaVersion: 1, userId, tenantId });

shell.description: Run user created outbox event tests

identity.approve: The event commits with the insert, carries no personal data, and has a version field from the start.

revise.reason: The outbox append runs on the pool connection rather than the transaction client, so a rollback leaves the event published.
revise.directive: Pass the transaction client into outbox.append and assert the rollback test leaves no row.

identity.title: Emit membership-changed webhooks to subscribers
identity.intent: Deliver a membership.changed webhook from src/identity/webhooks/membership-changed.ts whenever a membership moves between invited, active and suspended. Sign each delivery with the tenant's webhook secret and retry on non-2xx responses. The signing scheme and retry window are documented in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A status change produces one signed delivery per subscriber. A subscriber returning 500 is retried with backoff up to the configured limit.
thinking: Webhooks are the part of the system where a subscriber's bad day becomes our problem, so the retry and signing logic has to be boring and well tested.
The signature is an HMAC over the timestamp and body. Including the timestamp lets the receiver reject replays.
Doubt: retrying on every non-2xx includes 4xx responses, and retrying a 400 forever is pointless. I am restricting retries to 5xx and network errors.
The delivery worker reads from the outbox rather than being called inline, so a slow subscriber cannot block the membership write.
I will test the retry path with a stub server that fails twice and then succeeds, to confirm the backoff sequence.
identity.approve: Deliveries are signed with a timestamp, retries are limited to server and network failures, and the write path never waits on subscribers.

revise.reason: The success check accepts every status at or above 200, so a 3xx or 5xx response is recorded as delivered and never retried.
revise.finding: Delivery success check accepts any status
revise.directive: Limit the delivered branch to 2xx responses and route 5xx responses into the retry schedule.

identity.title: Sign token payloads for cross-system contracts
identity.intent: Produce signed access tokens in src/identity/tokens/sign.ts with a payload that other systems can verify offline. The payload includes tenant, subject, roles and an expiry, and it is signed with the active key from the key loader. The claim names and algorithm are fixed in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A signed token verifies with the published public key. A token whose expiry has passed fails verification with a typed error.
thinking: Other systems will verify our tokens without calling us, so the claim names are a public contract from the first commit.
I am using EdDSA because the keys are small and verification is fast. The algorithm name goes in the header, and the verifier pins it to avoid algorithm confusion attacks.
Doubt: the active key might rotate between signing and verification. The header carries the key id, so the verifier can fetch the right public key.
The expiry is short, fifteen minutes, because revocation for offline verifiers is best-effort. Longer expiry would make revocation a fiction.
I will verify the signed token in the test with the public key derived from the same fixture to catch encoding mismatches.
identity.approve: The algorithm is pinned, the key id travels in the header, and the expiry is short enough to be honest about revocation.

revise.reason: The header still advertises HS256 while the signature is produced with the Ed25519 key, so verifiers using the header will reject every token.
revise.finding: Token header algorithm does not match the signature
revise.directive: Set the header alg to EdDSA and add a test that verifies a token using only the published public key.

identity.title: Publish role grant events for downstream consumers
identity.intent: Emit a RoleGranted and RoleRevoked event from src/identity/events/role-grant.ts whenever a membership's role changes. Consumers in the billing and notifications systems read these events to decide on seat counts and mailing rights. The event fields are pinned in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Changing a role emits exactly one event with the old and new role. Setting a role to its current value emits nothing.
thinking: Two other systems depend on these events for money and mail decisions, so a spurious event is a real cost. The no-op case has to be explicit.
The event carries both the previous and the new role. Consumers should not need to reconstruct history by reading our tables.
Doubt: a role change that happens inside a bulk import could emit a burst of events. I am keeping one event per membership and noting the batching question as deferred.
The emit call goes through the same outbox helper as the user event, so every identity event shares one delivery path.
I will test the no-op case by comparing the emitted count before and after setting the same role.
identity.approve: Events fire only on a real role change and carry both sides of the change.

revise.reason: The emit condition has a stray always-true clause, so every save emits a role event even when the role is unchanged.
revise.finding: Role event fires on every save
revise.directive: Remove the always-true clause from the emit condition and keep the no-op test.

identity.title: Guard refresh rotation against concurrent reuse
identity.intent: Rotate refresh tokens in src/identity/tokens/refresh.ts so that each refresh token is consumed exactly once, using a row lock on the token family. If a consumed token is presented again, revoke the whole family. The reuse rule is written in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Two concurrent refreshes with the same token yield one success and one reuse error. The second presentation revokes every token in that family.
thinking: Refresh token rotation is where a stolen token does the most damage, so concurrency has to be handled in the database, not in application memory.
A SELECT FOR UPDATE on the family row serialises competing refreshes. Two requests cannot both observe the token as unused.
Doubt: revoking the whole family on reuse will also log out a legitimate user whose browser retried. That is the accepted trade-off, and I will say it plainly in the contract.
The migration adds a family id to each token row, so revocation is a single update rather than a scan.
I will run the race test with two parallel promises and a barrier so both requests reach the lock together.

edit.old: const row = await tx.one('SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE id = $1', [id]);
edit.new: const row = await tx.one('SELECT * FROM refresh_tokens WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE', [id]);

shell.description: Run concurrent refresh rotation race test

identity.approve: The row lock makes the single-use rule hold under real concurrency, and the race test proves it rather than assuming it.

revise.reason: The lock is taken on the token row but the family revocation reads the family table without a lock, so a racing revoke can miss tokens.
revise.finding: Family revocation runs without a lock
revise.directive: Take FOR UPDATE on the family row before revoking and add a race test covering the revoke path.

identity.title: Make invitation acceptance idempotent per token
identity.intent: Make the accept-invitation command in src/identity/commands/accept-invite.ts return the same membership when the same token is redeemed by the same user twice. A different user redeeming a used token still gets the already-used error. The idempotency rule is documented in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Accepting the same invitation twice as the same user returns the same membership id. A second user accepting it gets INVITE_ALREADY_USED.
thinking: Users double-click buttons and mobile networks retry requests, so the same acceptance will arrive twice. Returning an error on the second call would confuse a user who succeeded.
The rule is scoped to the same user. Letting any caller replay the token would turn the idempotency key into a second redemption path.
Doubt: the idempotent branch needs to compare user ids, and the token row stores the first redeemer's id. I need to make sure the comparison happens inside the locked transaction.
The response on replay has to be identical to the first response, including the membership id, so the client cannot tell the difference.
I will test replay by the same user, replay by a different user, and first acceptance, as three rows in one table.
identity.approve: Replays by the original user return the same membership and other users are still refused.

revise.reason: The replay branch returns the membership without checking that the caller is the original redeemer, so any holder of the token can replay it.
revise.finding: Replay path skips the redeemer check
revise.directive: Compare the caller's user id to the stored redeemer before returning the replay result.

identity.title: Retry outbound SSO metadata fetches with backoff
identity.intent: Fetch an enterprise identity provider's metadata document in src/identity/sso/metadata-fetch.ts with a bounded retry and exponential backoff. Cache a successful document for its declared max-age and never cache a failure. Retry limits and timeouts are recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A metadata endpoint returning 503 twice and then 200 succeeds on the third attempt. A failed fetch is not cached and the next call tries again.
thinking: The identity provider is a remote system we do not control, so the fetch needs timeouts and bounded retries. Unbounded retries would tie up workers during an outage.
Caching only successes is important. Caching a failure would lock a tenant out for the whole max-age window after one blip.
Doubt: the backoff uses jitter, but a test with random delays is flaky. I am injecting the random source so tests are deterministic.
The max-age header is parsed as an integer and clamped to a sane ceiling, so a provider sending a huge value cannot pin a stale document forever.
I will run the flaky-endpoint test with a fake clock to confirm the three attempts happen at the expected offsets.
identity.approve: Retries are bounded, jitter is injectable for tests, and failures never enter the cache.

revise.reason: The retry loop has no upper bound on attempts when the server returns a Retry-After header, so a misbehaving provider can hold a worker indefinitely.
revise.finding: Retry loop honours an unbounded Retry-After
revise.directive: Clamp the Retry-After delay to the configured maximum and count it against the attempt limit.

identity.title: Serialize password resets per account
identity.intent: Make the password reset flow in src/identity/commands/reset-password.ts take a per-account advisory lock so that two reset requests cannot race and issue two valid codes. A new request invalidates any earlier unused code. The lock key derivation is in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Two concurrent reset requests leave exactly one unused code. Using the older code after a newer request returns RESET_CODE_EXPIRED.
thinking: A reset code is a credential, and two valid codes at once double the window an attacker has. Serialising per account closes that.
I am using a Postgres advisory lock keyed on a hash of the tenant and user ids. That scopes the lock to one account and does not block the rest of the tenant.
Doubt: advisory locks are session-scoped, so a pooled connection that is not released would hold the lock. I am using the transaction-scoped variant to avoid that.
The older code is invalidated by marking it used, not by deleting it, so the audit history still shows the request.
I will verify the lock with two connections in the test and assert the second one waits for the first to commit.
identity.approve: The transaction-scoped lock serialises resets per account and the old code is marked used rather than deleted.

revise.reason: The reset path takes the session-level advisory lock and never releases it on the error branch, so a failed request holds the account lock until the connection is recycled.
revise.finding: Session advisory lock leaks on error
revise.directive: Switch to the transaction-scoped advisory lock so an error rollback releases it.

identity.title: Backfill normalized emails for legacy accounts
identity.intent: Write a backfill in migrations/0005_identity_backfill_canonical_email.sql that fills canonical_email for accounts created before normalisation existed. It runs in batches of 1,000 rows and is safe to re-run. The batch size and the collision handling are recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: After the backfill no row has a null canonical_email. Running the script twice changes nothing on the second run.
thinking: The backfill touches every account, so batching is needed to keep locks short. A single UPDATE over the whole table would block logins for minutes.
The script must be idempotent. It only updates rows where canonical_email is null, so a second run is a no-op.
Doubt: two legacy accounts may normalise to the same canonical address. I cannot silently pick one, so the script records collisions in a side table for a human to resolve.
The TypeScript wrapper prints the batch count and the number of collisions, so the operator sees the outcome without reading the database.
I will run the backfill twice against a copy of the fixture and compare the row checksums after each run.

edit.new: UPDATE users SET canonical_email = lower(trim(email)) WHERE canonical_email IS NULL AND id = ANY($1);

identity.approve: Batched, re-runnable, and collisions are surfaced instead of resolved by guesswork.

revise.reason: The backfill update has no null filter in one statement, so a re-run rewrites every canonical email and bumps every row version.
revise.directive: Add a WHERE canonical_email IS NULL filter to the batch update and assert a second run touches zero rows.

identity.title: Migrate refresh tokens to hashed storage
identity.intent: Move existing refresh tokens from plaintext columns to SHA-256 hashes in migrations/0006_identity_hash_refresh.sql. The migration adds a token_hash column, fills it, then drops the plaintext column in a later step. Hash format is recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: After the migration no plaintext refresh token remains in the table. An existing session can still refresh successfully.
thinking: Storing refresh tokens in plaintext means a database read is a session hijack. Hashing them is worth doing even though the tokens are random.
I am splitting the change into an add-and-fill step and a separate drop step, so a rollback between them does not lose any tokens.

Doubt: existing clients hold the raw token, and the hash of that raw token is what the lookup now needs. The fill step hashes the stored plaintext, so the client's token still matches after the change.
The drop is deliberately not in the same file. It runs only after the fill has been verified on production data.
I will test the round trip with a token issued before the migration and a refresh attempt after it.

edit.new: UPDATE refresh_tokens SET token_hash = encode(sha256(token::bytea), 'hex') WHERE token_hash IS NULL;

shell.description: Run refresh token hashing migration tests

identity.approve: The add-fill-drop split keeps every step reversible and the round-trip test proves old tokens still refresh.

revise.reason: The fill statement hashes the token column but the lookup now compares against the hex digest in a different case, so every migrated token fails to match.
revise.finding: Hash case mismatch breaks migrated lookups
revise.directive: Lowercase the hex digest in the fill step to match the lookup and add a test that refreshes a migrated token.

identity.title: Add a tenant_id column to membership rows
identity.intent: Add tenant_id to identity_memberships in migrations/0007_identity_membership_tenant.sql and backfill it from the parent user row. Index the column next to the user id so tenant-scoped reads stay fast. The column and index are noted in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Every membership row has a non-null tenant_id after the backfill. The new index is used by the tenant members query in EXPLAIN.
thinking: Membership rows were created before tenant scoping was enforced everywhere, so they may lack the column. The backfill has to fill it before the not-null constraint goes on.
The value comes from the parent user row, which is the source of truth for tenancy in the legacy model.
Doubt: a few legacy memberships point at users that were already deleted. Those orphans cannot be assigned a tenant, so the migration must remove them or stop, and stopping is the safer default.
The index order matters for the query. Tenant first, then user, because every read starts from the tenant.
I will run EXPLAIN against the members query in the test to confirm the planner picks the new index.

edit.old: ALTER TABLE identity_memberships ALTER COLUMN tenant_id SET NOT NULL;
edit.new: DO $$ BEGIN IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM identity_memberships WHERE tenant_id IS NULL) THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'orphan memberships'; END IF; END $$;

shell.description: Apply membership tenant migration to test database

identity.approve: The migration refuses to proceed on orphans, which is the safer default than inventing a tenant for them.

revise.reason: The migration sets the not-null constraint before the backfill runs on one code path, so it fails on any database with existing memberships.
revise.directive: Run the backfill statement before the ALTER TABLE SET NOT NULL and keep the orphan guard after it.

identity.title: Drop plaintext API key columns after backfill
identity.intent: Remove the legacy plaintext api_key column once every API key has a stored hash, in migrations/0008_identity_drop_api_key_plaintext.sql. The migration first asserts that no row still has a plaintext key, and only then drops the column. The removal is noted in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: The migration aborts if any row still holds a plaintext key. After a clean run the api_key column no longer exists.
thinking: Dropping a column is destructive and cannot be undone without a restore, so the guard has to run before the drop and fail loudly.
The guard counts rows where the plaintext column is not null. A non-zero count raises an exception and the whole transaction rolls back.
Doubt: the production dataset may include keys created by a script that wrote only the hash column. That is the desired state, so the guard should pass for them.
I am keeping the drop in a transaction with the guard, so it is all or nothing.
The test seeds one row with plaintext and asserts the migration refuses, then removes the row and asserts the drop succeeds.

edit.old: ALTER TABLE api_keys DROP COLUMN api_key;
edit.new: ALTER TABLE api_keys DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS api_key;

shell.description: Run API key column drop guard tests

identity.approve: The guard blocks the drop while plaintext rows remain, and the whole change is a single transaction.

revise.reason: The drop uses IF EXISTS, which turns a missing column into a silent success, so a wrong database name would pass without checking anything.
revise.finding: IF EXISTS hides a missing column
revise.directive: Remove the IF EXISTS clause so a missing column fails the migration loudly.

identity.title: Emit metrics for login success and failure
identity.intent: Record login outcomes as counters in src/identity/observability/login-metrics.ts, labelled by outcome and tenant tier but never by user id. Keep the metric names and label sets in contracts/identity.md so dashboards can depend on them. Use the existing metrics registry rather than a new client.
identity.acceptance: A successful and a failed login each increment the matching counter once. No metric carries a user id or email label.
thinking: Login counters are the first thing an on-call engineer reads during an incident, so the label set has to be stable and low cardinality.
User ids as labels would create one series per user. That would blow up the metrics store, so I am leaving them out entirely.
Doubt: tenant tier is a good label, but tenants can change tier. I will read the tier at emit time and accept that a historical series may split when a tenant upgrades.
I am reusing the shared registry, so the metric naming prefix matches the other systems.
The test scrapes the registry and asserts the exact label names, which catches a later edit that adds a high-cardinality label.
identity.approve: The labels are low cardinality and the scrape test guards against a future high-cardinality addition.

revise.reason: The counter still carries a user label in the failure branch, which would create one series per user on a busy tenant.
revise.finding: Failure branch adds a user label
revise.directive: Remove the userId label from the failure branch and keep the scrape test asserting the label set.

identity.title: Trace token issuance across service boundaries
identity.intent: Add spans around token issuance in src/identity/observability/trace-tokens.ts so a sign-in shows as one trace from the request through the signing step and the outbox write. Propagate the incoming trace context into the outbox event so consumers can join the trace. The span names are listed in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A sign-in request produces spans for issue, sign and outbox append under one trace id. The outbox event carries the trace id in its headers.
thinking: Sign-in is slow sometimes and nobody knows which step. Spans around the three steps make that visible in one view.
The trace id has to travel into the outbox row, otherwise the consumer side starts a new trace and the join is lost.
Doubt: the span attributes must not include the token or the subject id. Attributes are indexed and exported, so a raw token there would be a credential leak in the trace store.
I am using the existing tracer from the shared package and passing the context explicitly, not through async local storage, because the outbox write runs on a different tick.
The test asserts the span tree and checks that the outbox headers contain the same trace id.
identity.approve: One trace covers sign-in end to end, and the attributes carry the token kind rather than the credential.

revise.reason: The span attribute for the subject carries the raw user id, which is a personal identifier that the trace store should not index.
revise.finding: Span attribute exposes the subject id
revise.directive: Replace the subject attribute with a hashed subject key and assert the raw id is absent from span attributes.

identity.title: Log structured reasons for denied sign-ins
identity.intent: Write a structured log line in src/identity/observability/denial-log.ts for every denied sign-in, with a reason code from the closed error list and the tenant id. The log must never include the submitted password or the full email. The log schema is pinned in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A denied sign-in emits one JSON log line with a reason code and tenant id. The log line contains neither the password nor the full email.
thinking: Denied sign-ins are how support answers why can't I log in, so the log has to be specific enough to act on without leaking credentials.
The reason code comes from the same closed list as the error envelope, so the log and the response can never disagree about why.
Doubt: the full email is useful for support, but it is also personal data in logs that outlive the account. I am logging a masked email instead, with the domain and the first letter.
The log writer is a pure function that takes the event and returns the line, so the redaction is testable without a logger.
I will test that the password string never appears in the output by searching the serialised line for the fixture password.

shell.description: Run denied sign-in log redaction tests

identity.approve: The denial log is structured, redacted by a pure function, and checked against the fixture password.

revise.reason: The serialiser includes the request body as a debug field, which carries the submitted password into the log.
revise.finding: Request body is logged on denial
revise.directive: Drop the request body field from the denial log and assert the password fixture string is absent.

identity.title: Rate limit password attempts per account
identity.intent: Throttle password checks per account in src/identity/limits/password-attempts.ts using a sliding window of five attempts per fifteen minutes, keyed on the canonical email and the source address. A throttled request gets a retry-after value and no hint about the password. The window and keys are documented in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: The sixth attempt inside fifteen minutes is refused with a retry-after value. Attempts from a different address are counted separately.
thinking: Password guessing is cheap unless we make it expensive. A per-account window is the control that actually slows an attacker down.
I am keying on both the account and the source address. Keying on the account alone lets an attacker lock a real user out, and keying on the address alone is evaded with a botnet.
Doubt: a sliding window needs a sorted set or a counter bucket. A bucket is simpler and good enough at this scale, so I am using buckets.
The retry-after value is computed from the oldest attempt in the window, so the client can wait the exact time rather than guessing.
I will test the boundary at exactly fifteen minutes with a fake clock, since off-by-one errors live there.
identity.approve: The key combines account and address so one attacker cannot lock out a user and a botnet cannot evade the window.

revise.reason: The key uses the raw email rather than the canonical one, so a mixed-case attempt gets a fresh counter and the limit is bypassed.
revise.finding: Throttle key uses the raw email
revise.directive: Key the throttle on canonicalEmail and add a test with mixed-case attempts hitting one counter.

identity.title: Cache resolved permission sets per request
identity.intent: Memoise the resolved permission set for a membership inside one request in src/identity/perf/permission-cache.ts, so a route that checks permissions several times queries the membership once. The cache lives on the request context and is discarded afterwards. The scope of the cache is stated in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: A route checking three permissions issues one membership query. A second request does not see the first request's cached result.
thinking: Permission checks happen many times per request, and each one hitting the database is wasteful. A per-request cache removes the repeats without any shared state.
The cache must not outlive the request. A process-wide cache would keep a revoked role alive after the change.
Doubt: within one request a role change could happen in the same handler and a later check would read the stale value. The write path invalidates the cache entry, and I will test that exact sequence.
The cache key is the membership id, which is already scoped by tenant, so no cross-tenant reuse is possible.
I will measure the query count in the test with a counting wrapper rather than trusting the code path.
identity.approve: The cache is request scoped, invalidated on write, and the query count is measured instead of assumed.

revise.reason: The cache is a module-level Map that the code now points at, so entries from one request survive into the next.
revise.directive: Attach the cache to the request context and remove the module-level Map.

identity.title: Cap active sessions per user per tenant
identity.intent: Enforce a maximum of twelve active sessions per user per tenant in src/identity/limits/session-cap.ts. When a new sign-in would exceed the cap, the oldest active session is revoked rather than refusing the sign-in. The cap value and the eviction rule are written in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: The thirteenth sign-in revokes the oldest active session. The total active count never exceeds twelve.
thinking: A session cap protects against a leaked credential being used to pile up sessions. Evicting the oldest is friendlier than refusing a legitimate new device.
The eviction has to happen in the same transaction as the new session insert, otherwise two concurrent sign-ins could both see eleven and both insert.
Doubt: the oldest by creation time may be the session the user is actively using. I am using last-seen time instead, so the idle session is the one that goes.
The cap is read from tenant config, so a tenant with a higher limit does not need a code change.
I will test the concurrent case with two sign-ins against a count of eleven to prove the cap holds.

edit.new: ORDER BY last_seen_at ASC, id ASC

identity.approve: Eviction uses last-seen order inside the insert transaction, so the cap holds under concurrency.

revise.reason: The eviction count is read outside the transaction, so two concurrent sign-ins can both see eleven sessions and push the total to thirteen.
revise.finding: Session count read outside the transaction
revise.directive: Move the active-session count into the insert transaction and lock the user row before counting.

identity.title: Gate SSO login behind a tenant feature flag
identity.intent: Wrap the SSO login entry point in src/identity/rollout/sso-flag.ts so that it is refused unless the tenant's sso_enabled flag is on. Flag reads go through the shared flag client with a default of off. The flag name and default are recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: With the flag off, the SSO start endpoint returns FEATURE_DISABLED. Turning the flag on for one tenant does not enable SSO for another.
thinking: SSO is the riskiest login path to roll out, so it should sit behind a per-tenant flag that defaults off and can be reversed without a deploy.
The default must be off when the flag service is unreachable. A default of on would open SSO to every tenant during an outage.
Doubt: the flag is read on every start request, which adds a call. The shared client caches the value briefly, and I am relying on that rather than adding my own cache.
The refusal returns FEATURE_DISABLED rather than a 404, so support can tell a disabled tenant from a broken route.
I will test the per-tenant isolation explicitly by turning the flag on for one tenant and asserting the other still refuses.

edit.new: if (await flags.isEnabled('sso_enabled', req.tenantId, false)) return startSso(req);

shell.description: Run per-tenant SSO flag gate tests

identity.approve: The gate is per tenant, defaults off, and fails closed when the flag service is down.

revise.reason: The flag check reads a global flag rather than the tenant-scoped one, so enabling SSO for a pilot tenant opens it for all tenants.
revise.finding: SSO gate reads a global flag
revise.directive: Pass the request tenant id to the flag lookup and add a test with two tenants where only one is enabled.

identity.title: Revoke all sessions during emergency rollback
identity.intent: Provide an operator command in src/identity/rollout/revoke-all.ts that revokes every active session for a tenant, used when a credential leak is suspected. It writes an audit entry and emits a single revocation event. The procedure and its blast radius are documented in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Running the command revokes every active session for the named tenant only. Other tenants' sessions are untouched and an audit row is written.
thinking: This is a blunt instrument that logs out every user in a tenant, so it needs an explicit tenant argument and no default.
The command is a bulk update, and I want it to be one statement inside a transaction with the audit row, so the record and the effect cannot disagree.
Doubt: a bulk revoke with no confirmation is dangerous to type by mistake. I am requiring the tenant slug to be passed twice, which is an awkward but deliberate guard.
The emitted event carries a count rather than a list of user ids, which keeps the event small and avoids leaking membership detail.
I will test the cross-tenant case explicitly, since a wrong where clause here would be the worst kind of bug.

edit.new: UPDATE sessions SET status = 'revoked', revoked_at = now() WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND status = 'active';

identity.approve: The bulk revoke is scoped to one tenant, writes its audit row in the same transaction, and the cross-tenant case is tested.

revise.reason: The UPDATE has no tenant filter in the final shipped version, so one operator command revokes sessions across every tenant.
revise.finding: Bulk revoke has no tenant filter
revise.directive: Add the tenant_id predicate to the update and assert another tenant's sessions remain active in the test.

identity.title: Enforce retention on expired invitation records
identity.intent: Delete invitation rows older than ninety days in src/identity/rollout/retention.ts, in batches, once their status is accepted, expired or revoked. Active invitations are never touched. The retention window and the batch size are recorded in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: An expired invitation older than ninety days is removed. A pending invitation of the same age is kept.
thinking: Invitation rows hold hashed tokens and email addresses, so keeping them forever is a retention problem as well as a storage one.
The job deletes in batches of five hundred to keep transactions short, and it stops when a batch returns zero rows.

Doubt: a pending invitation older than ninety days is a stale credential, but deleting it silently could confuse a user who clicks an old link. I am deleting only terminal statuses, and an old pending one gets expired first by a separate rule.
The job is scheduled through the existing cron runner and logs the number of rows removed on each run.
I will test the boundary at exactly ninety days with a fixture dated on the edge.

edit.new: DELETE FROM invitations WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM invitations WHERE created_at < $1 AND status IN ('accepted','expired','revoked') LIMIT $2);

identity.approve: Only terminal invitations are deleted, in bounded batches, and the boundary is pinned by a test.

revise.reason: The delete statement removes invitations of every status, including pending ones, so a live invitation link stops working after ninety days.
revise.directive: Restrict the delete to accepted, expired and revoked statuses and assert a pending row survives.

identity.title: Write audit entries for privileged role changes
identity.intent: Append an audit record in src/identity/rollout/audit-role.ts for every change to owner or admin roles, with the actor, the target membership, the old and new role and the request id. Audit rows are append-only and written in the same transaction as the change. The audit record shape is pinned in contracts/identity.md.
identity.acceptance: Promoting a member to admin writes exactly one audit row in the same transaction. A failed role change writes no audit row.
thinking: Privileged role changes are the events an auditor will ask about first, so the record has to say who did it, to whom, and from what.
Writing the audit row in the same transaction as the change means a rollback removes both. A separate write could record a change that never happened.
Doubt: append-only is a convention unless the database enforces it. I am revoking update and delete on the audit table for the application role in the migration.
The actor is taken from the authenticated request context, never from a body field, so a client cannot claim to be someone else.
I will test the failed-change path by forcing a constraint violation and asserting the audit table count is unchanged.

edit.old: await tx.insert('role_audit', { actor: body.actor, target, from, to });
edit.new: await tx.insert('role_audit', { actor: ctx.actorId, membershipId: target.id, fromRole: from, toRole: to, requestId: ctx.requestId });

shell.description: Run privileged role audit write tests

identity.approve: The actor comes from the authenticated context, the audit row shares the change's transaction, and the table is append-only at the database level.

revise.reason: The audit row takes the actor from the request body, so a caller can record a role change under another administrator's name.
revise.finding: Audit actor comes from the request body
revise.directive: Take the actor id only from the authenticated request context and assert a body actor field is ignored.

catalog.title: Declare tenant-scoped identifiers for services and resources
catalog.intent: Introduce branded types for ServiceId, ResourceId and PriceRuleId in src/catalog/ids.ts, each carrying the TenantId it belongs to. Add a short section to contracts/catalog.md stating that identifiers cross system boundaries only as tenant-qualified pairs. Every later unit depends on these shapes, so they need to be settled first.
catalog.acceptance: Building an id without a tenant id fails to type-check. Each id round-trips through its string form in the identifier tests.
thinking: I am starting with the ids because every other module will import them, and changing them later would ripple everywhere.
A plain string alias is the tempting option, but it would let a ServiceId from one tenant reach a query for another. I will brand the type and carry the tenant as a field.
The string form needs a separator that cannot appear in a slug. I checked the slug rule and settled on a double colon.
Before writing the round-trip test I noticed the parser accepts an empty tenant segment. That would silently produce an id nobody owns, so I am rejecting it in the parser and adding a case for it.

edit.new: export type ServiceId = string & { readonly __brand: 'ServiceId'; readonly tenant: TenantId };

catalog.approve: The branded ids carry tenant scope where it cannot be forgotten, and the contract section makes that rule easy to hold reviewers to.

revise.reason: The id constructor accepts any tenant value, so a caller can mint an id for the wrong tenant.
revise.finding: Tenant is not checked at construction
revise.directive: Make the constructor take a TenantId and reject a mismatched tenant before building the id.

catalog.title: Scaffold the service and resource module layout
catalog.intent: Create the empty module files that the rest of the system will fill in: services.ts, resources.ts, pricing.ts and availability.ts under src/catalog/, each exporting a single placeholder type. Wire them into the package index so the test runner discovers them. Keep the layout flat, because the team decided against nested folders for this system.
catalog.acceptance: The package index re-exports every module and the typecheck passes with no unused exports.
thinking: This is pure scaffolding, so the goal is to get the shape right and not to add behaviour yet.
I looked at how the booking system organises its folders and decided to match it with a flat src/catalog directory.
My first draft exported default objects, which makes tree shaking worse and hides names in imports. I switched to named exports.
A layout test that only checks the files exist would pass even if the index forgot to re-export them, so I made it import each name from the index instead.
catalog.approve: Flat layout and named re-exports match the convention, and the test catches a forgotten re-export.

revise.reason: The layout test imports the modules directly and would miss a module that the index forgot to export.
revise.directive: Change the layout test to import every public name from the package index instead of the module files.

catalog.title: Load tenancy and region settings from environment config
catalog.intent: Read the default region, tenant isolation mode and per-tenant overrides from environment variables in src/catalog/config.ts, validating each one at startup. A missing region must stop the process rather than fall back to a guess. Document the variable names in contracts/catalog.md so operators can find them.
catalog.acceptance: Startup fails with a named variable when a required setting is absent, and each setting has a typed accessor.
thinking: Config is the first thing that can fail in production, so I want loud failures and no defaults that hide mistakes.
I am parsing every variable once at import time and returning a frozen object, which keeps the call sites simple.
The isolation mode accepts only two values, so I modelled it as a closed union rather than a free string.
I was tempted to default the region to the Postgres host, but that would route data to the wrong place silently. I removed the default and added a test for the missing case.
catalog.approve: Required settings fail loudly with the variable name, which is the behaviour operators need at three in the morning.

revise.reason: A silent default for the region would route tenant data somewhere the operator did not intend.
revise.directive: Remove the default for the region and require the variable at startup.

catalog.title: Enforce a tenant key on every listing table row
catalog.intent: Add a non-null tenant_id column and a composite primary key in migrations/catalog_0003_tenant_keys.sql for the services and resources tables. Mirror the check in src/catalog/repository.ts so that no insert path can omit the tenant. The composite key also becomes the basis for every index later in the system.
catalog.acceptance: A row insert without tenant_id is rejected by Postgres, and the repository refuses it before the query is sent.
thinking: The database constraint is the real guarantee, but the repository check gives a clearer error for the developer who made the mistake.
I wrote the migration with the composite key first and the column second, which reads backwards. I reordered it so the key is declared where a reviewer expects it.
Postgres will happily accept an empty string for tenant_id, which passes NOT NULL. I added a CHECK constraint so the empty case fails too.
I ran the migration against a scratch database to make sure it applies cleanly on an empty table and on a table with rows.

edit.new:
if (!row.tenant_id) throw new Error('missing tenant key');
  if (!row.service_id) throw new Error('missing id');

shell.description: Apply tenant key migration to scratch database

catalog.approve: The database refuses unscoped rows and the repository gives a clear message first, so either layer alone is enough to catch the bug.

revise.reason: The tenant check runs after the query is built, so the error message is generic and arrives too late.
revise.finding: Tenant check runs after query build
revise.directive: Move the tenant check to the start of the insert function, before any SQL string is assembled.

catalog.title: Model services with durations, buffers and capacity limits
catalog.intent: Define the Service type in src/catalog/services.ts with a duration, a buffer before and after, and a maximum concurrent booking count. Durations are stored in whole minutes and buffers may be zero but never negative. Record the shape in contracts/catalog.md so booking can rely on it without reading this code.
catalog.acceptance: A service with a negative buffer cannot be constructed, and a capacity of zero is rejected with a specific message.
thinking: A service is the unit that booking reads most, so the fields need to be exact and the constructor needs to enforce the invariants.
I modelled duration as minutes rather than a Date delta, because booking compares against whole-minute slots.
While writing the buffer check I realised a buffer larger than the duration is legal for some clinics that need a long clean-down, so I did not cap it.
The capacity field could be zero for a placeholder service, but a zero capacity silently blocks every booking, so I made it an error at construction.
catalog.approve: Exact minute fields and constructor-level invariants make the service shape trustworthy for booking.

revise.reason: The model allows a service with a zero capacity, which silently blocks all bookings.
revise.directive: Reject a capacity of zero in the service constructor with a message that names the service.

catalog.title: Represent resources such as rooms, chairs and equipment
catalog.intent: Add the Resource type in src/catalog/resources.ts with a kind discriminator covering room, seat and equipment, and a parent link so a chair can belong to a room. Keep the parent link optional and enforce that it stays within one tenant. The kinds are a closed union so that new kinds show up as compiler errors in every switch.
catalog.acceptance: A resource whose parent belongs to another tenant is rejected, and every switch over kind is exhaustive.
thinking: Resources are a tree in practice, and I want the model to express that without allowing cycles.
I used a discriminated union for kind so the compiler forces me to handle a new kind everywhere it matters.
Checking the parent tenant needs the parent loaded, which the pure model cannot do. I moved that check to the command layer and kept the model to shape only.
I was about to add a depth limit for the tree, but nobody has asked for it yet, so I noted it as deferred and moved on.
catalog.approve: A closed kind union with an explicit parent link is the right size for this, and the cycle concern is handled where it can be.

revise.reason: The parent check lives in the model, which cannot load the parent, so the check silently passes.
revise.directive: Move the cross-tenant parent check into the resource command handler where the parent is loaded.

catalog.title: Define price rules that vary by tenant and currency
catalog.intent: Create the PriceRule type in src/catalog/pricing.ts with a tenant, a currency and an amount in minor units. Rules are scoped to one service or resource and carry an effective-from timestamp. Currency is a three letter code checked against a fixed list, so that an unknown code fails before any money is stored.
catalog.acceptance: A price rule with an unknown currency code is refused, and amounts are always integers in minor units.
thinking: Money is where rounding bugs hide, so I am storing integers in minor units everywhere and never a float.
The currency list is short and fixed for now, so a literal union is clearer than a lookup table.
I wondered whether effective-from should be inclusive, and I checked the billing contract, which treats it as inclusive, so I matched that.
A rule with a negative amount is a discount that someone might want, but discounts are a billing concern, so I refuse negatives here.
catalog.approve: Integer minor units and a closed currency union keep money out of floating point, which is the risk I most want gone.

revise.reason: The amount field is a plain number, so a fractional value can be stored and rounded later.
revise.directive: Use the MinorUnits branded type for the amount and reject non-integer values at construction.

catalog.title: Encode recurring availability windows for each resource
catalog.intent: Describe recurring weekly windows in src/catalog/availability.ts, with a day, a start and end time in local minutes and a timezone taken from the resource. Overlapping windows on the same resource are merged on read. Explain the window format in contracts/catalog.md, since booking will expand it into concrete slots.
catalog.acceptance: Two windows that overlap on the same day expand to one merged window, and a window that ends before it starts is rejected.
thinking: Availability is the most error-prone part of this system, so I want the window math to be boring and well tested.
I represent times as minutes since midnight in the resource timezone, which avoids daylight saving bugs at the model level.
Merging overlaps is simple, but adjacent windows that touch at a single minute should also merge, and my first version missed that.
A window that crosses midnight is legal for a late venue, but the model cannot express it yet, so I reject it with a clear message and leave a note.
catalog.approve: Minute-based windows with explicit merge rules keep the availability math simple enough for booking to trust.

revise.reason: Adjacent windows that touch at one minute are not merged, so a resource shows a false gap.
revise.directive: Merge windows whose end equals the next start and add a test for the touching case.

catalog.title: Accept service creation commands with schema validation
catalog.intent: Validate the create-service command payload in src/catalog/commands.ts against a schema before any repository call. The schema covers name, duration, buffers and capacity, and rejects unknown keys. Keep validation in one function so that the HTTP layer and the import job share the same rules.
catalog.acceptance: A payload with an unknown key or a missing duration is rejected before the repository is touched.
thinking: Validation belongs at the boundary, so the command handler should refuse bad input before any side effect.
I am rejecting unknown keys rather than ignoring them, because a typo in a field name would otherwise pass quietly.
The import job will call the same validator, which is why it lives in commands.ts and not in the HTTP route.
