My first draft validated after normalising the name, which hid the original value in the error. I changed the order so the error quotes what the caller sent.

edit.new:
export function createService(input: unknown): ServiceDraft {
  const parsed = ServiceDraftSchema.parse(input);

catalog.approve: One validator shared by the route and the import job keeps the rules in one place, and the unknown-key rule catches typos.

revise.reason: Validation runs after the name is normalised, so the error shows a value the caller never sent.
revise.directive: Validate the raw input first and quote the original value in the error message.

catalog.title: Reject duplicate service slugs within one tenant
catalog.intent: Enforce a unique slug per tenant in src/catalog/services.ts and back it with a unique index added in migrations/catalog_0009_service_slug.sql. Two tenants may share a slug, so the uniqueness key must include the tenant. The repository maps the constraint violation to a domain error the command layer can return.
catalog.acceptance: Creating a second service with the same slug in one tenant returns a conflict, while the same slug in another tenant succeeds.
thinking: Slugs are shown in URLs, so a duplicate is a visible bug for a tenant admin and not just a data quality issue.
The unique index needs the tenant in it, or two tenants could never both name a service Massage. I included the tenant column first.
Postgres reports the violation with a code I can match, so I map that code and not the message text, which can change between versions.
I thought about normalising case before checking, then decided the slug rule already lowercases it on write, so the index is enough.

shell.command: psql -d tidewater_scratch -c 'CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ON catalog_services (tenant_id, slug);'

catalog.approve: The index carries the tenant and the code matching avoids brittle message parsing, which is the right way to map this error.

revise.reason: The conflict error is a generic Error, so the command layer cannot return a typed conflict to the caller.
revise.directive: Throw the SlugConflict domain error and let the command layer map it to a conflict response.

catalog.title: Return structured error envelopes for invalid listings
catalog.intent: Shape every catalog validation failure as an envelope with a code, a field path and a message, defined in src/catalog/errors.ts. Field paths follow the dotted form used by the other systems so the web console can highlight the offending input. Update contracts/catalog.md with the list of codes.
catalog.acceptance: Each validation failure returns an envelope with a code and a path, and the code list in the contract matches the enum.
thinking: Callers switch on the code, so the code list has to be closed and documented, not a string someone invents at the call site.
I used a discriminated union for the error kinds so that the envelope builder has to handle each one.
The path format is dotted to match the other systems, and I checked the operations system to confirm it parses the same way.
While writing the test I found that an array index in the path was rendered as brackets, which breaks the dotted rule, so I normalised it.
catalog.approve: A closed code list with a normalised path format gives callers something they can rely on.

revise.reason: The code list in the contract drifted from the enum, so a documented code is never returned.
revise.directive: Generate the contract code list from the enum or add a test that compares the two.

catalog.title: Version service updates with optimistic concurrency tokens
catalog.intent: Add a version column to services and resources and require callers to send the version they read when they update. A mismatch returns stale_version rather than overwriting. The version logic lives in src/catalog/services.ts so the resource path can reuse the same helper.
catalog.acceptance: An update with an outdated version returns stale_version and leaves the row unchanged.
thinking: Two admins editing the same service at once is ordinary, so the update path needs a version check instead of last write wins.
I put the check in a single UPDATE with a WHERE clause on the version, which avoids a read then write race.
The migration adds the column with a default of one, so existing rows start at a known version.
I checked whether the resource path could share this, and it can, so the helper takes the table name as a typed parameter rather than duplicating the logic.
catalog.approve: Checking the version inside the UPDATE avoids the read-then-write race and keeps the rule in one place.

revise.reason: The version is compared in application code after a read, which leaves a window for a concurrent write.
revise.directive: Move the version comparison into the UPDATE statement WHERE clause.

catalog.title: Serve paginated service lists with keyset cursors
catalog.intent: Return services for a tenant in pages using a keyset cursor over the slug and id, implemented in src/catalog/queries.ts. Offsets are not used because deep pages become slow on large tenants. The cursor is an opaque base64 string that the server validates on every request.
catalog.acceptance: Following the next cursor returns every service exactly once, and a tampered cursor returns invalid.
thinking: Keyset pagination is the only sane choice here, because the team has seen offset queries time out on tenants with thousands of services.
The cursor encodes the last slug and id, so ties on slug are broken by id and nothing is repeated.
I considered letting clients pass a raw slug as the cursor, but that leaks the ordering rule, so I made the cursor opaque.
The first page query had an off by one that dropped the boundary row, which the exactly-once test caught.

edit.new:
WHERE (slug, id) > ($2, $3)
  ORDER BY slug, id LIMIT $4

catalog.approve: Keyset ordering with an id tiebreak and an opaque cursor is exactly what the large tenants need.

revise.reason: The ordering uses only the slug, so services with the same slug can be skipped across a page boundary.
revise.directive: Add the id to both the ORDER BY and the cursor comparison.

catalog.title: Filter resources by location, tag and capacity
catalog.intent: Accept location, tag and minimum capacity filters for resource listing in src/catalog/queries.ts. Each filter is optional and combines with AND. Tags are matched exactly against a normalised lowercase set, and the query uses the index added for tenant keys.
catalog.acceptance: Combining a location and a tag returns only resources matching both, and an empty filter returns the full tenant list.
thinking: Filters are where listings get slow, so I want each one to use an index rather than a scan of the tenant.
Tags are stored as a text array, and a GIN index on it makes the containment check fast.
I normalised the filter value to lowercase before the query, because the stored tags are lowercase and a mixed case filter would match nothing.
When I combined all three filters the planner ignored the capacity index, so I checked the plan and accepted a scan for this small column.

edit.new:
AND r.location = $2
  AND ($3::text[] IS NULL OR r.tags @> $3)

catalog.approve: Optional AND filters with a GIN index on tags and lowercase normalisation cover the listing cases cleanly.

revise.reason: Tag filters are case sensitive in the query but the stored tags are normalised, so a mixed case filter returns nothing.
revise.directive: Lowercase the tag filter values before building the query parameter.

catalog.title: Search services by name prefix within a tenant
catalog.intent: Support a prefix search over service names in src/catalog/search.ts, restricted to the calling tenant. The search is a case insensitive prefix match and does not do full text yet. Results reuse the keyset pagination helper so the cursor behaviour is identical.
catalog.acceptance: A prefix search returns only services whose names start with the term, within the tenant, and paginates with the same cursor format.
thinking: Prefix search is enough for the admin screen, and full text can wait until someone asks for it with a real example.
The query uses lower(name) with a text pattern index, so the prefix match stays index friendly.
The search term can contain percent signs and underscores, which would act as wildcards, so I escape them before building the pattern.
My first version forgot the tenant predicate in the search path, which would have leaked names across tenants, so I added a test that fails without it.

edit.new: WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND lower(name) LIKE $2 ESCAPE '\\'

catalog.approve: Escaped prefix matching with the tenant predicate first is the safe form, and the cross-tenant test guards it.

revise.reason: The search term is not escaped, so a percent sign in the input matches far more rows than intended.
revise.directive: Escape percent and underscore characters in the term before building the LIKE pattern.

catalog.title: Expose a single service detail read with variants
catalog.intent: Return one service with its variants in a single read in src/catalog/queries.ts, avoiding a second round trip. A variant is a named tier such as a longer session, and each variant has its own price rule reference. The detail shape is documented for booking in contracts/catalog.md.
catalog.acceptance: The detail read returns the service and all its variants in one query, and a missing service returns not_found.
thinking: Booking calls the detail read on every quote, so one query matters more than the code looks.
I join variants with a lateral subquery so that a service with no variants still returns a row with an empty list.
A missing service must come back as not_found and never as an empty success, which would look like a free service to a caller.
I briefly wanted to cache the detail, but the version column is cheap to read, so I left caching out until the numbers ask for it.

edit.old: LEFT JOIN service_variants v ON v.service_id = s.id
edit.new: LEFT JOIN LATERAL (SELECT json_agg(v) AS variants FROM service_variants v WHERE v.service_id = s.id) vs ON true

catalog.approve: One query with a lateral join and an explicit not_found is what booking needs on every quote.

revise.reason: A service with no variants returns null for the variants field rather than an empty list.
revise.finding: Null variants instead of empty list
revise.directive: Coalesce the aggregated variants to an empty array so callers never receive null.

catalog.title: Publish a service-changed event through the outbox
catalog.intent: Write a service.changed event into the outbox table in the same transaction as every service update, through src/catalog/outbox.ts. The event payload carries the tenant, the service id and the new version, and nothing else. Consumers refetch the detail when they need more, which keeps the event small.
catalog.acceptance: An update and its outbox row commit or roll back together, and the payload contains only the tenant, id and version.
thinking: The event and the row change must commit together, otherwise a consumer could see an event for an update that never happened.
I put the outbox insert inside the same transaction callback as the update, so a failure of either rolls back both.
The payload is deliberately thin, because a fat payload would freeze the service shape that consumers depend on.
While testing the rollback I saw the outbox row survive when the update failed, which meant I had written it outside the transaction. I moved it inside.

edit.old: export async function publish(tx: Tx, evt: Event) {
edit.new:
export async function publish(tx: Tx, evt: ServiceChanged) {
  assertThinPayload(evt);

catalog.approve: Writing the outbox row inside the update transaction with a thin payload gives consumers a reliable signal.

revise.reason: The outbox insert runs on a separate connection, so an update that rolls back still publishes its event.
revise.directive: Pass the transaction handle into the outbox insert so both writes share one transaction.

catalog.title: Emit resource availability deltas to booking consumers
catalog.intent: Publish a delta event whenever a resource's availability windows change, from src/catalog/availability.ts through the outbox. The delta lists only the windows added and removed, so booking can patch its slot cache. Ordering within one resource is preserved by keying the outbox partition on the resource id.
catalog.acceptance: Changing a window produces one delta listing the added and removed windows, and deltas for one resource arrive in order.
thinking: Booking would rather patch than refetch the whole calendar, so the delta is worth the extra care.
I compute the delta by comparing the old and new window sets, keyed by day and start minute, which is cheap for a resource.
The partition key must be the resource id, or two deltas for one resource could be consumed out of order.
I initially emitted a delta even when nothing changed, which would wake booking for nothing, so I suppressed empty deltas.

edit.old: export function diffWindows(prev: Window[], next: Window[]) {
edit.new: export function diffWindows(prev: Window[], next: Window[]): WindowDelta | null {

catalog.approve: Keying the delta by resource and suppressing empty changes keeps booking's cache honest without waking it needlessly.

revise.reason: The delta is built from the window lists in input order, so reordered but identical windows produce a false change.
revise.directive: Sort both window sets by day and start minute before diffing them.

catalog.title: Define the cross-system service contract for booking
catalog.intent: Write the versioned contract that booking reads when it needs service data, in contracts/catalog.md, and mirror its types in src/catalog/contract.ts. The contract lists the fields booking may rely on, the events it may subscribe to and the error codes it must handle. Changes to the contract bump its version number in the file header.
catalog.acceptance: The contract types compile against the service model, and the contract header carries a version that the contract test checks.
thinking: This contract is the single thing booking can depend on, so I want the fields listed explicitly rather than implied by the model.
I mirror the types in contract.ts and have the contract test compare the two, so a drift is a red test and not a surprise.
I wondered whether booking needs the capacity field, and I checked its requirements, which do need it for the overbook check.
The version header is a plain string, and I added a test that fails if it is missing, because an unversioned contract is useless to a consumer.
catalog.approve: Mirrored types with a drift test and a versioned header make the contract something booking can trust without reading our code.

revise.reason: The contract lists capacity as optional but the model requires it, so booking will handle a missing field that never occurs.
revise.directive: Mark the capacity field as required in the contract and in the mirrored type.

catalog.title: Send webhook payloads when a price rule changes
catalog.intent: Deliver a signed webhook to each tenant's registered endpoint whenever one of its price rules changes, from src/catalog/webhooks.ts. The webhook reads the outbox rather than the write path, so a slow receiver cannot delay a save. The signature uses an HMAC over the body with the tenant secret.
catalog.acceptance: A price rule change produces one signed delivery per registered endpoint, and a receiver returning 500 is retried with backoff.
thinking: Webhooks are the part of this system a tenant's own engineers will see, so the payload and signature need to be exactly documented.
Reading from the outbox decouples delivery from the save, which is the reason I chose it over a direct call.
I sign the raw body bytes and not a re-serialised object, because re-serialising could change key order and break verification.
My first draft retried forever on a 500, which would hammer a dead endpoint, so I capped the attempts and recorded the failure.

shell.description: Run price rule webhook delivery tests

catalog.approve: Signing the raw bytes and reading from the outbox means a slow receiver never blocks a save, and the retry cap stops the hammering.

revise.reason: The signature is computed over a re-serialised body, so a receiver that verifies the raw bytes rejects every delivery.
revise.directive: Compute the HMAC over the exact raw body bytes that are sent on the wire.

catalog.title: Make service creation retry-safe with idempotency keys
catalog.intent: Accept an Idempotency-Key header on create-service in src/catalog/idempotency.ts and store the first response against the key for 24 hours. A retried request with the same key and body returns the stored response, and the same key with a different body returns a conflict. The store is a table in the tenant schema.
catalog.acceptance: Two identical create requests with one key create one service, and a reused key with a different body returns conflict.
thinking: Clients retry on timeouts, and a duplicate service with a timeout is a support ticket, so this is worth the table.
I hash the request body along with the key, so a reused key with a changed body is detected rather than silently replayed.
The stored response has to be written in the same transaction as the create, or a crash between them would allow a second create.
I first forgot to scope the key by tenant, which would let two tenants collide on a common key, so I added the tenant to the lookup.
catalog.approve: Hashing the body and scoping the key by tenant closes both the replay and collision risks I was worried about.

revise.reason: The idempotency lookup ignores the tenant, so two tenants sending the same key collide.
revise.directive: Include the tenant in every idempotency store lookup and write.

catalog.title: Serialise concurrent resource edits under row locks
catalog.intent: Take a row lock with SELECT FOR UPDATE on the resource before editing its parent or windows, in src/catalog/resources.ts. The lock is held for the shortest span possible, and the lock order is always parent first to avoid deadlocks. Two concurrent edits to one room then serialise rather than interleaving.
catalog.acceptance: Two concurrent edits to one resource both succeed in sequence, and the lock order test shows no deadlock across parent and child updates.
thinking: Resource edits touch a parent and several child windows, so without a lock two admins could produce a half applied state.
I lock the parent first everywhere, because two transactions that lock in opposite orders is the classic deadlock.
The lock is taken after validation, so a bad request never holds a lock while it fails.
Running the concurrency test I saw one transaction wait far too long, and I found I was locking the whole tenant table by mistake, so I narrowed it to the row.

edit.old: const row = await tx.query('SELECT * FROM resources WHERE id = $1', [id]);
edit.new: const row = await tx.query('SELECT * FROM resources WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE', [id]);

shell.description: Run concurrent resource edit lock tests

catalog.approve: Parent first lock ordering with the lock taken after validation is a careful, boring choice that avoids deadlocks.

revise.reason: The lock is taken on the child window rows before the parent, which reverses the lock order used elsewhere.
revise.directive: Lock the parent resource row first and then the child windows, matching the order used in every other path.

catalog.title: Retry failed outbox publications with bounded backoff
catalog.intent: Retry an outbox row whose publish failed, with exponential backoff capped at five minutes, implemented in src/catalog/outbox.ts. After the cap the row is marked dead and an alert is raised rather than retried forever. Backoff uses a stored attempt count so a restart does not reset it.
catalog.acceptance: A failing row is retried with growing delays, and after the maximum attempts it is marked dead.
thinking: A failing consumer should not hammer itself, and a dead row should stop consuming attention, so both limits matter.
The attempt count lives in the database, so a restart resumes the backoff instead of starting over at one second.
Five minutes is the cap the operations system uses, so I matched it rather than inventing a new number.
While testing I noticed the jitter could push a delay past the cap, so I clamp after applying jitter.

edit.new:
const base = Math.min(2 ** attempts * 1000, MAX_DELAY_MS);
  const delay = Math.min(base + jitter(base), MAX_DELAY_MS);

catalog.approve: Database-held attempts and a clamp after jitter give bounded, restart-safe retries that match the operations cap.

revise.reason: The attempt counter lives only in memory, so a restart resets the backoff to the shortest delay.
revise.directive: Store the attempt count on the outbox row and read it on every retry decision.

catalog.title: Guard price recalculation against stale snapshot reads
catalog.intent: Recalculate the effective price for a quote from a snapshot in src/catalog/pricing.ts, and reject the quote if the snapshot version has moved on by commit time. Booking holds the quote for a short window, so the check must compare the version and not the timestamp. A stale quote returns stale_version to the caller.
catalog.acceptance: A quote built from an old price snapshot is rejected at commit with stale_version, and a fresh one commits.
thinking: A quote that uses an old price is a financial error, so I want the staleness check strict and visible.
I compare the snapshot version and not the timestamp, because two price changes in the same millisecond would fool a timestamp check.
The check runs inside the same transaction as the booking commit, so a price change between quote and commit is caught.
I considered recomputing silently instead of rejecting, but that changes the amount the customer agreed to, so the rejection is the honest behaviour.
catalog.approve: Rejecting on a version mismatch rather than recomputing silently keeps the agreed price honest.

revise.reason: The check compares timestamps, so two price changes within one millisecond let a stale quote through.
revise.directive: Compare the snapshot version number instead of the snapshot timestamp.

catalog.title: Migrate legacy service rows into the tenant-scoped table
catalog.intent: Move rows from the legacy services table into the tenant-scoped table in migrations/catalog_0024_move_services.sql, using a script that copies in batches. The migration keeps the legacy table in place until the verification unit confirms the counts. Each batch commits on its own so a failure resumes from the last batch.
catalog.acceptance: After the migration every legacy service appears once in the new table with the correct tenant, and the batch resumes after a forced failure.
thinking: Real tenants depend on this data, so the migration is copy first and delete never, until verification has passed.
I copy in batches of five hundred rows, each in its own transaction, so a failure costs at most one batch.
The legacy rows have no tenant column for some very old tenants, and I found those by querying for nulls and assigning them to the owning account.
The first dry run duplicated rows because the batch cursor did not advance, so I fixed the cursor and added a test for a restart in the middle.

edit.new:
for (let cursor = ''; ; ) {
    const batch = await readBatch(cursor, BATCH);

catalog.approve: Copy-first batching with per-batch commits and a restart test is the safe way to move this data.

revise.reason: The batch loop restarts from the first row after a failure, so the copy duplicates every row already moved.
revise.directive: Resume the batch loop from the last committed cursor value instead of from the start.

catalog.title: Backfill resource tags from the free-text description field
catalog.intent: Derive a tags array for each resource from its free-text description in src/catalog/backfill.ts, matching a fixed list of known tags such as wheelchair and projector. Resources that match no tag keep an empty array. The backfill is idempotent so it can be run again after a fix.
catalog.acceptance: Running the backfill twice produces the same tags, and a resource with a known word in its description gains that tag.
thinking: Tags are only useful if the existing resources have them, so the backfill is worth the effort even though the matching is crude.
Matching is by whole word on a fixed list, which avoids a projector being tagged from the word project.
The backfill writes only when the tags change, so running it twice does not churn the rows.
I checked a sample of real descriptions and found several that mention a wheelchair ramp as a negation, so I accepted the false positives and recorded them for review.

revise.directive: Match tags only on whole words after splitting the description on word boundaries.

The up step backfills the existing rows to the tenant default currency. The down step drops the column only after confirming no rows depend on it.
catalog.acceptance: Applying then reverting the migration leaves the table as it started, and existing rows gain the tenant default currency.
thinking: Currency is a change that could need undoing after a billing discussion, so I want the down step to be real and tested.
The up step sets the default for existing rows before making the column not null, which avoids a long lock on a populated table.
The down step refuses to run if a row has a currency that differs from the tenant default, because dropping it would lose information.
I first wrote the down step without that guard and it would have silently discarded the currency of a non-default row, so I added the check and a test that proves it.

catalog.title: Verify backfill counts against the source table
catalog.intent: Write a verification script in src/catalog/backfill.ts that compares row counts and a per-tenant checksum between the legacy and new service tables. The script exits non zero on any mismatch and prints the tenants that differ. Legacy deletion is gated on this script passing.
catalog.acceptance: The script exits zero when counts and checksums match and exits non zero with the differing tenant list when one row is missing.
thinking: A migration is only as trustworthy as its check, so I want the verification to compare content and not just row counts.
Counts can match while a row is wrong, so the per-tenant checksum hashes the slug, duration and capacity together.
The script must be read only, because running it should never change anything, and I enforced that with a read only transaction.
When I first ran it on the scratch copy it reported a mismatch that was just a timezone difference in an audit timestamp, so I excluded timestamps from the checksum.
catalog.approve: Checksums that exclude timestamps and a read only run catch wrong data that counts would miss.

revise.reason: The verification compares only row counts, so a row with a wrong duration passes the check.
revise.finding: Counts alone do not verify content
revise.directive: Add a per tenant checksum over slug, duration and capacity to the comparison.

catalog.acceptance: A service update produces a parent span with child spans for the write and the outbox publish, and the trace context reaches the outbox row.

The trace context has to travel with the event, or the consumer's work appears as an orphan trace that nobody can connect.
I checked that the span attributes do not include the slug, because names can contain personal details and traces are retained longer than I would like.

revise.reason: The span attributes include the service slug, which is a free text name that may hold personal details.

catalog.title: Log structured diagnostics for rejected availability rules
catalog.intent: Emit a structured log line from src/catalog/availability.ts whenever an availability rule is rejected, with the rule kind, the resource id and the reason code. The log is a single JSON object with stable keys, so the operations system can aggregate it. Free text messages are kept out of the log line.
catalog.acceptance: A rejected rule writes exactly one JSON log line with the kind, resource and reason keys, and no free text field.
thinking: When a rule is rejected the operator needs to know why without reading the database, so the log carries the reason code.
Stable keys matter more than pretty output, since the operations system parses these lines without a human in the loop.
I initially logged the whole rule object, which included a free text note from the admin, so I narrowed the log to the typed fields.
A rejected rule can be retried by the admin, so the log says rejected and not failed, which avoids a false alarm.

revise.reason: The rejection log writes the whole rule object, including a free text note the admin typed.
revise.directive: Log only the kind, resource id and reason code instead of the full rule object.

catalog.title: Benchmark keyset pagination against deep offsets

catalog.acceptance: The benchmark prints the last page timing for both strategies, and the keyset timing stays under the agreed budget.
thinking: The argument for keyset is mostly theory until I measure it on a tenant of realistic size, so I am measuring it.
I seed fifty thousand services in a transaction and time the last page for each strategy, which is the case that hurts offsets.
The benchmark must not run in the parallel test tier, because a timing bound is unreliable on a busy host.

catalog.title: Cap the number of variants a service may carry
catalog.intent: Enforce a maximum of twelve variants per service in src/catalog/services.ts, checked inside the same transaction that adds a variant. The limit protects the detail read from a service that grows without bound. The cap is a named constant and the error is a quota error.
catalog.acceptance: Adding a thirteenth variant returns a quota error and leaves the existing variants unchanged.
thinking: A service with hundreds of variants would make the detail read slow, so the cap is a real protection and not a formality.
I put the limit in a named constant in quotas.ts so the number is visible and can be changed in one place.
The count and the insert must share a transaction, or two concurrent adds could both pass a count of eleven.
The first version counted variants outside the transaction, and the concurrency test showed two inserts both succeeding past the cap, so I moved the count inside.

revise.reason: The variant count is checked outside the insert transaction, so concurrent adds can exceed the cap.
revise.directive: Count and insert the variant inside a single transaction so the cap holds under concurrency.

catalog.title: Throttle bulk resource imports per tenant quota
catalog.intent: Limit bulk resource imports to a set number of rows per tenant per hour in src/catalog/import.ts, returning a quota error with the reset time when the limit is hit. The counter lives in the same store as the idempotency keys. Imports larger than one batch are split so that the limit applies per batch and not per file.
catalog.acceptance: An import that would exceed the hourly row quota is refused with the reset time, and a smaller import in the same hour succeeds.
thinking: Bulk imports are the easiest way for one tenant to load the shared database, so a per tenant limit is the protection I want.
The counter is a row per tenant and hour, and I increment it atomically so two imports cannot both squeeze under the limit.
I return the reset time in the error, because an admin who hits the limit needs to know when to try again.
I was going to limit by file rather than by row, but a single file could hold a hundred thousand rows, so I counted rows.

const allowed = await quota.consume(tenant, rows.length);
  if (!allowed.ok) throw new QuotaExceeded('import_rows', allowed.resetAt);

catalog.approve: Counting rows atomically per tenant and hour, with the reset time in the error, is a fair limit that an admin can act on.

revise.reason: The quota check and the counter increment are separate statements, so two concurrent imports can both pass.
revise.directive: Increment the counter and compare it to the limit in one atomic statement.

catalog.title: Hide new service types behind a tenant feature flag
catalog.intent: Gate the new service type field behind a per tenant flag read through src/catalog/flags.ts. Tenants without the flag see the field ignored, and the write path refuses it with a clear error. The flag is removed after rollout, so the code path stays short.
catalog.acceptance: A tenant without the flag cannot set the new type, and a tenant with it can, and the flag lookup is cached for one minute.
thinking: Rolling out a new field to every tenant at once is how a surprise reaches a customer, so I am gating it.
The flag is read once per request and cached for a minute, which keeps the database off the hot path.
When the flag is off I refuse the field rather than ignoring it, because silent ignoring would lose the value the caller meant to store.
I checked the flag name against the naming rule and it was fine, but I had nearly used a plural, which would have confused the removal later.

catalog.title: Document the rollback path for price rule changes

The steps reference the snapshot table and the outbox. The document is reviewed with the on-call rota before it is marked final.
catalog.acceptance: The rollback section names each table and command, and a dry run of the steps on scratch data restores the prior price.
thinking: On-call needs rollback steps they can follow at night without asking me, so the section has to be literal and not descriptive.
Rolling back a price means restoring a snapshot and emitting a new event, not deleting history, so the steps say so explicitly.
I wrote a rollback helper in pricing.ts so the steps and the code agree, and the test runs the helper against scratch data.

catalog.title: Apply a retention window to archived services
catalog.intent: Delete archived services older than the retention window in src/catalog/retention.ts, run as a scheduled job with a batch size and a dry run flag. The window is ninety days from the archive timestamp. Deletion goes through the same audit path as a manual delete, so nothing disappears without a record.
catalog.acceptance: The dry run lists the services it would delete without deleting them, and a live run removes only services past the window.
thinking: Deleting data is irreversible, so the dry run comes first and I want it to be the default.
The window is measured from the archive timestamp and not the last edit, because the archive is the moment the tenant stopped using the service.
Each deletion writes an audit row before the delete, so a crash between the two leaves a record rather than a silent loss.
I checked whether a live booking could reference an archived service and found that booking keeps its own copy, so the deletion is safe for them.

catalog.acceptance: A deletion writes exactly one audit row in the same transaction, and a rolled back deletion leaves no audit row.
thinking: Audit is the record someone reads after an incident, so it has to be complete and written with the change, not after it.
Writing the audit row in the same transaction means a rolled back delete leaves no false record, which is the behaviour I want.
I store the actor as a role and not a user id here, because the catalog only knows roles and the identity system owns the user mapping.
The application role has insert and select on the audit table but no update or delete, which I checked with a grant test.

The status column is tempting as a free-form string, but the contract lists five states, so I'll make it a checked enum in the migration.
Wait, I almost forgot tenant_id needs to be NOT NULL here and not added in a later migration. Adding it later would mean a backfill I'd rather never write.

booking.acceptance: The barrel exports the command and query entrypoints as empty typed stubs and the project typechecks with no unused exports.

Hmm, the layout test might be overkill for a stub, but it does catch someone deleting the barrel export by accident.

Parse and validate once at startup so bad values stop the process instead of failing a customer request later. The shape is recorded in contracts/booking.md so the catalog team sees the same keys.

The lead-time default could live in code, but then two environments can disagree silently, so I'll make every rule explicit.

The contract doc gets the same key list, which is the only place a catalog engineer will look for them.

revise.directive: Treat an empty slot length variable as a missing required value and throw at startup.

The repository takes a TenantContext argument, not a raw string, so the compiler flags any call site that forgets it. Cross-tenant reads must return not found, never forbidden, to avoid leaking existence.
booking.acceptance: A repository call with a tenant context from another tenant returns not found, and the test covers get, list and cancel.
thinking: The repository is where tenancy leaks happen, so I'm putting the tenant filter in one helper that every query must call.
Returning forbidden would tell an attacker that a reservation id exists, so every cross-tenant path returns not found.
I was going to type tenant_id as string, but a branded TenantId stops someone passing a resource id by mistake.
The tenancy test runs each operation twice, once in the right tenant and once in the wrong one, which is the only check that matters.

booking.approve: Every repository function takes a tenant context and the cross-tenant case is covered for each operation.

booking.title: Model the time slot as a half-open interval
booking.intent: Represent a slot in src/booking/domain/slot.ts as a start inclusive and end exclusive pair so back-to-back slots never overlap by accident. Provide a constructor that rejects zero or negative durations and a helper that tests containment. The domain type is the only place interval arithmetic is written.
booking.acceptance: Two slots that touch at one instant do not overlap, and a zero-length slot throws InvalidSlot.
thinking: Half-open intervals are the one piece of arithmetic that every later unit depends on, so I'm writing its tests first.
If I make the end inclusive, a slot ending at 10:00 and one starting at 10:00 would collide, and that is the classic off-by-one.
The constructor should throw rather than normalise a reversed pair, because a reversed pair means an upstream bug.
I'll keep the helper pure so the same function serves the overlap check and the availability calculation.
booking.approve: Slots are half-open, touching slots do not overlap, and invalid durations are rejected at construction.

revise.reason: The overlap helper treats a slot that ends exactly at the other slot's start as overlapping.
revise.directive: Change the comparison to strict inequality on both bounds.

booking.title: Enforce a minimum lead time on slots
booking.intent: Reject a requested slot that starts sooner than the resource's minimum lead time in src/booking/domain/lead-time.ts. The check takes the clock as an argument so tests do not depend on wall time. The rule reads the lead time from the resource config that the catalog publishes.
booking.acceptance: A slot starting inside the lead window returns a LeadTimeViolation, and a slot exactly at the boundary is accepted.
thinking: The lead time check needs a clock, and I'd rather pass it in than reach for Date.now inside the domain.
Boundary behaviour matters here: a slot exactly at the minimum lead should be accepted, so I'm using greater-or-equal.
I'm second-guessing whether the lead time should compare in UTC or in the resource's local zone, and the answer is UTC since the zone belongs to presentation.
The violation carries the earliest permitted start so the caller can offer it back to the customer.
booking.approve: Lead time is compared in UTC with an injected clock and the boundary is inclusive.

revise.reason: The check compares against the wall clock directly, so the test that sets a fixed time is flaky near midnight.
revise.finding: Wall clock read inside domain check
revise.directive: Accept the current instant as a parameter and remove the direct Date call.

booking.title: Represent recurring availability as rules
booking.intent: Store weekly availability as rules in src/booking/domain/availability-rule.ts, each with a weekday set, a time window and an effective date range. Expanding rules into concrete slots happens elsewhere; this module only validates and stores them. A rule that overlaps another rule for the same resource is rejected at write time.
booking.acceptance: A rule with an end before its start is rejected, and two overlapping rules for one resource produce a single validation error.
thinking: Rules are easier to reason about as data than as generated slots, so I'm keeping them unexpanded in storage.
The overlap check has to consider weekdays as well as times, since a Monday rule does not clash with a Tuesday rule.
I'm not sure a date range should be inclusive on both ends, so I'm checking the contract wording before I encode it.
The contract says effective_to is exclusive, which matches the half-open slot model, so I'll keep the semantics consistent.
booking.approve: Rules validate their date range and weekday set, and overlapping rules for one resource are caught on write.

revise.reason: A rule with an empty weekday set is accepted and then silently produces no slots.
revise.directive: Reject rules with no weekdays during validation with a named error.

booking.title: Derive resource capacity from slot overlap
booking.intent: Compute how many concurrent reservations a resource can take in src/booking/domain/capacity.ts from its configured seat count and the overlap of requested slots. A studio with four chairs and a venue with one room use the same function. The result feeds the create command so over-capacity requests are refused before any write.
booking.acceptance: Four overlapping requests against a capacity of three return exactly one capacity error, and non-overlapping requests never count against each other.
thinking: Capacity is really a sweep over the timeline, so I'll count active intervals at each start point rather than comparing every pair.
A naive pairwise count would be quadratic and ugly, and resources can have hundreds of holds in a busy day.
I think I need to double check the sweep handles an end point and a start point at the same instant, because that is where I'd miscount.
Since the half-open model makes an end-at-start pair non-overlapping, I'll process ends before starts at equal instants.
booking.approve: Capacity uses a single sweep, ends are processed before starts at equal instants, and the error is raised before any write.

revise.reason: The sweep processes starts before ends at the same instant, so a back-to-back request is wrongly refused.
revise.directive: Sort end events before start events when their timestamps match.

booking.title: Accept appointment requests through the command handler
booking.intent: Implement the create command in src/booking/commands/create.ts so an authenticated caller can request a slot. The handler validates input, runs the domain checks and writes one reservation row inside a single transaction. It returns the new reservation id and never returns partial state on failure.
booking.acceptance: A valid request returns a held reservation with an id, and a request with a missing resource id returns a validation error without touching the database.
thinking: The handler is the first place where all the domain pieces meet, so I'll wire it through the existing transaction helper.
Validation runs before the transaction opens, which means a bad request never costs a connection from the pool.
I'm checking whether the lead-time rule should run inside the transaction, and it should, because the clock could move between check and write.
The return value is the id only, and the full row is a separate read, which keeps the command honest about what it changed.
booking.approve: The handler validates before opening a transaction, runs domain checks inside it, and returns only the id.

revise.reason: The handler opens the transaction before validation, so every rejected request holds a pooled connection.
revise.directive: Move input validation above the transaction open and return early on failure.

booking.title: Validate requested party size against resource limits
booking.intent: Check the party size on a create request against the resource's configured minimum and maximum in src/booking/commands/validate-party.ts. The limits come from catalog through the config module, so the validator reads them rather than hard-coding them. Failures return a field-level error the client can show next to the input.
booking.acceptance: A party size one above the maximum returns a field error naming partySize, and a size equal to the minimum is accepted.
thinking: Party size is a plain integer, but the client sends it as a string sometimes, so I'll coerce once at the edge and then trust the type.
I'll return a field error rather than a generic message, because the form needs to know which input to highlight.
Wait, the minimum of one is not the same as the default of two in config, and I should read the resource value and not the default.
The validator stays a pure function so the command tests can reuse it without a database.

edit.new: if (size < limits.min || size > limits.max) return fieldError('partySize', 'out_of_range');

booking.approve: Party size is checked against resource limits read from config, and each failure names the field.

revise.reason: The validator checks only the upper bound, so a party size of zero reaches the capacity check and fails there with a confusing message.
revise.directive: Add the minimum bound check and return the same field error shape.

booking.title: Return a structured error envelope on conflicts
booking.intent: Map domain and conflict failures into one error envelope in src/booking/errors.ts with a stable code, a message and a field path when one applies. The HTTP layer and the event consumers read the same shape, so a client never parses free text. Conflicts return HTTP 409 with the envelope and no internal detail.
booking.acceptance: A capacity conflict serialises to code capacity_exceeded with status 409, and no stack trace appears in the body.
thinking: A stable envelope matters more than a pretty message, because the client keys on the code and the message is only for humans.
I'm keeping a closed union of error codes so a new failure cannot appear without the compiler asking where it should map.
The envelope must not carry the SQL error text, since that would expose the schema to any caller who triggers a constraint.
I'll add the status mapping in one table so the HTTP layer does not decide statuses on its own.
booking.approve: The envelope has a closed code set, a single status table, and no internal detail in the body.

revise.reason: A database unique violation leaks the constraint name into the message field returned to the caller.
revise.directive: Map unique violations to a generic conflict code and drop the raw database message.

booking.title: Cancel a reservation and release its slots
booking.intent: Add a cancel command in src/booking/commands/cancel.ts that moves a held or confirmed reservation to cancelled and frees its slot interval. The cancel is a no-op on an already cancelled row, which keeps retries from a flaky client safe. The release happens in the same transaction as the status change.
booking.acceptance: Cancelling twice returns the same cancelled reservation both times, and the slot becomes available for a new create in the same test.
thinking: Cancellation is where an idempotency bug would most hurt, so I'm writing the double-cancel test before the handler.
The release and the status change must commit together, or a crash between them leaves a cancelled row still holding a slot.
I was about to return an error on second cancel, but a client retry would then look like a failure, so the result stays the same.
I'll check the outbox write happens in the same transaction later, which is a separate unit, so for now I leave a note in the handler.
booking.approve: Cancel is idempotent, releases the slot in the same transaction, and the retry test passes.

revise.reason: The cancel handler releases the slot before updating status, so a failed status update leaves the slot free on a live reservation.
revise.directive: Reorder the two writes inside one transaction so both commit or neither does.

booking.title: List reservations for a resource by date range
booking.intent: Implement the list query in src/booking/queries/list.ts that returns reservations for one resource between two instants. The query uses the starts_at index and returns rows ordered by start time. It rejects ranges longer than thirty-one days so one request cannot scan a whole year.
booking.acceptance: A thirty-two day range returns a range_too_large error, and a seven day range returns only rows that start inside it.
thinking: The list query is the first read path, so I want its shape fixed before any pagination goes on top.
A range guard is cheap and stops a careless client from asking for everything, which would be a real cost problem.
I'm checking the boundary: a range that starts inside the window but ends after it should still be included when it overlaps.
The ordering is by starts_at then id, because two reservations can share a start and the tie must be stable.

shell.description: Run resource date range list tests

booking.approve: The list is ordered with a stable tie-breaker, the range guard is enforced, and overlapping rows are included.

revise.reason: Rows that begin before the range and end inside it are excluded, so the first hour of a multi-hour hold disappears.
revise.finding: Overlapping rows excluded at range start
revise.directive: Select rows where starts_at is before range end and ends_at is after range start.

booking.title: Paginate reservation listings with opaque cursors
booking.intent: Add cursor pagination to the list query in src/booking/queries/cursor.ts. The cursor encodes the last starts_at and id as an opaque base64url string, and the client never sees the raw fields. A malformed cursor returns a validation error rather than falling back to the first page.
booking.acceptance: Walking three pages of a fixture returns every row exactly once, and a tampered cursor returns invalid_cursor.
thinking: Opaque cursors keep the wire contract free to change, so the client treats the token as a string and nothing more.
A tampered cursor should be an error, because silently restarting from page one would hide a client bug.
I'm not sure the page size default should be twenty or fifty, so I'll read the catalog's list limit before I pick one.
Keyset pagination on starts_at and id avoids the drift that offset pagination gives when rows are inserted mid-walk.

shell.description: Run cursor encode and decode tests

booking.approve: Cursors are opaque, keyset-based, and a tampered token fails loudly with invalid_cursor.

revise.reason: The cursor decoder accepts a token with extra fields and ignores them, so a future field silently changes the walk.
revise.directive: Reject any decoded cursor that contains keys outside the expected pair.

booking.title: Filter reservations by status and assignee
booking.intent: Extend the list query in src/booking/queries/filter.ts to accept an optional status set and an assignee id. Filters combine with AND and an empty filter list means no filtering. The filter builder is a small function that appends parameterised clauses, so no request value is ever spliced into SQL.
booking.acceptance: Filtering by two statuses returns only those statuses, and a value containing a quote character is passed as a bound parameter.
thinking: Filters are where string-built SQL sneaks in, so I'm making the builder return a parameter list and never a raw fragment.
A status set of one and a status set of two should go through the same clause, which keeps the builder small.
Hmm, the assignee filter should match on the assignee column but also include unassigned rows when asked, and I'll defer that until the contract says so.
The builder is pure, so I can unit test the generated SQL and the parameter order without a database.
booking.approve: Filters are parameterised, combine with AND, and no request value reaches the SQL text.

revise.reason: The status filter is built by interpolating the requested value into the SQL string.
revise.directive: Replace the interpolation with a bound parameter array and add a test with a quote character.

booking.title: Fetch a single reservation with its audit summary
booking.intent: Implement the get query in src/booking/queries/get.ts that returns one reservation and a short summary of its last three audit entries. The audit rows come from a separate table, so the query joins them with a limit applied per reservation. The result type makes the audit list optional so a reservation with no history still renders.
booking.acceptance: A reservation with five audit rows returns exactly three summary entries, newest first, and an unknown id returns not found.
thinking: I'll fetch the reservation row first and the audit summary second, since a missing reservation should return before any audit read.
Limiting audit rows to three in SQL is cheaper than pulling all of them and trimming in code.
The newest-first ordering needs a descending index on the audit table, which I'll confirm in the migration unit later.
Not found is the right answer for an id from another tenant, which the tenancy test already covers.

edit.new: const audit = await auditRepo.recent(ctx, id, { limit: 3 });

booking.approve: Get returns the reservation with a three-entry audit summary and not found for unknown ids.

revise.reason: The audit summary is fetched without a limit and trimmed in memory, so a long-lived reservation loads thousands of rows.
revise.finding: Audit summary not limited in SQL
revise.directive: Push the three-row limit into the audit query and drop the in-memory slice.

booking.title: Emit a reservation created event to the outbox
booking.intent: Write a reservation.created event into the outbox table from src/booking/events/emit.ts inside the same transaction as the insert. The payload carries the reservation id, tenant id and slot interval and nothing from the customer record. The event name and payload are recorded in contracts/booking.md for the analytics consumer.
booking.acceptance: A committed create leaves exactly one outbox row with the reservation.created type, and a rolled back create leaves none.
thinking: The outbox write belongs inside the create transaction, so a reservation can never exist without its event.
I'm keeping the payload small, because the analytics consumer does not need customer details and they should not travel.
The rollback test matters more than the commit test here, since a leaked event after a rollback is the real failure mode.
I'll version the event name in the payload so a later schema change does not break the existing consumer.
booking.approve: The event is written in the same transaction, the payload is minimal, and the rollback case leaves no row.

revise.reason: The outbox insert runs after the transaction commits, so a crash between them loses the event.
revise.directive: Move the outbox insert inside the same transaction as the reservation insert.

booking.title: Publish webhook deliveries for status transitions
booking.intent: Fan out status transition events to subscribed tenant webhooks from src/booking/events/webhooks.ts. Each delivery is signed with the tenant secret and carries the outbox event id so receivers can deduplicate. Delivery itself is handled by the outbox relay; this module only builds and signs the payload.
booking.acceptance: A confirmed transition produces one signed delivery per subscription, and the signature verifies with the tenant secret.
thinking: Signing has to be deterministic over the exact bytes sent, so I'm serialising the body once and signing that string.
The outbox event id doubles as the delivery id, which lets a receiver deduplicate without a separate counter.
I need to check whether secrets are rotated per tenant or globally, and the contract says per tenant, so the lookup goes through the tenant context.
A subscription that is disabled should produce no delivery, and the test covers that case explicitly.

shell.description: Run webhook signing and fan-out tests

booking.approve: Deliveries are signed over canonical bytes, carry the event id, and disabled subscriptions are skipped.

revise.reason: The signature is computed over the pretty-printed body while the wire body is minified, so receivers always fail verification.
revise.directive: Sign the exact serialised string that is sent on the wire.

booking.title: Define the availability contract for search
booking.intent: Write the availability section of contracts/booking.md and the matching type in src/booking/contracts/availability.ts so the search system can index open slots. The contract lists the fields, their units and the update events that signal a change. Search reads only this shape and never reaches into the booking tables.
booking.acceptance: The contract type matches the documented fields, and the test fails if a field is added to the type without a contract entry.
thinking: Search must not query our tables, so the contract is the only thing it can depend on and it has to be explicit.
I'll pick minutes for duration and UTC instants for times, since search otherwise guesses at time zones.
The test that compares type fields to the contract text is a little brittle, but it is the only thing that stops them drifting apart.
Units are the most common source of cross-team bugs, so each field gets its unit in the contract line.

shell.description: Check availability type against contract doc

booking.approve: The contract fields are typed, their units are documented, and drift between type and doc fails the test.

revise.reason: The contract doc omits the updatedAt field that the type now carries, so the drift test passes only because it skips optional fields.
revise.directive: Require every exported field to appear in the contract section without an optional exemption.

booking.title: Consume catalog resource updates for resource rules
booking.intent: Subscribe to catalog.resource.updated in src/booking/events/consume-catalog.ts and refresh the cached resource rules when a limit changes. The handler is idempotent on the event id and ignores events for resources the booking system has never seen. Stale cache entries are dropped rather than patched in place.
booking.acceptance: Replaying the same catalog event twice leaves the cache unchanged, and an event for an unknown resource is acknowledged without error.
thinking: The catalog is owned by another system, so I depend only on its event and never read its tables.
Replays happen after every outbox retry, so the handler must produce the same cache state on a second pass.
I was going to patch the cached rule in place, but dropping the entry is simpler and removes a class of partial-update bugs.
An unknown resource is not an error, since catalog publishes for every resource and most are not bookable here yet.
booking.approve: The consumer drops stale rules, is idempotent on replay, and acknowledges unknown resources.

revise.reason: The consumer writes the new rules into the cache before checking the event id, so a replay overwrites a newer rule with an older one.
revise.directive: Check the processed event id first and skip the write when it was already applied.

booking.title: Hold a slot for ten minutes during checkout
booking.intent: Add a hold step in src/booking/commands/hold.ts that reserves a slot in the held state with an expiry ten minutes out. The hold blocks other requests for the same interval and is converted to confirmed on payment success. An expired hold returns its slot automatically through the expiry sweep.
booking.acceptance: A held slot rejects an overlapping create until expiry, and after ten minutes the same slot can be held again.
thinking: A hold is just a reservation with an expiry, so I'm reusing the reservation row and not adding a second table.
The expiry is stored as an instant, not a duration, so the sweep compares against now without recomputing the start.
I need to be careful the sweep and the create path agree on whether an expired hold still blocks, or two customers could both see a free slot.
The ten minute value comes from config, but the test pins it so a config change cannot quietly break the expiry test.

shell.description: Run hold expiry and overlap tests

booking.approve: Holds block overlapping creates, expire after ten minutes, and the expiry boundary is covered.

revise.reason: The hold expiry is set to one minute instead of ten, so the expiry test passes only because it advances the clock by a minute.
revise.directive: Set the hold window to ten minutes and update the test to advance the clock past it.

booking.title: Reject overlapping reservations for the same resource
booking.intent: Enforce in src/booking/commands/overlap.ts that no two active reservations for one resource share an instant. The check runs inside the create transaction with a row lock on the resource so two concurrent requests cannot both pass. Cancelled and expired rows are excluded from the overlap test.
booking.acceptance: Two concurrent creates for the same slot produce one success and one overlap error, and a create after a cancel succeeds.
thinking: Two concurrent creates are the real test, so I'm writing a race test with two connections before touching the handler.
The row lock on the resource serialises writers without a global lock, which is the cheapest correct option here.
I need to exclude cancelled rows from the overlap query, or a cancelled reservation would block its own slot forever.
I'm not sure the lock should be on the resource row or on a tenant advisory key, and the resource row is what the catalog already locks, so I'll use it.

edit.new: WHERE resource_id = $1 AND status IN ('held', 'confirmed') FOR UPDATE

booking.approve: Concurrent creates are serialised by the resource lock and cancelled rows never block a slot.

revise.reason: The overlap query omits the row lock, so two concurrent creates both see an empty slot and both insert.
revise.directive: Take a FOR UPDATE lock on the resource row before running the overlap query.

booking.title: Make the create endpoint idempotent on a client key
booking.intent: Accept an Idempotency-Key header on create in src/booking/commands/idempotency.ts and store the first response against it for twenty-four hours. A repeat with the same key and body returns the stored response, and a repeat with a different body returns a conflict. The keys are scoped to the tenant so two tenants can reuse a key safely.
booking.acceptance: Two identical creates with one key return the same reservation id, and the same key with a different body returns idempotency_mismatch.
thinking: Idempotency is a retry safety net, so the stored response must be the exact one the first caller received.
I'm hashing the request body to detect a reused key with a different payload, and a hash mismatch is a client bug to surface.
The scope is tenant plus key, because a global key namespace would let one tenant probe another tenant's keys.
Wait, storing the response before the transaction commits could cache a reservation that was then rolled back, so the store goes in the same transaction.
booking.approve: Idempotent replays return the stored response, mismatched bodies are rejected, and keys are tenant scoped.

revise.reason: The idempotency record is written after the transaction commits, so a crash between them lets a retry create a second reservation.
revise.directive: Write the idempotency record inside the same transaction as the reservation.

booking.title: Retry outbox deliveries with capped exponential backoff
booking.intent: Configure the outbox relay retry policy for booking events in src/booking/events/retry.ts with exponential backoff capped at five minutes and a maximum of twelve attempts. A permanent failure moves the event to a dead-letter state and raises an alert. The policy is a pure function so the schedule can be checked without sleeping.
booking.acceptance: The delay after the eighth attempt equals the five minute cap, and the twelfth failure marks the event dead-lettered.
thinking: The backoff schedule is pure arithmetic, so I'm computing the delays in a table and testing the table.
Capping at five minutes keeps a long outage from pushing retries out to hours, which would delay every downstream system.
I should check whether jitter belongs here, and I'll add it so a fleet of relays does not retry in lockstep.
The dead-letter state is a status, not a deletion, so an operator can replay the event after fixing the consumer.

edit.new: const delay = Math.min(base * 2 ** attempt, CAP_MS) * jitter(attempt);

shell.description: Run retry schedule and cap tests

booking.approve: The schedule is capped, dead-lettering happens at twelve attempts, and the schedule is tested without sleeping.

revise.reason: Jitter is applied after the cap, so the eighth attempt can exceed the five minute ceiling.
revise.directive: Apply jitter before the cap so the final delay never exceeds five minutes.

booking.title: Backfill slot rows from legacy calendar exports
booking.intent: Write a backfill in src/booking/migrate/backfill-slots.ts that converts legacy calendar export rows into reservation slots. The job runs in batches of five hundred keyed by legacy id and records its checkpoint so it resumes after a crash. Rows that cannot be mapped are written to a rejects table rather than dropped.
booking.acceptance: A rerun after a simulated crash skips already converted rows, and an unmappable row lands in the rejects table.
thinking: The backfill is one-shot and touches real rows, so the checkpoint has to be durable before any write is trusted.
Batching by legacy id gives a stable resume point, which a timestamp would not, since timestamps can repeat.
A legacy row with a zero duration is not a slot, and I was going to coerce it to thirty minutes, but that would invent data, so it goes to rejects.
The rerun test is the proof, so I'm running the backfill twice and checking the row count does not change.

edit.old: const batch = await legacy.nextBatch({ after: checkpoint, size: 500 });
edit.new: const batch = await legacy.nextBatch({ after: checkpoint, size: BATCH_SIZE });

shell.description: Run backfill resume and reject tests

booking.approve: Backfill resumes from its checkpoint, rejects are recorded rather than dropped, and the rerun is idempotent.

revise.reason: The backfill advances its checkpoint before writing the batch, so a crash mid-batch skips rows permanently.
revise.directive: Advance the checkpoint only after the batch commits in the same transaction.

booking.title: Add a non-overlap exclusion constraint in Postgres
booking.intent: Add a Postgres exclusion constraint in migrations/booking/0025_no_overlap.sql using a tstzrange of the slot and the resource id, restricted to active statuses. The database enforces the rule even if an application path skips the lock. The constraint name is documented in contracts/booking.md so the error mapper can recognise it.
booking.acceptance: An insert that overlaps an active row fails with the named exclusion violation, and a cancelled row does not block it.
thinking: The application lock is correct but a database constraint is the backstop when someone writes a new path and forgets it.
I need the range to be half-open to match the domain, so I'm using the bounds argument explicitly as [) in the range.
The partial index on active statuses is the piece that makes cancelled rows stop blocking, and I'd forgotten it until the test failed.
I'll map the constraint violation in the repository so the error envelope gets a stable code and not a raw database message.
booking.approve: The exclusion constraint enforces overlap in the database, uses half-open ranges, and ignores cancelled rows.

revise.reason: The exclusion constraint uses closed bounds, so a slot ending at the next slot's start is rejected.
revise.directive: Build the tstzrange with bounds that exclude the end instant.

booking.title: Migrate reservation status enum to text with check
booking.intent: Convert the reservation status column from a Postgres enum to text with a check constraint in migrations/booking/0026_status_text.sql. Postgres enums are hard to extend in a transaction, and the check is easier to change. The allowed values match the list in src/booking/schema.ts exactly.
booking.acceptance: The migration applies and rolls back cleanly, and a value outside the allowed set fails the check.
thinking: Enums feel safe until you need to add a value inside a transaction, which Postgres will not let you do cleanly.
The check constraint lists the same values as the TypeScript constant, so the two lists must not diverge; I'll generate the SQL from the constant.
Wait, the migration has to rewrite existing rows with the same values, so the cast from enum to text has to happen before the check is added.
The rollback test proves the down migration restores the enum type and I'm not relying on the up path alone.

shell.description: Run status enum to text migration tests

booking.approve: The status column is text with a generated check that matches the TypeScript list, and the rollback is tested.

revise.reason: The down migration drops the check constraint but does not restore the enum type, so a rollback leaves an unusable column.
revise.directive: Recreate the enum type and cast the column back in the down migration, then test the round trip.

booking.title: Dual-read legacy reservation ids during cutover
booking.intent: During cutover, have src/booking/queries/legacy-id.ts resolve a legacy reservation id to the new id before falling back to a not found. The mapping table is read-only and is dropped after the cutover window. Callers see only the new id in responses, so the legacy id never leaks into the contract.
booking.acceptance: A legacy id resolves to the same reservation as the new id, and an unmapped legacy id returns not found without error.
thinking: Dual reads are scaffolding, so I'm keeping this module small and marking it for deletion at the end of the cutover window.
The response always carries the new id, which means the legacy id is a lookup input only and never an output.
I need to be sure an unmapped id is a plain not found, not an error, since most old links point at reservations that were never migrated.
The mapping table is read-only here, so this module cannot accidentally create new mappings during a normal request.
booking.approve: Legacy ids resolve for lookup only, responses carry new ids, and unmapped ids are a plain not found.

revise.reason: The legacy resolver looks up the mapping without a tenant filter, so a legacy id from one tenant resolves another tenant's reservation.
revise.directive: Pass the tenant context into the mapping lookup and filter on it.

booking.title: Emit a metric for reservation conversion rate
booking.intent: Record a counter and a histogram in src/booking/observability/metrics.ts for hold-to-confirm conversion and time spent holding. The metric names follow the platform convention with the system label set to booking-scheduling. Labels stay low cardinality so a tenant id is never a label value.
booking.acceptance: A confirmed hold increments the conversion counter once, and no metric label contains a tenant or reservation id.
thinking: Conversion is the number the product team will ask about first, so the counter has to fire exactly once per confirmation.
A tenant id as a label would explode the series count, so I'm checking every label value against a closed list.
I wonder if the histogram buckets should match the ten minute hold, and they should, so the top bucket is the expiry.
The test reads the registry and asserts on label names, which catches a stray high-cardinality label before it ships.
booking.approve: Metrics are counted once per confirmation, labels are closed, and the tenant id never appears as a label.

revise.reason: The conversion counter increments on hold creation as well as on confirmation, which doubles the reported rate.
revise.directive: Increment the conversion counter only on the confirmed transition.

booking.title: Trace the hold-to-confirm path across services
booking.intent: Add spans in src/booking/observability/trace.ts around the hold, payment callback and confirm steps so one trace links the whole checkout. The trace context travels in the outbox event headers so the analytics consumer joins the same trace. Spans carry the reservation id as an attribute but never the customer name.
booking.acceptance: A checkout produces one trace with three named spans sharing a trace id, and the customer name is absent from span attributes.
thinking: A single trace across checkout is the only way to see where a customer waited, so I'm threading the context through the outbox.
The payment callback arrives on a different request, so the trace id has to be carried in the hold record and not the process.
I'm worried about putting the customer name anywhere near a span, so the test asserts its absence explicitly.
The span names are fixed strings, which keeps the trace UI readable and stops names from carrying ids.

edit.new: const span = tracer.startSpan('booking.hold', { attributes: { reservation_id: id } });

booking.approve: One trace spans the checkout, the trace context rides the outbox, and no customer name reaches a span.

revise.reason: The trace context is read from the request in the payment callback, which is a different request, so the spans start a new trace.
revise.finding: Trace context not carried across callback
revise.directive: Restore the trace context from the stored hold record in the payment callback handler.

booking.title: Log structured diagnostics for rejected slot requests
booking.intent: Emit a structured log line from src/booking/observability/diagnostics.ts whenever a create is rejected, with the rejection code, resource id and a request correlation id. The line never includes the request body, since bodies can hold customer data. Logs are written at warn level and the fields are typed so a missing one fails the build.
booking.acceptance: A capacity rejection produces one warn log with code capacity_exceeded and a correlation id, and the body does not appear in the line.
thinking: Rejections are where operators look first, so the log has to say what failed without saying who asked.
Typing the log fields means a new rejection code cannot be logged without the compiler knowing about it.
I was going to log the request body for debugging, then I remembered customer data sits in it, so I'm dropping that field entirely.
The correlation id comes from the request context and not a new uuid, so the log joins to the access log.
booking.approve: Rejections log typed fields with a correlation id, and no request body reaches the log.

revise.reason: The diagnostic line logs the full request body including the customer email on every rejection.
revise.directive: Remove the body field from the log call and assert its absence in the test.

booking.title: Index reservations by resource and start time
booking.intent: Add a composite index on reservations(tenant_id, resource_id, starts_at) in migrations/booking/0031_index_resource_time.sql to serve the list query. The index leads with tenant_id because every query filters on it first. An EXPLAIN check in the test confirms the planner uses it for the range query.
booking.acceptance: EXPLAIN for the list query shows an index scan on the new index, and the migration rolls back by dropping that index only.
thinking: The list query is the hot path, so I'll check the plan on a populated fixture instead of guessing from the column order.
Leading with tenant_id is deliberate, since a leading resource id would not help a query that starts from a tenant.
I'm not sure the planner will choose the index for a small table, so the test seeds enough rows to make the choice honest.
The down migration drops only this index and nothing else, which keeps rollback from touching the constraint from unit twenty-five.

edit.new: WHERE tenant_id = $1 AND resource_id = $2 AND starts_at >= $3

shell.description: Run index plan check for list query

booking.approve: The index serves the list query, leads with tenant id, and the plan check confirms the index scan.

revise.reason: The index leads with starts_at, so the planner scans the whole table for a single tenant's resource.
revise.directive: Reorder the index so tenant_id and resource_id lead and starts_at follows.

booking.title: Apply per-tenant quota to reservation creation
booking.intent: Enforce a daily create quota per tenant in src/booking/limits/quota.ts using a token bucket held in the shared cache. A tenant over quota gets a rate_limited error with a retry-after value. Limits are read from the tenant plan through the catalog contract, not from a hard-coded number.
booking.acceptance: The tenth create in a bucket of ten succeeds and the eleventh returns rate_limited with a positive retry-after.
thinking: A token bucket is simple to reason about and tolerates short bursts, which fits a booking flow where people double-click.
The retry-after value has to come from the bucket refill rate, so I'm computing it instead of returning a fixed sixty seconds.
I need to make sure the bucket is keyed by tenant and not by caller, or one busy user would starve the whole tenant.
The cache is shared, so the decrement must be atomic, and I'm using the cache's compare-and-set rather than a read then write.

edit.new: const current = await cache.incrementWithin(key, bucketCapacity, refillWindowMs);

booking.approve: Quota is per tenant, atomic on the shared cache, and returns a computed retry-after.

revise.reason: The bucket is read and then written without atomicity, so two concurrent creates both see room and both pass.
revise.directive: Use the cache's atomic increment within the bucket limit and reject when it reports over capacity.

booking.title: Cap the number of open holds per customer
booking.intent: Limit each customer to a fixed number of open holds in src/booking/limits/open-holds.ts so one person cannot lock up a resource with many expiring holds. The count is taken inside the hold transaction and the limit is read from the resource config. Exceeding the cap returns hold_limit_reached with the current count.
booking.acceptance: A customer with three open holds and a cap of three is refused a fourth, and confirming one hold frees a slot under the cap.
thinking: The cap guards against a single customer hoarding a resource, which is more likely than a malicious flood.
The count must run inside the same transaction as the hold insert, or two parallel holds can both see two and both pass.
I'm checking whether the cap counts expired holds, and it should not, since they are about to be swept and would unfairly block the customer.
The error carries the current count so the client can tell the customer how many holds are open without a second request.

edit.new: WHERE customer_id = $1 AND status = 'held' AND expires_at > now()

booking.approve: The hold cap is counted inside the transaction, ignores expired holds, and reports the current count.
