revise.reason: The open-hold count includes holds that have already expired, so a customer is blocked by holds the sweep has not yet cleared.
revise.directive: Exclude holds whose expiry is in the past from the open-hold count.

booking.title: Gate waitlist promotion behind a feature flag
booking.intent: Put waitlist promotion in src/booking/rollout/waitlist-flag.ts behind the booking-waitlist flag so it can be turned on per tenant. When a held slot expires, the next waitlisted customer is promoted only when the flag is on. The flag is read once per sweep so a mid-sweep toggle cannot split one batch between behaviours.
booking.acceptance: With the flag off no promotion occurs, and with it on exactly one waitlisted customer is promoted per expired slot.
thinking: Waitlist promotion changes customer-visible behaviour, so it sits behind a flag from the first commit.
Reading the flag once per sweep is a small decision that prevents a half promoted batch if someone flips it at the wrong moment.
I need to make sure a flag that is absent defaults to off, not on, since the safe state for a new behaviour is off.
The test runs with the flag both off and on, so the disabled path is exercised as much as the enabled one.
booking.approve: Waitlist promotion is off by default, the flag is read once per sweep, and both states are tested.

revise.reason: The flag is read inside the per-slot loop, so a toggle mid-sweep promotes some customers and not others.
revise.directive: Read the flag once before the sweep loop and pass the value into each iteration.

booking.title: Roll back a failed batch of slot releases
booking.intent: Provide a rollback path in src/booking/rollout/release-rollback.ts for a bulk slot release that went wrong. The release writes a batch id on every row it touches, so the rollback can restore exactly those rows and nothing else. Rollback refuses to run on a batch older than seven days.
booking.acceptance: A rollback restores only the rows with the batch id, and a rollback request for a batch older than seven days returns an error.
thinking: A bulk release without a batch id is impossible to undo cleanly, so every row carries the id it was released under.
The seven day refusal is a guard against restoring a slot that has since been legitimately taken by someone else.
I'm double checking the restore only touches rows still in the released state, since a row confirmed since then must not flip back.
The rollback is a deliberate operator action, so it logs the batch id and the row count for the audit trail.

edit.old: UPDATE reservations SET status = 'held' WHERE batch_id = $1
edit.new: UPDATE reservations SET status = 'held' WHERE batch_id = $1 AND status = 'released'

booking.approve: Rollback is scoped to the batch id and released rows, refuses old batches, and logs what it restored.

revise.reason: The rollback restores every row with the batch id, including rows that were confirmed after the release.
revise.directive: Restrict the rollback update to rows still in the released state.

booking.title: Set retention on cancelled reservations to ninety days
booking.intent: Add a retention job in src/booking/rollout/retention.ts that deletes cancelled reservations ninety days after their cancellation. The job deletes in small batches so it never holds a long lock, and it writes a count to the audit log. Expired holds are excluded because they are swept separately.
booking.acceptance: A reservation cancelled ninety one days ago is deleted and one cancelled eighty nine days ago is kept, and each run writes one audit count.
thinking: Retention is a deletion, so the window and the batch size are both pinned in the contract before the code is written.
The boundary test uses ninety one and eighty nine days, which avoids arguing about the exact instant the window closes.
Deleting in batches of two hundred keeps each transaction short, and a single big delete would block the create path for seconds.
I'm checking that the job never touches a row that is still held, since the status filter is the only thing protecting it.

edit.new: DELETE FROM reservations WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND cancelled_at < $1 AND id IN (SELECT id FROM reservations WHERE status = 'cancelled' AND cancelled_at < $1 LIMIT $2)

shell.description: Run retention window and batch delete tests

booking.approve: Retention deletes only cancelled rows past ninety days, in short batches, with an audit count per run.

revise.reason: The retention window is measured from the created date instead of the cancellation date, so long-held reservations are deleted while still recent.
revise.directive: Measure the ninety day window from cancelled_at instead of created_at.

booking.title: Record an audit entry for every status change
booking.intent: Write an audit row in src/booking/audit/record.ts for every transition of a reservation's status, with the actor role, the prior status and the new status. The write happens in the transition transaction so an audit gap is impossible. Audit rows are append-only and the repository exposes no update method for them.
booking.acceptance: Each transition writes exactly one audit row with prior and new status, and no code path can update an existing audit row.
thinking: The audit row lives in the same transaction as the transition, so there is no state where a change happened unrecorded.
Recording the actor as a role rather than a user id keeps personal identifiers out of the audit table by default.
I was going to add an update method for corrections, and I've decided against it, because a correction should be a new row.
The migration revokes update and delete on the audit table from the application role, which turns the append-only rule into a database fact.

edit.old: await tx.insert('reservation_audit', { reservation_id, prior, next, actor_role });
edit.new: await tx.insert('reservation_audit', { reservation_id, prior, next, actor_role, recorded_at: now });

shell.description: Run audit transition and append-only tests

booking.approve: Every transition writes one audit row in the same transaction, the table is append-only, and the actor is a role.

revise.reason: The audit insert runs after the transition commits, so a crash between them leaves a status change with no audit row.
revise.directive: Write the audit row inside the same transaction as the status change.

billing.title: Create the invoice schema with tenant-scoped tables
billing.intent: Add the first billing tables for invoices, invoice lines and charge attempts, each keyed by tenant_id so no query can cross tenants by accident. The DDL goes in migrations/0001_billing_schema.sql and the row types in src/billing/schema.ts. Record table ownership in contracts/billing.md so catalog and booking know which tables are ours.
billing.acceptance: The migration applies cleanly to an empty database and every billing table has a non-null tenant_id with an index that leads on it. A test asserts that inserting an invoice row without tenant_id fails.
thinking: The brief is three tables and one rule: every row carries tenant_id. I'll start with the invoice header because the line and attempt tables hang off it.

I was going to use a single uuid primary key everywhere, but a composite key of (tenant_id, id) puts the tenant predicate into every lookup. That costs a little index width. It is worth it, because a forgotten WHERE clause then fails to find the row instead of leaking it.
Checked the identity migration to see how it names foreign keys. It uses fk_<table>_<column>, so I'll match that rather than invent a convention for billing.
The row types in schema.ts are plain interfaces for now. Money columns are bigint minor units, and I'll leave the money type itself for unit 6.
Before I trust the index I want the planner to prove it. The test runs EXPLAIN on a tenant-scoped select and asserts the index name appears, instead of assuming it does.
testOutput: ok 2 - invoice lines index leads with tenant_id
billing.approve: Every row carries the tenant key and the migration applies clean, so this foundation can merge.

revise.reason: The invoice_attempts table has no index that leads with tenant_id, so tenant-scoped reads would scan the table.
revise.directive: Add a composite index on invoice_attempts that begins with tenant_id.

billing.title: Scaffold the invoicing module and its public entry point
billing.intent: Create the src/billing module with index.ts as the only surface other systems may import. Internal files stay under src/billing/internal so nothing outside the module reaches past the entry point. Add a stub section per public function to contracts/billing.md so the surface is documented from day one.
billing.acceptance: Importing the module from index.ts exposes createBilling and nothing from internal files. A test fails if another system imports src/billing/internal directly.
thinking: Scaffolding is mostly deciding what is public. I want index.ts to be the one door and everything else behind it.
Thought about putting the boundary check in lint, but a test is cheaper to read and runs in the same suite. I'll grep the import graph inside the test.
The contracts file gets a heading per public function now, even empty. An undocumented export is the first thing that drifts.
Caught a mistake while wiring the barrel: I had re-exported a type from internal/ that the caller should never build by hand. Pulled it back out and kept only the function.
Keeping the scaffold small. No config reads yet, that is unit 2.
billing.approve: The entry point is the only door and the contract file documents it, which is what I wanted from the scaffold.

revise.reason: The barrel re-exports an internal type, so callers can construct internal state directly.
revise.directive: Remove the internal type export from index.ts and expose only the factory function.

billing.title: Load currency and tax settings from tenant config
billing.intent: Read the default currency, the supported currency list and the tax rounding mode from environment config in src/billing/config.ts. Failing fast on a bad value is more useful than a silent fallback, so the loader throws a named error. Note the accepted codes in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Startup fails with BillingConfigError when BILLING_DEFAULT_CURRENCY is missing or not in the supported list. A valid environment loads with the rounding mode set to half-even.
thinking: Config is a boundary, so this is where I want strictness. A default currency that quietly becomes USD would corrupt every total downstream.
I considered reading the whole config into a loose record and validating later. Validating at load into a typed object is simpler and keeps the error at startup.
Checked how the other systems name their environment variables. They are prefixed by system, so BILLING_ it is.
The rounding mode has one legal value for now. I left it as a union type rather than a free string so a typo fails compilation.
Ran the loader against an empty environment and got a stack trace instead of the named error. The error class was not exported from the barrel, so I fixed the import and reran.
testOutput: ok 3 - valid env loads half-even rounding
billing.approve: The config fails loudly on bad input and the accepted currencies are written down where catalog can read them.

revise.reason: The loader falls back to USD when the variable is unset, which hides a missing deployment setting.
revise.directive: Throw BillingConfigError when BILLING_DEFAULT_CURRENCY is unset instead of defaulting.

billing.title: Derive tenant-scoped keys for every invoice row
billing.intent: Write the key helpers in src/billing/keys.ts that build storage and cache keys from a branded TenantId and the record id. Every key begins with the tenant so a scan of one tenant's prefix can never return another's rows. The helpers are the only place that concatenates key strings.
billing.acceptance: Two tenants with the same invoice id produce different keys. A test confirms every helper output starts with the tenant prefix.
thinking: A key helper is small, but a mistake here spreads everywhere, so I want it to be the single place that knows the format.
I'll brand TenantId so a raw string cannot be passed where a tenant is expected. That turns a whole class of mix-ups into a compile error.
The first draft interpolated the invoice id before the tenant. Flipping the order made prefix scans work, so the tenant comes first.
Checked schema.ts to make sure the row types already carry tenant_id, so the key and the row cannot disagree.
Wondering whether a separator collision is possible if a tenant id contains a colon. Ids are uuids in this system, so I'll assert the format in the test instead of escaping.

edit.new: export function invoiceKey(tenantId: TenantId, id: InvoiceId) {

testOutput: ok 2 - same invoice id differs across tenants
ok 3 - tenant id with colon is rejected
billing.approve: The branded tenant type and prefixed keys make cross-tenant collisions visible at compile time.

revise.reason: The invoice key helper accepts a plain string for the tenant, so an unbranded id can slip through.
revise.directive: Change the tenant parameter type to the branded TenantId and update the callers.

billing.title: Model invoices as an aggregate with line items
billing.intent: Define the Invoice aggregate in src/billing/invoice.ts so that lines, totals and status are changed only through its methods. Lines live in src/billing/line-item.ts and the aggregate owns their sum. Keep the contract for the aggregate's public shape in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Adding a line recomputes the subtotal and total in one call. A test shows that an invoice cannot be edited after it is finalized.
thinking: The aggregate is where the invariants live, so the rule that totals equal the sum of lines goes here and nowhere else.
I was tempted to store the total as a column and update it from callers. I'd rather recompute it inside addLine so nobody can forget.
Finalized invoices are immutable. The method checks status first and throws, and I'll test that the throw happens before any line is added.
Noticed that line amounts are still plain numbers. That is wrong for money, but unit 6 introduces the type, so I'll note it and move on.
Ran the aggregate test and it passed, but the total was off by one line because the new line was pushed after the sum. Reordered the two statements.
billing.approve: Totals are derived inside the aggregate and finalized invoices cannot drift, which matches the invariant we wrote down.

revise.reason: The total is stored as a separate field that addLine does not update, so it can disagree with the lines.
revise.directive: Remove the stored total field and derive it from the lines inside the aggregate.

billing.title: Define the subscription lifecycle state machine
billing.intent: Encode subscription states and their legal transitions in src/billing/subscription-state.ts as a table, not a chain of ifs. Trialing, active, past due and canceled each have a short list of allowed moves. Describe the transitions in contracts/billing.md so booking can rely on them.
billing.acceptance: A transition not in the table throws an IllegalTransitionError. Every state has at least one test covering its allowed exits.
thinking: State machines rot when the rules are spread across handlers. A table makes the whole rulebook readable in one screen.
I initially let canceled return to active for reactivations. On reflection a reactivation is a new subscription in our model, so canceled is terminal.
Wrote the table as a map from state to allowed next states. The test iterates it and checks every pair, which catches an accidental omission.
Checked how past_due recovers. A successful payment moves it back to active, and that edge is the one most likely to be forgotten, so I gave it its own test.
Changed the status union to include canceled, and the compiler immediately flagged two switch statements in the older code that now need the new case.
billing.approve: Canceled as terminal and the recovery edge from past due match what the product team described.

revise.reason: The transition table allows canceled to move back to active, which would resurrect a closed subscription.
revise.directive: Remove the canceled to active transition and add a test that asserts canceled has no exits.

billing.title: Represent money as integer minor units with currency
billing.intent: Introduce a Money value in src/billing/money.ts holding an integer amount in minor units and an ISO currency code. Arithmetic refuses to mix currencies, so adding dollars to euros throws instead of producing a number. Document the representation in contracts/billing.md for the other systems.
billing.acceptance: Adding two amounts in different currencies throws CurrencyMismatchError. Floating point input is rejected when constructing a Money value.
thinking: Money is where the cheapest bug in the system hides, so I want the type to refuse the bad operation rather than trust the caller.
The representation is an integer count of minor units. Floats are rejected at construction, because a value like 10.1 would silently round in some later step.
I considered a library for decimal money and decided against it. The operations we need are add, subtract and multiply by an integer, and that does not justify a dependency.
Replaced the plain number amounts in line-item.ts with Money. The compiler flagged every site that used the old field, which was the point.
Realised the currency check must run before the arithmetic, not after. Reversing that order would produce a number first and then fail on a value that is already wrong.
billing.approve: Integer minor units with a hard currency check is exactly the representation the other systems need.

revise.reason: The Money constructor accepts a non-integer amount and rounds it silently.
revise.directive: Make the Money constructor throw when the amount is not a safe integer.

billing.title: Compute prorated charges when a plan changes mid-cycle
billing.intent: Write the proration calculation in src/billing/proration.ts that credits the unused part of the old plan and charges the new plan for the remainder of the period. Days are counted in the tenant timezone, not UTC, and the rule is written up in contracts/billing.md. Results are rounded through the Money type from unit 6.
billing.acceptance: A plan change on day 10 of a 30-day cycle produces the expected credit and charge to the minor unit. A change on the first or last day produces no proration.
thinking: Proration has an answer that is easy to get almost right. The tricky part is which day counts, so I'll pin it down in the contract first.
Counted days in UTC at first, which gave the wrong result for a tenant whose cycle starts late in the evening local time. The test caught it, so the day boundary now uses the tenant zone.
The rounding of each side has to be symmetric. If credit and charge round in different directions the customer ends up a cent off, so I round both with the same mode.
Checked the first-day and last-day edge cases by hand against a calendar before writing them into the test. A change on the last day should produce no credit at all.
Kept the function pure, taking the period and the two plans, which makes it trivial to test without a database.
testOutput: ok 1 - mid-cycle change credits remaining days
ok 2 - first day change has no proration
ok 3 - last day change has no proration
ok 4 - tenant zone decides day boundary
billing.approve: The tenant timezone boundary and symmetric rounding are the two things that would have cost us a support ticket, and both are covered.

revise.reason: Credit and charge are rounded in different modes, so a plan change can leave the customer a minor unit short.
revise.directive: Round the credit and the charge with the same rounding mode from config.

billing.title: Create invoices from a validated charge request
billing.intent: Accept a charge request in src/billing/create-invoice.ts and validate its shape before any row is written. Validation lives in src/billing/validate-request.ts and returns a discriminated result, so the handler never inspects raw input. The request format is listed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A request with no lines or a negative amount is rejected before a row is written. A valid request returns the created invoice id.
thinking: The write path starts at the boundary, so validation runs first and the handler only sees a value it can trust.
I want the validator to return a result union rather than throw, because the caller needs to map each failure to a specific error code.
Caught a case where an empty lines array passed because the check only tested for undefined. Changed it to require at least one line.
The handler inserts the invoice and its lines in one transaction, and I'll confirm that a failure midway leaves no orphan lines.
Before merging I'll grep for any other caller that builds an invoice directly, since that path would skip validation entirely.
billing.approve: Validation runs before any write and returns specific codes, so callers can react to each failure.

revise.reason: The empty-lines check only tests for undefined, so an invoice with zero lines is created.
revise.directive: Require at least one line in validate-request.ts and return NO_LINES otherwise.

billing.title: Reject duplicate payment method attachments per tenant
billing.intent: Stop the same card fingerprint from being attached twice to one tenant's customer in src/billing/payment-methods.ts. The check runs in the attach path and is backed by a unique index in migrations/0009_payment_method_unique.sql, so a race cannot slip past it. Note the conflict response in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Attaching a second method with the same fingerprint returns a DUPLICATE_PAYMENT_METHOD error. A concurrent double attach leaves exactly one row.
thinking: An application check alone loses to a race, so the unique index is the real guarantee and the check is only there to return a nice error.
The fingerprint is scoped by tenant and customer, not globally. The same card can legitimately belong to two tenants.
Ran the concurrent attach test twice to be sure. The first run passed by luck, so I added a barrier to force both inserts to start together.
Wrote the migration to create the index concurrently so the table does not lock during a production deploy.
Checked whether the existing rows already have duplicates. They do not, so the index will create cleanly without a cleanup step.

edit.new: const existing = await repo.findByFingerprint(tenantId, customerId, fingerprint);

testOutput: ok 2 - same card across tenants allowed
ok 3 - concurrent attach leaves one row
billing.approve: The unique index backs the check, so the concurrent case is closed and not just tested for once.

revise.reason: The duplicate lookup omits the customer, so the same card cannot be attached to two customers of the same tenant.
revise.directive: Include the customer id in the duplicate lookup and in the unique index.

billing.title: Return structured error envelopes for declined charges
billing.intent: Map provider decline codes into a stable error envelope in src/billing/errors.ts with a machine code, a retryable flag and a human message. The charge path in src/billing/charge.ts returns the envelope instead of throwing a raw provider error. The envelope shape is fixed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Every known decline code maps to one envelope with retryable set correctly. An unknown provider code produces an UNKNOWN_DECLINE envelope and is logged, not swallowed.
thinking: Callers should never parse provider strings. Mapping once in errors.ts means the rest of the system sees one vocabulary.
The retryable flag is the field I care most about. Insufficient funds may be retried later, while a stolen card must never be, so I mapped each code explicitly.
An unknown code is the dangerous case. Treating it as retryable would hammer a card that is permanently declined, so unknown is non-retryable and logged.
Ran the mapping table against the provider's documented list, and found two codes I had transcribed with the wrong casing. Fixed them and added a test that fails on any mismatch.
Thought about a default branch that returns a generic error, then decided against it. Failing loud on an unmapped code is what surfaces the gap.
billing.approve: Retryable is set deliberately per code and unknown declines fail safe, which is the behavior I want on a card.

revise.reason: Unknown provider decline codes are marked retryable, which would keep retrying a permanently declined card.
revise.directive: Mark UNKNOWN_DECLINE as non-retryable and log the raw provider code.

billing.title: Record refunds against a settled charge only
billing.intent: Create refunds in src/billing/refund.ts that reference a settled charge and cannot exceed the amount still refundable on it. The refund total is checked against the charge inside the same transaction that writes the refund row. The refund flow is described in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A refund larger than the remaining balance on the charge is rejected. A refund against an unsettled charge returns CHARGE_NOT_SETTLED.
thinking: Refunds are money leaving, so the rule is simple: only settled charges, and never more than what is left on them.
I check the remaining balance inside the transaction that inserts the refund. Checking it outside would let two refunds each pass against the same balance.
Partial refunds stack, so the balance is the settled amount minus the sum of prior refunds, not a single flag on the charge.
Checked charge.ts for how settled is represented. It is a status plus a settled_at timestamp, and I only read the status.
Noticed the refund test passed with a zero amount, which is meaningless. Added a rejection for non-positive refunds.

shell.description: Run refund balance and settlement tests

billing.approve: The balance is checked inside the transaction against prior refunds, so a stacked refund cannot exceed what was charged.

revise.reason: The over-refund check compares against the original charge amount and ignores earlier refunds on it.
revise.directive: Compare the requested amount against the remaining refundable balance, not the original charge.

billing.title: List invoices with cursor pagination by due date
billing.intent: Serve the invoice list from src/billing/queries/list-invoices.ts ordered by due date and then id, using an opaque cursor built from those two values. Offset pagination would skip rows when invoices are created during a read, so it is not used. The query shape goes in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Paging through a tenant with 250 invoices returns each invoice exactly once. A cursor from another tenant is rejected with INVALID_CURSOR.
thinking: Listing is read-heavy and runs against the replica, so the query has to be index-friendly from the start.
The cursor is due date plus id together, because due dates are not unique and paging on the date alone would drop rows at the boundary.
Encoded the cursor as base64 of a small JSON object and then checked that decoding a tampered cursor fails cleanly rather than returning a partial page.
Wondered whether the cursor should carry the tenant. It does, and a cursor from another tenant is rejected, which is cheaper than a silent empty page.
Ran the 250-invoice test with a page size of 40 to force several boundaries. Every invoice appeared exactly once across pages.
billing.approve: The composite cursor handles equal due dates, and the tenant check on the cursor closes the cross-tenant case.

revise.reason: The query orders by due date only, so invoices sharing a due date can be skipped at a page boundary.
revise.directive: Add id as a secondary order key and include it in the cursor.

billing.title: Filter subscriptions by status and renewal period
billing.intent: Add status and renewal window filters to the subscription list in src/billing/queries/list-subscriptions.ts. Filters combine with AND, and an empty filter returns all subscriptions for the tenant. The filter grammar is written into contracts/billing.md next to the list endpoint.
billing.acceptance: Filtering by status and a renewal window returns only subscriptions matching both. An unknown status value returns a 400 rather than an empty list.
thinking: Filters are where people quietly pass the wrong value, so an unknown status should be an error and not an empty result.
The status list comes from the state machine module, so the filter cannot accept a status the lifecycle does not define.
Renewal window is an inclusive start and exclusive end, which I'll state in the contract so nobody guesses.
Caught a subtle one: an empty status array means no filter in my first draft, but a caller reading it could expect no results. I made it explicit and tested both.
Spot-checked the generated SQL for the window. The index on renewal_at is used, which is what matters for a large tenant.
testOutput: ok 1 - status and window combine with AND
billing.approve: Unknown filter values fail loudly and the window boundary is written down, which removes the ambiguity I was worried about.

revise.reason: An unknown status value is ignored, so the list silently returns every subscription for the tenant.
revise.directive: Return a 400 for any status value not defined in the lifecycle table.

billing.title: Expose a read-only statement of account per customer
billing.intent: Build the statement of account in src/billing/queries/statement.ts, listing a customer's invoices, payments and refunds in date order with a running balance. It reads only and writes nothing. The statement's fields are pinned in contracts/billing.md so the customer portal can render it without guessing.
billing.acceptance: The final running balance equals the sum of invoices minus payments and refunds. The statement for a customer with no activity returns an empty list and a zero balance.
thinking: A statement is a reconciliation view, so its running balance is a check on the ledger as much as a display.
I compute the balance by walking the sorted entries, and the test asserts the final balance matches the independent sum. Two calculations agreeing is the point.
Considered caching the statement, but it changes whenever a payment lands, so the read stays live and uncached for now.
Checked the ordering on ties. Two entries on the same timestamp are ordered by their id so the running balance is stable across calls.
The zero-activity case returned null in the first draft and the portal would have crashed on it. Changed it to an empty list with a zero balance.
testOutput: ok 1 - running balance matches independent sum
ok 2 - empty customer returns zero balance
billing.approve: The balance reconciles against an independent sum and the empty case no longer crashes the portal.

revise.reason: Statement entries with equal timestamps are returned in arbitrary order, so the running balance changes between calls.
revise.directive: Order statement entries by timestamp and then by id before computing the running balance.

billing.title: Aggregate usage totals for a metered period
billing.intent: Sum recorded usage events into per-meter totals for a billing period in src/billing/usage.ts. Only events inside the period boundaries count, and late-arriving events for a closed period are dropped with a logged warning. The meter definitions are listed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Totals for a period equal the sum of in-window events per meter. An event timestamped after the period close is excluded and produces a warning.
thinking: Usage arrives out of order, so the period filter is on the event timestamp, not on the moment we received it.
Dropping a late event for a closed period is a choice I want to make visibly. It is logged so the drop is never invisible.
Summing quantities as floats would accumulate error over a month of events, so quantities are integers in the smallest unit of the meter.
Checked the period boundary against the proration rule from unit 7 so both systems agree on what counts as inside the period.
The aggregator first grouped by meter name, and a renamed meter produced two totals. Grouping by the meter id fixed it.
testOutput: ok 1 - in-window events summed per meter
ok 2 - late event for closed period dropped
ok 3 - renamed meter groups by id
billing.approve: Grouping by meter id and dropping late events visibly gives totals I can defend to the customer.

revise.reason: Late usage events for a closed period are added to the total and change an invoice that was already finalized.
revise.directive: Exclude events timestamped after the period close and log a warning for each one.

billing.title: Publish invoice finalized events through the outbox
billing.intent: Write an invoice.finalized event into the outbox in the same transaction as the finalize step, using src/billing/events.ts for the payload type. The separate publisher in src/billing/outbox-publisher.ts reads the outbox and forwards it. The event schema is documented in contracts/billing.md for analytics and notifications.
billing.acceptance: The outbox row exists if and only if the invoice is finalized in the same transaction. The published payload validates against the event schema.
thinking: Writing to the outbox inside the finalize transaction is what stops us from announcing an invoice that was rolled back.
I considered publishing directly after commit. That reintroduces the dual-write problem, so the outbox row is the single write and the publisher is a separate loop.
The payload carries the invoice id, tenant id and totals, and nothing that would need a second lookup on the consumer side.
Checked the publisher's ordering guarantee. Events for one invoice are delivered in insert order because I key the outbox by invoice id.
Injected a failure after the outbox insert in a test to confirm the invoice rolls back with it. Both rows vanished together, which is correct.
testOutput: ok 1 - outbox row written with finalize
billing.approve: The outbox write shares the finalize transaction, so an event can never describe an invoice that was rolled back.

revise.reason: The event payload is typed as invoice.created, so consumers subscribed to finalized invoices receive the wrong type.
revise.directive: Set the event type to invoice.finalized and update the payload schema to match.

billing.title: Accept provider webhooks after signature checks
billing.intent: Handle incoming payment provider webhooks in src/billing/webhooks/provider-webhook.ts, verifying the HMAC signature and the timestamp window before any payload is parsed. A webhook that fails verification is rejected with a 401 and never reaches the reconciler. The accepted event types are listed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A webhook with a bad signature returns 401 and writes nothing. A replayed webhook older than five minutes is rejected.
thinking: Webhooks are an unauthenticated door by default, so verification has to come before parsing, or a malformed body could get into the parser unchecked.
The signature is computed over the raw body bytes. Re-serializing the parsed JSON would change whitespace and break every valid signature, so I read the raw buffer.
Added a five minute timestamp window to stop replays. I thought about a nonce store, but the window is enough for the threat here and avoids a table.
Compared signatures with a constant time comparison, since a plain string equality leaks timing information.
The first test passed with a correct signature over a modified body, which should have been impossible. The test was signing the parsed object, not the raw body, so I fixed the test.
testOutput: ok 3 - valid signed raw body accepted
billing.approve: Verification runs on the raw body before parsing and the comparison is constant time, which is the right order for an open endpoint.

revise.reason: The signature is compared with plain string equality, which leaks timing information to an attacker.
revise.directive: Replace the string equality check with a timing-safe comparison of the two signature buffers.

billing.title: Expose entitlement snapshots to booking and catalog
billing.intent: Provide a read-only entitlement snapshot in src/billing/entitlements.ts that tells booking and catalog which plan features a tenant currently holds. The snapshot is versioned so a consumer can detect a stale copy. The snapshot fields are fixed in contracts/billing.md as a cross-system contract.
billing.acceptance: A tenant on an expired plan gets a snapshot with the feature flags off. The snapshot version increases on every change to the entitlement set.
thinking: Booking should not ask billing whether a feature is on for every request. A snapshot that consumers cache keeps the hot path off our database.
The version is a monotonically increasing integer on the entitlement row, so a consumer can tell a newer snapshot from an older one without comparing contents.
Expiry is evaluated against the clock at read time, so a plan that expires at midnight is off immediately, not after the next sweep.
Considered sending full snapshots as events, but the contract says consumers pull, so I kept this read-only and version-stamped.
Checked the contract file: booking already documented a feature key format, and I matched it exactly instead of inventing a second spelling.
testOutput: ok 1 - expired plan yields features off
billing.approve: The snapshot is versioned and matches booking's feature keys, which is the whole job of this contract.

revise.reason: Entitlements for a plan in past_due status are still reported as active until the expiry date passes.
revise.directive: Report features off for any plan whose status is not active, regardless of expiry.

billing.title: Reconcile provider webhook events against local charges
billing.intent: Match each verified provider event against the local charge attempt in src/billing/reconcile.ts and apply the state change it describes. An event for an unknown charge is parked rather than dropped, so a late-arriving charge can be matched later. Reconciliation outcomes are described in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A succeeded event moves the matching attempt to settled exactly once even if the event is delivered twice. An event with no matching charge is parked and visible in the reconcile queue.
thinking: Providers deliver events out of order and more than once, so reconcile has to be a function of the current local state, not of the event arrival order.
An event for a charge we have not yet recorded is common when the provider is faster than our write. Parking it means the match can happen on the next pass.
I want a duplicate delivery to be a no-op. The settled transition checks the current status first and returns without writing if it is already settled.
Checked how the attempt status is stored and found a race between two deliveries. A conditional update on the expected prior status closes it.
Wrote the parked-event test first, and it failed because the handler dropped unknown events silently. Changed it to park them.
testOutput: ok 1 - duplicate succeeded event settles once
billing.approve: Duplicate deliveries are a no-op and unknown charges are parked rather than lost, which is the behavior I wanted from reconcile.

revise.reason: Events for charges not yet recorded are dropped without a trace, so a late charge never settles.
revise.directive: Park events with no matching attempt in the reconcile queue instead of returning early.

billing.title: Guard invoice finalization against concurrent edits
billing.intent: Make finalize in src/billing/finalize.ts compare the invoice version it read against the stored version before writing, and reject the call when another writer got there first. The version column is added to the aggregate in src/billing/invoice.ts. Callers see the conflict as a documented error in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Two concurrent finalize calls on the same invoice result in one success and one VERSION_CONFLICT. A finalize that succeeds increments the version by one.
thinking: Finalize is the moment the invoice becomes immutable, so two writers racing into it is the worst case and needs a real guard.
Optimistic locking on a version column is simpler than a row lock held across the provider call, and the lock would be held far too long here.
The version check and the status write are one conditional update. Checking then writing in two statements would reintroduce the race.
I had the version increment in the wrong place and the second writer still succeeded. Moved the increment into the same statement as the status change.
The concurrency test uses two real connections, because a single connection serializes the calls and proves nothing.
testOutput: ok 1 - one finalize wins under race
billing.approve: The conditional update closes the race in one statement and the test uses two real connections to prove it.

revise.reason: The finalize write does not check the version it read, so a concurrent edit can be overwritten.
revise.directive: Use a conditional update that matches the version read at the start of finalize.

billing.title: Deduplicate charge requests with idempotency keys
billing.intent: Store the caller's idempotency key with the charge in src/billing/idempotency.ts so a retried request returns the original result instead of charging again. Keys are scoped to the tenant and expire after 24 hours. The header name and the replay behavior are fixed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Two requests with the same key and body return the same charge id and create one attempt. The same key with a different body returns IDEMPOTENCY_MISMATCH.
thinking: Idempotency is the guard against a network retry double charging a card, so this is probably the most important unit in the write path.
The key alone is not enough. I also store a hash of the body, so reusing a key for a different charge is rejected rather than replayed.
The key is scoped to the tenant, otherwise two tenants could collide on a common client-generated value.
Thought about storing the full response, but the charge id is enough to rebuild it, and it avoids a second copy of the response that could drift.
Hit a case where the first request failed before writing anything. The key was still stored, so the retry would be wrongly rejected. I now store the key only after the attempt row exists.
testOutput: ok 1 - same key and body replays result
ok 2 - same key different body rejected
ok 4 - failed first attempt allows retry
billing.approve: Replay is keyed on tenant and body hash and a failed first attempt can still be retried, which is the safe behavior.

revise.reason: The body hash uses JSON.stringify directly, so key order changes the hash and an identical retry is rejected.
revise.finding: Body hash depends on key order
revise.directive: Hash a canonical serialization of the body with sorted keys.

billing.title: Retry failed charge captures with bounded backoff
billing.intent: Retry transient capture failures in src/billing/retry.ts with exponential backoff capped at five attempts and a maximum total delay of two minutes. Only envelopes marked retryable are retried, and each attempt is recorded on the charge. The retry policy is stated in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A retryable failure is retried up to five times and then parked. A non-retryable failure is never retried.
thinking: A retry loop without a cap is how a single bad charge keeps a worker busy forever, so the cap is the first thing I write.
Backoff is exponential with jitter. Without jitter a burst of failed captures would all retry together and hit the provider in a spike.
Only retryable envelopes from unit 10 enter the loop. A non-retryable failure short-circuits, which the test checks by counting provider calls.
Thought about retrying inside the provider client, but the attempt must be recorded on the charge, so the retry lives in the charge path where the record is.
Ran the test with a fake clock. The total delay came out to 1 minute 50 seconds, which is inside the two minute cap, so the bound holds.

edit.new: const delay = Math.min(2 ** attempt * 1000 + jitter(), MAX_DELAY_MS);

testOutput: ok 1 - retryable failure parked after five attempts
ok 3 - total delay under two minutes
billing.approve: Jitter and the two minute cap are in place, and the test counts provider calls so the non-retryable case is proven.

revise.reason: The backoff delay has no upper bound, so a late attempt can wait far longer than the two minute budget.
revise.directive: Clamp each computed delay to the maximum delay constant before scheduling the next attempt.

billing.title: Lock subscription rows during renewal sweeps
billing.intent: Make the renewal sweep in src/billing/renewal-sweep.ts claim due subscriptions with a row lock and SKIP LOCKED, so two sweep workers never bill the same subscription. A worker that crashes mid-sweep releases its locks when its transaction ends. The sweep's ordering guarantees are noted in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Two concurrent sweeps bill each due subscription exactly once. A subscription already locked by one worker is skipped by the other rather than waited on.
thinking: The sweep runs on several workers in production, so the claim has to be exclusive, or we bill a customer twice on the same renewal.
SKIP LOCKED means the second worker moves on instead of queueing behind the first. Waiting would make the sweep serial and slow for no benefit.
The lock is released by the transaction ending, so a crashed worker cannot hold a subscription forever. I verified this by killing the process mid-batch in a test.
Considered an advisory lock per tenant, but per row is finer grained and keeps one slow tenant from blocking the others.
The first version selected the due rows and then locked them in a second query, which left a window. Merged both into one statement.
testOutput: ok 2 - locked row skipped not waited on
billing.approve: The claim is one statement with SKIP LOCKED, so two workers cannot bill the same renewal and neither blocks on the other.

revise.reason: The sweep selects due subscriptions without a lock, so two workers can both bill the same renewal.
revise.directive: Lock the due subscription rows with SKIP LOCKED in the same statement that selects them.

billing.title: Backfill invoice totals from legacy line item rows
billing.intent: Populate the new total column on historical invoices from their legacy line item rows, using the backfill script in src/billing/backfill/invoice-totals.ts. The migration in migrations/0024_backfill_invoice_totals.sql only adds the column. The backfill runs in batches and is idempotent so an interrupted run can be restarted.
billing.acceptance: After the backfill every invoice total equals the sum of its legacy lines. Running the backfill twice changes nothing on the second run.
thinking: A backfill that is not idempotent is a trap on a live table, so the first thing I check is that a second run writes no rows.
I split the schema change from the data change. The migration only adds the nullable column, and the backfill fills it in batches afterwards.
Batches are keyed by invoice id and not by offset, so a restart resumes from the last id without re-reading finished rows.
Verified the totals against the legacy sums on a sample of historical invoices before trusting the query. Two invoices had a voided line that the legacy sum included, so I excluded voided lines.
Wrote the script to log progress every ten thousand rows so a long run is observable from the outside.

edit.new: WHERE total IS NULL AND voided = false

testOutput: ok 1 - totals match legacy line sums
ok 2 - second run writes no rows
billing.approve: The backfill is idempotent and excludes voided lines, which is what the legacy sums should have been doing.

revise.reason: The backfill sums voided legacy lines, so totals on a few invoices are higher than the amount actually billed.
revise.directive: Exclude voided legacy lines from the backfilled total.

billing.title: Migrate stored card tokens to the vault format
billing.intent: Move stored card tokens from the old column format into the vault format in src/billing/vault-migration.ts. The schema change is in migrations/0025_card_token_vault.sql and runs before the rewrite. Tokens are re-wrapped in place and the original ciphertext is never logged.
billing.acceptance: Every stored token decrypts under the new vault key after the migration. A dry run reports the count of tokens to migrate without writing.
thinking: Card tokens are the most sensitive data in this system, so the migration is written to be re-runnable and to log counts only.
A dry run goes first. It reports how many tokens will be rewritten and writes nothing, and I want the number before anyone flips the flag.
The re-wrap decrypts with the old key and encrypts with the new one in the same step. The plaintext exists in memory only for the duration of that call.
Checked the logging path. An error message can include the token, so the error handler logs the token id and never the value.
Found one token that failed to decrypt under either key. Rather than skip it, the migration stops and reports the id, since a silent skip would lose a customer's card.

shell.description: Run card token vault migration tests

testOutput: ok 2 - rewrapped tokens decrypt under new key
billing.approve: Dry run, re-runnable rewrap, and a halt on any undecryptable token are the right safeguards for card data.

revise.reason: The migration error log includes the raw token value, which would write card material to the log.
revise.directive: Log only the token id in the rewrap failure path and remove the token value from the log call.

billing.title: Add a tax rate snapshot column to invoices
billing.intent: Store the tax rate applied to each invoice as a snapshot on the invoice row, so a later rate change does not alter a finalized invoice. The column is added in migrations/0026_invoice_tax_snapshot.sql and written in src/billing/invoice.ts when the invoice is finalized. The snapshot rule is recorded in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A finalized invoice keeps its original tax rate after the tenant rate changes. New invoices populate the snapshot column on creation.
thinking: Tax rates change, and a finalized invoice must not change with them, so the rate is copied onto the row at finalize time rather than looked up later.
The column is nullable in the migration because existing rows have no snapshot. Those rows are not rewritten here, since the backfill for them is a separate decision.
I want the rate stored as a decimal string, not a float, so the value round trips without drift through the database.
Checked finalize to find the exact point the rate is read. It has to be read in the same transaction that sets the status, or a rate change between the two could split them.
Ran the test that changes the tenant rate after finalize. The stored snapshot kept the old value, which is the outcome the contract promises.
testOutput: ok 1 - finalized invoice keeps original rate
ok 3 - rate read inside finalize transaction
billing.approve: The rate is frozen at finalize inside the same transaction, so a rate change cannot split an invoice from its tax.

revise.reason: The tax rate is read outside the finalize transaction, so a rate change between the two steps can split status from tax.
revise.directive: Read the tenant tax rate inside the finalize transaction and store it as the snapshot in the same write.

billing.title: Backfill ledger entries for already settled payments
billing.intent: Create ledger entries for payments that settled before the ledger existed, using src/billing/ledger.ts and the backfill in migrations/0027_ledger_backfill.sql. Each historical payment gets exactly one debit and one credit entry. The backfill is verified against the settled payment totals before the ledger is trusted.
billing.acceptance: The sum of ledger debits equals the sum of settled payments for each tenant. Re-running the migration does not insert duplicate entries.
thinking: A ledger is only useful if it balances, so the backfill is judged by whether its totals match the settled payments and nothing else.
The migration inserts entries with a deterministic id derived from the payment id, which makes a re-run a no-op on conflict.
Each payment produces one debit and one credit with the same amount, and the test asserts that pairing for every settled row.
I initially planned to backfill refunds as well. Refund history is a separate migration that depends on this one, so I kept it out of this unit.
Ran the balance check against the staging snapshot and the debit total was short by one payment. The payment had a zero amount and was filtered out, which is correct, but the check had counted it.
testOutput: ok 1 - debits equal settled totals per tenant
billing.approve: Deterministic ids make the backfill re-runnable and the balance check ties it back to the settled payments.

revise.reason: Ledger ids are random uuids, so re-running the backfill inserts a second copy of every historical entry.
revise.directive: Derive each ledger entry id deterministically from the payment id and entry side.

billing.title: Emit a metric for dunning retry outcomes
billing.intent: Count each dunning retry by outcome in src/billing/metrics.ts, with the outcome label drawn from a closed set so dashboards never see an unknown value. The counter is incremented in the dunning loop in src/billing/dunning.ts. The metric name and labels are documented in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Every dunning retry increments exactly one outcome counter. An outcome outside the closed set fails to compile.
thinking: Metrics are only useful if the label values are finite, so the outcome is a closed union and not a free string.
The increment sits in the loop right after the outcome is decided, so a retry that fails before deciding is counted under its own error label.
Thought about a histogram for retry latency, but the question on the dashboard is how many succeed, not how long, so a counter is the honest choice.
Checked the metric name against the existing convention and matched the billing prefix on every series.
The test forces each outcome and asserts exactly one increment, which catches a path that double counts.
testOutput: ok 3 - each outcome counted exactly once
billing.approve: A closed outcome set keeps the dashboard labels finite and the test proves each retry is counted once.

revise.reason: The dunning loop increments the counter twice when a retry is exhausted, inflating the exhausted series.
revise.directive: Increment the outcome counter once, after the outcome is decided, in the exhausted branch.

billing.title: Trace each charge attempt across the provider call
billing.intent: Wrap every provider call made from src/billing/charge.ts in a trace span that carries the attempt id, the tenant and the provider's request id. Spans end in a finally block so a thrown error still closes them. The span names and attributes are listed in contracts/billing.md for the operations team.
billing.acceptance: Each charge attempt produces one span with the attempt id attribute, including when the provider call throws. No span carries the card number or token.
thinking: A trace is only useful if it is closed on every path, so the span end goes in a finally block around the provider call.
I attach the provider request id as an attribute after the response, not before, since it does not exist until then.
Card data must never leak into a span attribute, so the tracing helper takes an explicit allow list of fields rather than serializing the whole attempt.
Checked whether the attempt id is a safe attribute. It is an internal uuid with no customer data, so it is fine to include.
The test throws from the mocked provider and asserts the span still ended. Without the finally, the span would stay open and show as a leak.

shell.description: Run charge attempt trace span tests

testOutput: ok 1 - span ends when provider throws
ok 3 - no card fields in attributes
billing.approve: The allow list keeps card data out of spans and the finally block closes the span on the error path too.

revise.reason: The span attributes accept an open record, so a caller can attach the full attempt including the token.
revise.directive: Restrict span attributes to an explicit allow list of identifier fields.

billing.title: Log structured diagnostics for failed invoice runs
billing.intent: When an invoice run fails for a tenant, emit one structured diagnostic record from src/billing/diagnostics.ts with the run id, the failing stage and the error code, and no free text from the customer. The run driver in src/billing/invoice-run.ts calls it once per failure. The record fields are listed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A failed run produces exactly one diagnostic record with a stage from the closed set. The record contains no customer name, email or address.
thinking: Diagnostics go to logs that many people read, so the record is built from identifiers and codes only, never from customer text.
The stage is a closed union matching the run's phases, so an operator can filter on it without guessing spellings.
Calling the diagnostic from one place, the run driver, means a failure in a helper cannot emit a second record for the same run.
Looked at the old error path, which logged the whole invoice object. That is exactly what leaked customer fields, so I removed it.
The test feeds a customer name into the input and asserts it is absent from the emitted record, which is the property that matters.

edit.new: log.error({ runId, stage, code }, 'invoice run failed');

shell.description: Run invoice run diagnostic record tests

testOutput: ok 1 - one record per failed run
ok 3 - no customer fields in record
billing.approve: One record per failure, built only from identifiers and codes, is the diagnostic I would want on call.

revise.reason: The failure log serializes the whole invoice object, which includes the customer name and billing address.
revise.directive: Log only the run id, stage and error code in the diagnostic record.

billing.title: Batch invoice generation to bound database load
billing.intent: Generate invoices for a run in fixed-size batches in src/billing/batching.ts so one large tenant cannot hold a long transaction open. Each batch commits on its own and the run driver resumes from the last committed batch. The batch size and its reasoning are stated in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A run over 10,000 subscriptions commits in batches of 500 and resumes correctly after a simulated crash. No single transaction covers more than one batch.
thinking: A single transaction over ten thousand subscriptions would hold locks for minutes, so I want the batch boundary to be a hard limit in code.
The batch size is a constant of 500 for now. I'll make it configurable only when a measurement shows it needs to change.
Each batch commits and records the last id it finished. A crash resumes from that id, so the batch that was in flight is simply redone.
Considered paging by offset, but a concurrent insert would shift the window and skip a subscription. Keyset paging by id avoids that.
The first version forgot to reset the transaction between batches and two batches shared one. The test that counts open transactions caught it.

edit.new: const batch = await nextBatch(db, cursor, BATCH_SIZE);

testOutput: ok 1 - run commits in batches of 500
ok 2 - resume after crash skips committed batches
billing.approve: Keyset batches with a commit per batch bound the lock time and the resume point is obvious from the code.

revise.reason: The batch size is hardcoded at five thousand, which holds locks long enough to block the renewal sweep.
revise.finding: Batch size too large for locks
revise.directive: Set the invoice batch size to 500 and make the batch its own transaction.

billing.title: Enforce per-tenant caps on invoices per run
billing.intent: Limit how many invoices one tenant can generate in a single run, using the cap in src/billing/limits.ts and the run driver in src/billing/invoice-run.ts. A tenant over the cap is deferred to the next run and recorded, not failed. The cap value and its reasoning are documented in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A tenant with more invoices than the cap generates exactly the cap in the first run and the remainder in the next. Other tenants in the same run are unaffected.
thinking: A single very large tenant should not starve everyone else's run, so the cap is per tenant and is applied before a batch is built.
Deferral is the choice I want, not failure. A tenant over the cap is not wrong, it is just big, so the remainder waits for the next run.
The cap is read from configuration so an operator can raise it for a specific tenant without a deploy.
I checked whether deferring could ever drop an invoice. The deferred set is persisted with the run, so the next run picks it up explicitly.
Ran the starvation test with one large tenant and two small ones. The small tenants finished in the first run, which is the property we wanted.
testOutput: ok 1 - tenant over cap defers remainder
ok 2 - deferred set persisted with run
billing.approve: Deferral with a persisted set means the large tenant is slowed down, not dropped, and the others keep their schedule.

revise.reason: Over-cap invoices are marked failed instead of deferred, which triggers a dunning notice to the customer.
revise.directive: Persist over-cap invoices as deferred to the next run instead of marking them failed.

billing.title: Cache active price books with a short expiry
billing.intent: Cache the active price book for each tenant in src/billing/price-book-cache.ts with a five minute expiry, so charge creation does not read the price table on every call. An explicit invalidate runs on price book publish. The cache behavior and its staleness bound are written in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A price book change is visible to new charges within five minutes, and immediately after publish invalidates the entry. A cache miss reads the database exactly once.
thinking: Price lookups are on the hot path of every charge, so a short cache is worth it, but the staleness has to be a number we can state.
Five minutes is the bound I'll document. A tenant that publishes a price book sees the change at once because publish invalidates the entry directly.
Two concurrent misses for the same tenant would read the table twice, so the cache coalesces in-flight loads into one promise.
I double checked that the expiry is measured from load time and not from last read, since a sliding expiry would never refresh a busy tenant's prices.
The coalescing test found a bug where a failed load was cached as an empty book. Failures now evict and are not stored.

shell.description: Run price book cache expiry tests

testOutput: ok 1 - change visible within five minutes
billing.approve: Expiry measured from load, coalesced loads and no cached failures give a staleness bound I can state plainly.

revise.reason: A failed price book load is cached as an empty book, so charges are priced at zero until the entry expires.
revise.directive: Evict the cache entry when a load fails and never store the failure result.

billing.title: Gate the new proration engine behind a flag
billing.intent: Route proration through the new engine only when a tenant's flag is on, keeping the old path in src/billing/proration.ts for everyone else. The flag check lives in src/billing/flags.ts and defaults to off. The flag name and rollout order are described in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: With the flag off the output matches the old engine exactly. With the flag on, the new engine is called and its result is returned.
thinking: The new proration engine is a risk to every plan change, so it goes out behind a flag and the flag defaults to off.
The test runs the same input through both paths and asserts equal output with the flag off. That is the proof that the gate changes nothing by default.
I want the flag read once per request and passed down, not read inside the calculation, so one request cannot see two different answers.
Thought about a percentage rollout, but that is a decision for later. For now the flag is per tenant and an operator sets it by hand.
Found that the new engine rounds half up where the old one rounded half even. The flag test caught the mismatch, and I'll fix it before any tenant turns the flag on.
testOutput: ok 1 - flag off matches old engine
ok 2 - flag on calls new engine
ok 3 - flag read once per request
billing.approve: The gate defaults to off and the equality test shows the old path is untouched, which is the safe way to ship this.

revise.reason: The proration flag defaults to on, so every tenant is switched to the unreleased engine without an operator choosing it.
revise.directive: Default the proration engine flag to off so tenants opt in explicitly.

billing.title: Write the rollback path for a failed cutover
billing.intent: Write the rollback in src/billing/rollback.ts that returns charges and invoices to the pre-cutover path if the new billing write path fails its health check. Rollback markers are recorded in migrations/0035_rollback_markers.sql so an operator can see which rows were written under which path. The rollback procedure is written up in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A failed health check reverts the write path flag and records a rollback marker. Rows written after the marker are identifiable by path version.
thinking: A cutover is only safe if the way back is written and tested, so the rollback is a first class function, not a runbook step.
Rows written under the new path carry a path version, so a rollback leaves a clear boundary and nobody has to guess which rows to reconcile.
The marker is inserted before the flag flips, so if the process dies between the two steps the marker still exists to tell an operator what happened.
I considered rolling back by deleting the new rows. That is destructive and unnecessary, so the rows stay and are simply tagged.
Ran the failed health check test and the flag reverted, but the marker was written after the flip. Swapped the order so the marker always comes first.
testOutput: ok 1 - failed health check reverts flag
ok 3 - rows tagged by path version
billing.approve: Rollback tags rows instead of deleting them and the marker goes down before the flip, so a crash mid-rollback is still explainable.

revise.reason: The rollback deletes the rows written under the new path, which destroys the evidence needed to reconcile the cutover.
revise.directive: Tag the rows written under the new path instead of deleting them during rollback.

billing.title: Apply retention rules to expired payment records
billing.intent: Purge or anonymize payment records past their retention window in src/billing/retention.ts, keeping the ledger totals intact. Records under legal hold are excluded by a check that runs before any delete. The retention periods per record type are published in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: A payment past retention is anonymized and its ledger amount is preserved. A record under legal hold is never touched, and the sweep reports the count it skipped.
thinking: Retention is destructive by nature, so the default is anonymize and the delete path is reserved for records with nothing else depending on them.
Ledger amounts are kept because the totals are what auditors need. Only the personal fields are cleared, so the arithmetic still reconciles.
The legal hold check runs before anything is changed, and a held record is counted and skipped rather than silently passed over.
I want the sweep to be idempotent. Anonymizing an already anonymized record is a no-op, which the test covers by running the sweep twice.
Checked the retention periods against the contract. The contract says seven years for ledger, and I used that value instead of a number from memory.

edit.new: await db('payments').where({ id }).update({ customer_name: null, email: null });

testOutput: ok 3 - legal hold skipped and counted
ok 4 - second sweep is a no-op
billing.approve: Anonymize-first with ledger amounts kept and holds checked before any change is the conservative choice I would make.

revise.reason: The retention sweep hard deletes payment rows, which removes ledger amounts the auditors still need.
revise.directive: Anonymize the personal fields and keep the ledger amount instead of deleting the payment row.

billing.title: Record an audit trail for manual credit adjustments
billing.intent: Write an audit record for every manual credit adjustment made by an operator, in src/billing/audit.ts, with the actor, the amount, the reason code and the previous balance. The credit path in src/billing/credits.ts appends the record in the same transaction as the balance change. The audit record fields are fixed in contracts/billing.md.
billing.acceptance: Every manual credit writes exactly one audit record in the same transaction. A credit without a reason code is rejected before any write.
thinking: A manual credit is a person changing money, so every one leaves a record, and the record has to commit or fail with the change.
The audit row is written in the same transaction as the balance update. Writing it after commit would allow a balance change with no trail if the process died between the two.
The reason code is required and comes from a closed list, so a credit cannot be made with a note like 'fix' that tells an auditor nothing.
I stored the previous balance on the audit record as well as the new one, so the change can be checked without replaying the whole ledger.
Ran the credit path with the audit insert forced to fail. The balance change rolled back too, which is the atomicity I was after.
testOutput: ok 1 - credit writes one audit record
ok 2 - audit failure rolls back balance
billing.approve: The audit row commits with the balance change and the reason code list means every credit can be explained later.

revise.reason: The credit path accepts any free text as the reason, so the audit trail cannot be filtered to a known set of causes.
revise.directive: Validate the reason against the closed reason code list and reject anything else before writing.

notifications.title: Define the delivery channel table schema
notifications.intent: Create the delivery channel table that holds one row per tenant and channel kind, with an enabled flag and provider settings as jsonb. Use a composite primary key of tenant_id and channel_kind so every lookup from src/notifications/channels/registry.ts stays tenant-scoped. Record the table's guarantees in contracts/notifications.md so booking and billing know what they may rely on.
notifications.acceptance: The migration applies cleanly on an empty database and rolls back to nothing. Inserting a second row with the same tenant and channel kind fails with a unique violation.
thinking: The first decision is the key shape. A row per tenant and channel kind is the natural grain, and the composite key makes the tenant part impossible to forget in a query.
I was going to store provider settings in separate columns, one per provider. That falls apart the moment a fourth provider appears, so jsonb with a validated shape in schema.ts is the better trade.
Before writing the migration I checked whether the identity system already defines a tenant_id type. It does, as a uuid, so I reuse that instead of inventing a text column that would drift.
The down migration is trivial because nothing reads this table yet. I still wrote it so the migration runner can round trip in the test.
I want the schema test to hit the unique constraint directly, because a model-level check would pass even if the database accepted duplicates.
notifications.approve: The composite key and the unique-constraint test are exactly the guardrail this table needed.

revise.reason: The migration adds the push kind to the enum but the contract still lists only two channel kinds.
revise.directive: Update the channel kind list in contracts/notifications.md to match channelKinds.

notifications.title: Scaffold the dispatch module and public exports
notifications.intent: Create the src/notifications/dispatch/ folder with an index.ts that exports only the command, query and types other systems may import. Keep provider adapters and the outbox writer private to the folder so src/notifications/index.ts stays the single door. Mention the export list in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Importing from src/notifications/index.ts compiles and exposes sendMessage and getMessage. A lint rule fails when another system imports a file under dispatch/internal directly.
thinking: The scaffold is mostly a question of what goes into the public barrel. I want the smallest surface that booking and billing can call, so I start with two functions and their types.
I first wrote the barrel to re-export everything from dispatch, and then I noticed that would leak the provider adapter types into other systems. I narrowed it.

There is a lint rule in the repo that forbids deep imports across systems. I checked its config to confirm the pattern matches src/notifications/dispatch/internal/ and it does, so no custom rule is needed.
The export test is a short static check rather than a runtime one. It reads the barrel's named exports and compares them to a fixed list, which catches accidental additions in review.
I left the internal folder empty for now. Creating placeholder files would only add noise until the provider work lands.

notifications.approve: A narrow barrel with a deep-import check is how the boundary stays honest.

revise.reason: The barrel still exports the outbox writer, which other systems should never call directly.
revise.directive: Remove the outbox writer from the re-exports in src/notifications/index.ts.

notifications.title: Load per-tenant channel settings from config
notifications.intent: Read each tenant's channel defaults from the tenancy config and parse them in src/notifications/config/channel-settings.ts. Fall back to the platform defaults when a tenant has no override, and reject unknown channel kinds at load time. Document the precedence order in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A tenant with an override gets its value and a tenant without one gets the platform default. An unknown channel kind throws a ConfigError naming the tenant.
thinking: The settings loader sits between the tenancy config and the channel registry, so its job is mainly precedence. Tenant override first, platform default second, and no third layer.
I wanted to load settings lazily on first use, but that would hide a bad config until a message is sent. Loading eagerly at startup fails loud, which matches how the other systems treat config.

The defaults file exports a frozen object. I double checked that the tenancy loader returns plain objects, because a frozen default merged with a plain override would otherwise throw in strict mode on write.
I added the ConfigError with the tenant id in the message so the on-call engineer sees which tenant is misconfigured without digging.
The test covers an unknown kind but not an empty override object, which should simply use defaults. I added that case before calling the unit done.
notifications.approve: Loading eagerly and failing loud on an unknown kind is the right call for config.

revise.reason: The loader silently accepts a null override, which means a tenant can be disabled by accident.
revise.finding: Null override disables a channel silently
revise.directive: Treat a null override as absent and fall back to the platform default.

notifications.title: Derive tenant-scoped keys for dedupe records
notifications.intent: Build the dedupe key from tenant id, recipient id, template id and a caller-supplied dedupe token, in src/notifications/dedupe/key.ts. Hash the components with a fixed separator so distinct inputs cannot collide. Note the key format in contracts/notifications.md because replays depend on it.
notifications.acceptance: Two requests with the same components produce the same key, and changing any one component changes it. Keys are 64 hex characters.
thinking: A dedupe key that collides across tenants would be a silent data leak, so the tenant id goes first and is never optional.
My first draft joined the parts with a colon. Then I realized a recipient id could contain a colon, and two different inputs could produce the same string. I switched to length-prefixed encoding.
The hash is sha256 over the encoded string. I confirmed that node:crypto is already a dependency in the package, so I am not adding anything new.
I wrote a property-style test that generates random components and checks that changing one field always changes the key. It runs a few hundred cases in well under a second.
The contract note matters here because a future change to the encoding would break replays of messages already queued. I wrote the format version into the key prefix so a change is detectable.
notifications.approve: Length-prefixing closes the collision hole, and the property test is what proves it.

revise.reason: The key omits the template version, so a template edit would reuse the dedupe slot of the old body.
revise.finding: Template version missing from dedupe key
revise.directive: Add the template version as a fourth component in buildDedupeKey.

notifications.title: Model a recipient as a validated value object
notifications.intent: Represent a message recipient as a branded value in src/notifications/domain/recipient.ts, with separate constructors for email addresses and phone numbers. Validation happens once at construction, so downstream code never re-checks the address. Describe the accepted formats in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Constructing a recipient from a malformed address returns a typed error and never throws. A valid address round trips through toString unchanged.
thinking: The value object is where the illegal states get shut out. A recipient is either a verified-format email or a normalized phone number, and nothing else reaches the send path.
I considered a single regex for both kinds, but the two formats have different normalization rules. Two small constructors read more clearly than one clever function.
Phone normalization to E.164 needs a library, and I checked the repo for an existing one before adding it. The catalog system already uses one, so I import that rather than adding a second.
The branded type needs a unique symbol so that a plain string cannot be passed where a recipient is expected. I verified the compiler rejects that with a tsc check in the test file.
I deliberately left mailbox-level validation out of scope, since we cannot know a mailbox exists without sending. The contract says so explicitly.

edit.new: export function emailRecipient(raw: string): Result<Recipient, InvalidRecipient> {

notifications.approve: Validating once at construction and returning a typed result keeps the send path clean.

revise.reason: The phone constructor accepts numbers without a country code and stores them ambiguously.
revise.finding: Phone numbers stored without country code
revise.directive: Reject any phone input that does not normalize to E.164 with a country code.

notifications.title: Enforce quiet hours before any send occurs
notifications.intent: Check each recipient's quiet-hours window against the tenant's local time in src/notifications/policy/quiet-hours.ts before a message is queued.
