A send that falls inside the window is deferred to the window's end rather than dropped. Note the deferral rule in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A send requested at 22:30 local time with a 21:00 to 08:00 window is scheduled for 08:00. A send outside the window is queued immediately.
thinking: Quiet hours are a policy decision, so they belong in the policy folder and not inside the dispatcher. The dispatcher should only ask whether a time is allowed.
The tricky part is windows that cross midnight. I wrote the check as a wrap-around comparison and then tested 23:00 and 02:00 explicitly to make sure both sides of midnight work.
Time zones are the real risk. I use the tenant's configured zone through Intl and not the server's local clock, because the server runs in UTC and that would be wrong for every tenant outside it.

I first implemented deferral as a drop, which is what the spec literally said. Then I reread the spec and the intent is that the message still arrives, just later, so I changed it to a scheduled time.
The test uses a fixed clock injected through the constructor. That keeps the test deterministic and avoids any sleeping.

edit.new: if (inWindow(now, window)) return { action: 'defer', until: window.end };

notifications.approve: Deferring instead of dropping matches what the tenant actually wants, and the midnight cases are covered.

revise.reason: The window end is computed in the server zone, so deferred sends land at the wrong local hour.
revise.directive: Compute the window end in the tenant time zone before returning the deferral.

notifications.title: Represent a message template with typed placeholders
notifications.intent: Define a template as a list of literal segments and named placeholders in src/notifications/templates/model.ts. Placeholder names are a closed union so a typo fails at compile time. Keep the template format documented in contracts/notifications.md for the catalog system authors.
notifications.acceptance: Parsing a template with an unknown placeholder name fails with a typed error. Rendering with all placeholders supplied produces the expected string.
thinking: A template is data, not code, so I refuse to evaluate anything inside braces. The parser only recognizes a fixed set of placeholder names.
I wrote the placeholder names as a const array and derived the union type from it. Adding a new placeholder then means editing one list, and the compiler finds every switch that needs updating.
The parser is a small state machine over characters. I considered a regex, but a regex would make the error positions useless when an author writes an unclosed brace.
Rendering a template with a missing value should not silently emit an empty string. I made the render function require every placeholder, which pushes the check to the caller at compile time.
I added a fixture template that mirrors the booking confirmation copy so the test exercises a realistic shape and not just toy input.

edit.new:
export const placeholderNames = ['recipientName', 'startsAt', 'resourceName'] as const;
export type PlaceholderName = (typeof placeholderNames)[number];

shell.description: Run template parser and render tests

notifications.approve: A closed placeholder union and an error position on unclosed braces is exactly what authors need.

revise.reason: The parser accepts nested braces and produces a template that renders the inner text twice.
revise.directive: Reject nested braces in parseTemplate with a positioned error.

notifications.title: Reject sends to unsubscribed recipients explicitly
notifications.intent: Check the suppression list before queueing any message in src/notifications/policy/suppression.ts, and return a typed rejection that names the reason. Suppression is keyed by recipient and channel, so an email opt-out does not block SMS. Document the rejection codes in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A send to a suppressed recipient on the same channel returns a suppressed rejection. A send on a different channel to the same recipient is accepted.
thinking: The suppression check has to happen before anything is written, so a suppressed send never reaches the outbox. That makes it a precondition, not a post-filter.
I initially keyed suppression by recipient alone. Then I realized a customer who replies STOP to SMS may still want email, so the key must include the channel.
The rejection is a value, not an exception, because callers in booking need to show a reason to a user. Throwing would force them to catch and reshape the error.
I checked how the identity system records consent and it stores it per channel as well, so the two sides agree on the key shape.
The test covers both channels for the same recipient, which is the case that would have hidden the original bug.
notifications.approve: Keying by channel and returning a value instead of throwing is the right shape for this check.

revise.reason: The suppression lookup runs after the outbox write, so a suppressed message still appears in the queue.
revise.directive: Move the suppression check ahead of the outbox write in the send path.

notifications.title: Accept send requests through a typed command
notifications.intent: Expose a sendMessage command in src/notifications/dispatch/send-message.ts that takes a validated request object: tenant, recipient, channel, template and variables. The command is the only write entry point, so validation of every field lives behind it. Describe the request shape in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A well-formed request returns an accepted result with a message id. A request missing the tenant is rejected before any database call.
thinking: The send command is the front door for every caller, so I want its request type to be exhaustive. A caller cannot skip the tenant or pass a channel that does not exist.
I separated the request type into its own file so the contract doc can point at one place. The command file only holds the orchestration.
I first let the command accept raw strings for the channel and then parse them inside. Moving the parse to the request constructor means the command only ever receives typed input.
The test for a missing tenant asserts that the database stub was never called. That is the property that matters, since a rejected request must not touch storage.
I hesitated over returning the message id before the outbox write commits. I left that to the next unit, where the transaction boundary is set.

edit.new: export async function sendMessage(req: SendMessageRequest): Promise<SendResult> {

notifications.approve: The typed request means the command can only be reached with valid input, which is the whole point.

revise.reason: The command still accepts an untyped request object from the HTTP layer, bypassing the constructor.
revise.directive: Build the SendMessageRequest through its constructor in the HTTP handler before calling sendMessage.

notifications.title: Validate template variables before queuing a message
notifications.intent: Check that every placeholder in the chosen template has a supplied variable, and that each value fits its declared type, inside src/notifications/dispatch/validate-variables.ts. Validation runs before the message row exists, so a bad request leaves no trace. List the variable rules in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A request missing a required variable returns a validation error naming that variable. A request with extra variables is accepted and the extras are ignored.
thinking: Variable validation is where the template model meets the request, so I want it as a pure function. It takes a template and a variable map and returns either the map or a list of errors.
The extra variables case needed a decision. Rejecting extras would break callers that pass a shared context object, so I ignore them and say so in the contract.
I was going to validate types with a runtime schema library. Then I checked the template model, which already knows each placeholder's type, so the check is just a switch.
The error list collects every missing variable at once. Returning only the first one would make authors fix errors one request at a time.
The test feeds a template with three placeholders and omits two, and it checks that both missing names appear in the result.
notifications.approve: Collecting every missing variable at once saves the caller a round trip per field.

revise.reason: The check treats an empty string as present, so a required name with no value is queued and sent blank.
revise.directive: Reject empty strings for required placeholders in validateVariables.

notifications.title: Return structured errors for invalid channel choices
notifications.intent: Map an unsupported or disabled channel to a structured error in src/notifications/dispatch/channel-errors.ts, with the tenant, the requested kind and the list of enabled kinds. Callers display these fields directly, so the shape is part of the contract. Record the error codes in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Requesting a disabled channel returns the channel_disabled code with the enabled kinds listed. Requesting an unknown kind returns the unknown_channel code.
thinking: The two failure cases look similar but mean different things to a caller. A disabled channel is a configuration state, and an unknown kind is a bad request, so they get different codes.
I added the list of enabled kinds to the error because a caller shown only a rejection would have no next step to offer.
The error builder is a plain function, not a class, so it serializes cleanly into the HTTP response without a custom mapper.
I briefly considered reusing the ConfigError from the settings loader. It is the wrong abstraction, since this is a per-request rejection and not a startup failure.
The test asserts the exact set of error keys, which catches a field being added later without the contract being updated.

edit.new: return { code: 'channel_disabled', tenantId, requested: kind, enabled };

notifications.approve: Giving the caller the enabled kinds turns a dead end into a next step.

revise.reason: The unknown channel error returns the same code as a disabled channel, so callers cannot tell them apart.
revise.finding: Unknown and disabled share one code
revise.directive: Return the unknown_channel code for kinds outside the closed channel list.

notifications.title: Persist queued messages inside the command transaction
notifications.intent: Insert the message row and its first delivery attempt in one transaction inside src/notifications/dispatch/queue.ts. The transaction also commits the dedupe record, so a retried command cannot queue twice. Describe the commit guarantee in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: If the attempt insert fails, no message row remains. A retried request with the same dedupe key returns the original message id.
thinking: Atomicity is the reason this unit exists. A message row without an attempt row would be stuck forever, because the worker only picks up attempts.
I used a single transaction with three statements: dedupe insert, message insert, attempt insert. A unique violation on the dedupe insert short-circuits to the existing message.
The migration adds the messages table with a foreign key to the channel table, and I checked that the foreign key cascade is restrict, so a channel cannot disappear under a queued message.
The test kills the second insert with a forced error and then queries the message table to confirm nothing remains. That is the observable guarantee, not the internal call order.
I want to revisit the isolation level later, but read committed is enough for this unit because the unique constraint carries the real guarantee.
notifications.approve: The single transaction and the forced-failure test prove the stuck-message gap is closed.

revise.reason: The retry path returns a new message id on a duplicate dedupe key instead of the original one.
revise.finding: Retry returns a new message id
revise.directive: Return the existing message row when the dedupe insert hits a unique violation.

notifications.title: List a recipient's messages with cursor pagination
notifications.intent: Add a listMessages query in src/notifications/query/list-messages.ts that pages through one recipient's messages using an opaque cursor. The cursor encodes the created time and id, so pages stay stable while new messages arrive. Document the cursor format in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Paging through 25 messages with a page size of 10 returns every message exactly once. A tampered cursor returns an invalid_cursor error.
thinking: Offset pagination would skip or repeat messages as new ones arrive, so I went straight to keyset pagination on created time and id.

The cursor is base64url over a small JSON payload. I considered signing it, but the cursor only selects a position inside a query that is already tenant-scoped, so tampering can at worst change the page.
A tampered cursor should fail loud, not fall back to the first page. Silently restarting would make a client loop forever on a broken cursor.
I found the id tiebreaker was missing in my first query and two messages with the same timestamp could be skipped at a page boundary. The test with 25 rows created in one transaction caught it.
The page size is capped at 100 in the query, which I kept small because the list view only ever shows a screen of results.
notifications.approve: The id tiebreaker and the tampered-cursor failure are the two cases pagination always gets wrong.

revise.reason: The list query has no upper bound on page size, so a client can request the whole table in one call.
revise.finding: Page size has no upper bound
revise.directive: Clamp the requested page size to the maximum of 100 in listMessages.

notifications.title: Filter delivery history by channel and status
notifications.intent: Let callers narrow the delivery history by channel kind and by status in src/notifications/query/filters.ts. Each filter is optional and combines with the others using AND. Mention the supported filter fields in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A filter for sms and failed returns only rows matching both. Omitting both filters returns the same rows as the unfiltered list.
thinking: The filter module builds a where clause from a plain object, and each field is optional. I keep the builder pure so it can be tested without a database.
I want the status filter to accept only the closed status union, not any string, so a misspelled status fails at the boundary rather than returning an empty page.
Combining filters with AND is the only sensible default. I checked whether any caller expects OR and none does, so I documented AND and moved on.
The test compares the generated clause against an expected structure, which is brittle. I replaced it with a check that runs the filter against an in-memory list of rows.
Omitting both filters should be identical to the unfiltered list, and I confirmed that by reusing the same fixture rows for both queries.
notifications.approve: Typed status values and AND-combined filters keep the history query predictable.

revise.reason: An empty status string is treated as no filter, which hides a client bug that should surface.
revise.directive: Reject an empty status filter value with a validation error.

notifications.title: Expose a single message by id with tenant checks
notifications.intent: Implement getMessage in src/notifications/query/get-message.ts so it returns one message only when the message belongs to the caller's tenant. A message from another tenant looks exactly like a missing one, to avoid leaking existence. Record the not-found behaviour in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Fetching an existing message with the right tenant returns it. The same id under another tenant returns not_found, identical to a random id.
thinking: The obvious implementation fetches by id and then compares the tenant in code. That leaks timing and it is one forgotten check away from a leak, so I put tenant in the where clause.
Returning forbidden for another tenant's message would tell an attacker the id exists. I return not_found in both cases so the two responses cannot be told apart.
I checked the shared query helpers and they already build tenant filters, so I reuse one instead of writing a new where clause by hand.
The test runs the same lookup with a valid id under a foreign tenant and with a nonexistent id, and asserts the two responses are deep-equal.
I was unsure whether the identity system expects a tenant error code for this case, so I checked its error catalog and it uses not_found there too.

edit.new: const row = await db.select().from(messages).where(and(eq(messages.id, id), eq(messages.tenantId, tenantId)));

notifications.approve: Making a foreign tenant indistinguishable from a missing message is the right default.

revise.reason: The lookup filters by tenant after fetching the row, which returns the row body before the check runs.
revise.directive: Move the tenant condition into the where clause so the foreign row is never selected.

notifications.title: Sort inbox results by creation time descending
notifications.intent: Order the inbox view by created time, newest first, with id as the tiebreaker, in src/notifications/query/inbox.ts. The inbox reuses the list pagination cursor so the sort and the cursor stay in step. Note the ordering in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Two messages created in the same millisecond come back in id order every time. The newest message is always first on page one.
thinking: The inbox is a thin wrapper over the list query with a fixed sort. The risk is that the sort and the cursor drift apart, so I derive both from one constant.
I wrote the test to insert two rows with an identical timestamp to exercise the tiebreaker, since the bug only shows up when two rows collide.
The inbox view should never show a stale order after a new message lands, and keyset pagination guarantees that for the newest-first direction.
I considered adding a secondary sort by status, but nothing in the spec asks for it, so I left it out rather than build for a future that has not been asked for.
The query uses the same index as the list view, which I confirmed with an explain output in the scratch notes before accepting the change.
notifications.approve: Deriving the sort and the cursor from one constant is what keeps them from drifting apart.

revise.reason: The inbox sort is duplicated in the list view, so a change to one silently leaves the other behind.
revise.directive: Import the shared sort constant from the list query instead of redefining it.

notifications.title: Write outbox rows for every queued delivery
notifications.intent: Append an outbox row for each queued delivery in src/notifications/events/outbox.ts, inside the same transaction that persists the message. Other systems subscribe to the outbox, so the row carries the tenant id, message id and status. Describe the outbox row shape in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Queueing one message produces exactly one outbox row in the same transaction. A rolled back queue leaves no outbox row.
thinking: The outbox row must commit or roll back with the message, otherwise a subscriber would see an event for a message that never existed.
I wrote the outbox table with an identity column for ordering, since the relay reads in insert order and needs a monotonic cursor.
The payload is a small JSON document with ids and status only. I deliberately leave the message body out so the event stream cannot leak content.
The test rolls back a queue call on purpose and checks the outbox table is empty, which is the property that matters rather than a count after a successful call.
I noticed the queue module now calls two inserts after the outbox addition, so I moved the outbox insert into the same helper to keep the transaction in one place.
notifications.approve: The outbox row sharing the message transaction is the guarantee subscribers depend on.

revise.reason: The outbox payload includes the rendered message body, which copies recipient content into the event stream.
revise.finding: Message body leaks into outbox payload
revise.directive: Remove the rendered body from the outbox payload and keep only ids and status.

notifications.title: Emit a webhook when a delivery reaches a terminal state
notifications.intent: When a delivery becomes delivered, failed or bounced, enqueue a webhook call in src/notifications/webhooks/emit.ts. The webhook targets are configured per tenant and signed with the tenant's secret. Record the webhook payload and signature scheme in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A delivery moving to delivered enqueues one webhook per configured target. A delivery moving to queued enqueues none.
thinking: Only terminal states should fire a webhook, so the emitter checks the new status against a closed set before doing anything.
Signing uses HMAC with the tenant secret over the raw body. I put the signature in its own module so the scheme can be checked against a fixed test vector.
I first called the target URL inline during the state transition. That would couple the transition to a slow external host, so the emitter only enqueues and a worker performs the call.
I was worried about sending the webhook before the state commit, which would announce a state that could still roll back. The emitter reads from the outbox, so it only ever sees committed rows.
The test pins a known body and secret to a known signature, which catches any change to the canonical serialization.
notifications.approve: Reading from committed outbox rows means a webhook can never announce a state that rolled back.

revise.reason: The emitter fires for the queued state, so every send announces a webhook before it has happened.
revise.directive: Restrict the emitter to the terminal status set before enqueueing.

notifications.title: Publish a contract for the delivery status event
notifications.intent: Write the delivery status event schema into contracts/notifications.md, with its version, its fields and the rule for adding fields. Export a matching type from src/notifications/events/delivery-status.ts so the producer and the document cannot drift. Other systems read this contract before subscribing.
notifications.acceptance: The exported type and the contract table list the same fields. A test fails if a field is added to the type without a matching contract row.
thinking: The contract is the thing other systems will actually read, so I write it before the type and then make the type follow it.
I considered generating the markdown table from the type, but that makes the doc an output nobody reads closely. A test that compares the two is simpler to reason about.
The versioning rule is additive only. New fields are optional, and a removed field needs a new event name, which I wrote into the contract so future authors see it.
The contract test parses the markdown table with a regex. It is a little fragile, but the table format is stable and the failure message names the missing field.
I realized the event name had a typo in an earlier unit's contract section, so I corrected it while I was here.

shell.description: Check status event type against contract

notifications.approve: The contract test is what keeps the document honest after the next field is added.

revise.reason: The contract table omits the version field that the type now requires, so consumers cannot tell which shape they received.
revise.directive: Add a version row to the delivery status table in contracts/notifications.md.

notifications.title: Consume booking confirmation events into sends
notifications.intent: Subscribe to the booking confirmation event and queue a confirmation message in src/notifications/events/consume-booking.ts. The consumer maps the booking payload to a template and recipient, and it ignores events for tenants without the confirmation channel enabled. Document the consumed event in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A booking confirmed event queues exactly one confirmation message. A redelivered event does not queue a second message.
thinking: Consuming events is the inbound side of the contract, so redelivery is the default case rather than the exception. The consumer must be idempotent by design.
The dedupe key from the earlier unit already covers this, provided I build it from the booking event id. I checked that the booking event carries a stable id before depending on it.

I briefly wondered whether the consumer should read the recipient from the booking payload or look it up in identity. The payload already carries the contact, and a lookup would add a cross-system call on the hot path.
The test delivers the same event twice and asserts a single queued message. It also checks an event for a disabled tenant produces nothing.
I deferred the retry policy for consumer failures to a later unit, since the current path only needs to handle the happy case and the redelivery case.
notifications.approve: Building the dedupe key from the booking event id is what makes redelivery safe.

revise.reason: The consumer builds the dedupe key without the event id, so two different bookings for one recipient collapse into one message.
revise.finding: Dedupe key drops booking event id
revise.directive: Include the booking event id in the dedupe key passed from the consumer.

notifications.title: Guard concurrent dispatch with row-level locks
notifications.intent: Lock each message row with select for update skip locked before a worker attempts delivery, in src/notifications/dispatch/worker-lock.ts. Two workers may run at once, and the lock ensures one attempt per message at a time. Describe the locking rule in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Two concurrent workers claiming the same pending message result in exactly one attempt. A locked row is skipped rather than waited on.
thinking: Two workers racing on one row would double-send, which is the worst failure in this system. The lock is the guarantee, so I test it with real concurrent transactions.
I used skip locked so a busy worker moves on to the next row instead of queuing behind a slow send. Waiting would make throughput depend on the slowest provider.
The lock has to be released by the transaction end, and I confirmed the attempt write happens inside the same transaction, so a crash cannot leave a half-claimed row.
The test spawns two workers against a single pending row and counts attempts. My first version was flaky because the second worker ran before the first claimed, so I added a barrier.
I double checked the isolation level for the claim query and read committed with a row lock is enough here.
notifications.approve: The barrier-based concurrency test is what makes the one-attempt guarantee believable.

revise.reason: The claim query runs outside the attempt transaction, so the lock is released before the attempt is written.
revise.directive: Run the claim select and the attempt update inside one transaction.

notifications.title: Make send requests idempotent by client key
notifications.intent: Accept an optional client idempotency key on send requests and store it with the dedupe record in src/notifications/dispatch/idempotency.ts. A repeated request with the same key returns the original result rather than queuing again. Note the key lifetime in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Sending twice with the same idempotency key returns the same message id and queues one message. A key reused for a different recipient returns a conflict error.
thinking: Client keys are a different thing from the internal dedupe key. The client key is chosen by the caller and must be scoped to the tenant, so I store it with the tenant id in the same row.
A reused key with a different body is a caller bug, not a retry. Returning the original result for it would silently drop the new body, so I return a conflict.
I set the key lifetime to 24 hours in the contract, since callers retry within minutes and a longer window only costs storage.
The check happens inside the send transaction so two concurrent requests with the same key cannot both pass it. The unique constraint on tenant and key carries that.
The test sends the same key twice with the same body and once with a different body, and checks the three outcomes distinctly.

edit.new: const existing = await findByKey(tenantId, clientKey, { forUpdate: true });

notifications.approve: Treating a reused key with a changed body as a conflict is the correct call and the test shows it.

revise.reason: The idempotency lookup runs without the tenant id, so a key collides across tenants.
revise.directive: Scope the findByKey call by tenant id before comparing keys.

notifications.title: Retry transient provider failures with jittered backoff
notifications.intent: Retry provider calls that fail with a timeout or a 503 response, using exponential backoff with full jitter in src/notifications/dispatch/retry.ts. Permanent rejections are never retried. Describe the retry classes in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A provider returning 503 twice then 200 results in a delivered attempt. A provider returning a permanent 400 is marked failed after one call.
thinking: The retry module needs to know what is transient, and that is a property of the provider's response, so I classify responses in a separate module first.
I chose full jitter over equal jitter because it spreads the herd better when a provider comes back. The formula is random between zero and the capped exponential delay.
The test injects a fake random source so the delays are deterministic. Without that the assertions would depend on the clock and be flaky.
I almost retried on every 5xx. Then I checked the provider docs and a 500 can mean the request body was rejected, which is permanent, so only 503 and timeouts retry.
The retry loop is bounded by the attempt ceiling in the next unit, so for now I set a fixed three attempts to keep the behaviour testable.

edit.new: const delay = Math.floor(rand() * Math.min(cap, base * 2 ** attempt));

notifications.approve: Excluding 500 from the transient set and injecting the random source make this both correct and testable.

revise.reason: The jitter helper uses the full base delay as its upper bound, so retries do not respect the cap.
revise.directive: Bound the jittered delay by the configured maximum before sleeping.

notifications.title: Stop retrying after the configured attempt ceiling
notifications.intent: Stop the retry loop after the configured maximum attempt count and mark the delivery as exhausted in src/notifications/dispatch/ceiling.ts. The ceiling is read from the tenant channel settings, with the platform default when unset. Record the exhausted state in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A delivery with a ceiling of 4 makes exactly 4 provider calls before becoming exhausted. The exhausted state is terminal and emits no further attempts.
thinking: The ceiling is a tenant policy, so it comes from the settings loader I wrote earlier, not from a constant in the retry module.
I counted attempts from zero and then realized the ceiling in the spec means total calls, not retries after the first. I changed the comparison to match the spec wording.
Exhausted is a terminal state, so I added it to the closed status union. The terminal set in the webhook emitter now needs it too, and I updated that reference.
The test uses a ceiling of four and a provider that always fails, and it counts calls to make sure the boundary is exact.
I left the question of whether exhausted deliveries should be re-queued by an operator for a later operations unit.
notifications.approve: Counting total calls against the ceiling and testing the exact boundary removes an off-by-one that would have shipped.

revise.reason: The exhausted status is not added to the terminal set, so exhausted deliveries never fire their webhook.
revise.directive: Add the exhausted status to the terminal status set used by the webhook emitter.

notifications.title: Backfill delivery attempts from the legacy log
notifications.intent: Copy historical send records from the legacy log table into delivery attempts in batches, in src/notifications/backfill/attempts.ts. Each batch commits independently and the job can resume from the last committed id. Describe the backfill guarantees in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Re-running the backfill after a crash produces no duplicate attempt rows. Every legacy row in the fixture has exactly one matching attempt afterwards.
thinking: A backfill runs against production-shaped data, so I want it resumable and idempotent before I think about speed. The resume cursor is the last legacy id that committed.
I wrote the insert with on conflict do nothing keyed by the legacy id. That makes a re-run harmless and removes the need for a clever resume step.
The migration only adds a unique index on the legacy reference column. I checked that no existing attempt rows already carry a null there, since the index would fail on nulls.
The test kills the job after the second batch and restarts it, then counts rows. The count must match the fixture exactly, not just be non-zero.
I considered running the backfill as one transaction for simplicity, but a long transaction over the legacy table would hold locks for minutes, so I kept batches.
notifications.approve: The idempotent insert and the kill-and-restart test are what make this safe to run twice.

revise.reason: The backfill advances the resume cursor before the batch commits, so a crash skips the batch entirely.
revise.directive: Advance the resume cursor only after the batch transaction commits.

notifications.title: Migrate channel preferences to the new column shape
notifications.intent: Move each tenant's channel preferences from the old flat columns into the jsonb settings column, in migrations/0005_channel_prefs.sql with a helper in src/notifications/migrate/prefs.ts. Unknown legacy values are logged and mapped to the platform default. Record the new shape in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: Every tenant row has a settings value matching its old flat columns after the migration. A legacy value outside the known list is mapped to the default and logged once.
thinking: This migration reshapes live data in a system only we depend on, so I avoid a long-lived compatibility layer and write one forward migration plus a small defaulting helper.
The old columns hold free text for the channel, and a few rows have values nobody expected. I map those to the platform default and log them, rather than failing the whole migration.
I checked the row count before writing the helper, and the legacy table is small enough that a single update statement is fine without batching.
The test seeds one row for each known value and one odd value, and asserts the odd one lands on the default with a single log line.
I need to remember to delete the helper once the migration has run everywhere, so I noted that in the file header rather than leaving it as a permanent surface.
notifications.approve: Logging the odd legacy value once and defaulting it is the right balance for a small live table.

revise.reason: The migration helper stays in the source tree with no removal date, so it will outlive the transition.
revise.finding: Migration helper has no removal plan
revise.directive: Mark the helper for deletion in the file header with the release it can be removed in.

notifications.title: Add a partial index for pending deliveries
notifications.intent: Add a partial index on the attempts table covering only rows in the pending status, in migrations/0006_pending_index.sql. The worker polls on this predicate, so the index keeps the poll cheap as history grows. Document the index purpose in src/notifications/dispatch/worker-lock.ts beside the query it serves.
notifications.acceptance: The explain plan for the pending poll uses the partial index. The migration applies and reverses cleanly.
thinking: The poll query scans for pending attempts on every tick, and as history grows that scan gets expensive. A partial index covers just the rows the poll cares about.
I checked the plan on a seeded table of about two hundred thousand rows. Without the index it sequential scans, and with it the plan switches to an index scan.
The index predicate has to match the query text exactly, or Postgres will ignore it. I copied the where clause from the lock query into the migration to make the match obvious.
The test asserts on the explain output and fails if the plan falls back to a sequential scan. That is brittle across Postgres versions, so I pinned the test to the version in the compose file.
I thought about indexing the full status column, but a partial index is smaller and only the pending rows ever matter to the poll.

shell.description: Check pending poll uses partial index

notifications.approve: The explain assertion is what proves the index is actually used, not just created.

revise.reason: The index predicate omits the lockedAt condition, so the poll query can never match the index it was built for.
revise.finding: Index predicate differs from poll query
revise.directive: Make the partial index WHERE clause identical to the poll query predicate.

notifications.title: Verify backfill row counts against the source table
notifications.intent: Compare row counts and a checksum of the legacy ids against the migrated attempts after the backfill runs, in src/notifications/backfill/verify.ts. A mismatch fails the job and writes the differing id range to the log. Describe the verification step in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A verified backfill reports matching counts and checksums. A deliberately deleted row causes a mismatch report naming its id range.
thinking: Counts alone can match while rows are wrong, so I add a checksum over the sorted legacy ids. Two cheap checks that catch different failures.
The checksum is computed in chunks by id range so the verifier never loads the whole table into memory. The chunk size is a constant I can tune later.
I had the verifier compare totals first and only dig into ranges on a mismatch. That keeps the happy path to two queries.
The test deletes one row on purpose and checks the reported range contains that id. A report that says only that counts differ would not help the operator.
I want to be sure the verifier never mutates data, so the test runs it against a read-only role and confirms it still passes.

edit.new: if (src.count !== dst.count || src.checksum !== dst.checksum) return fail('mismatch', rangeOf(src, dst));

notifications.approve: Pairing a count with a checksum and naming the bad id range is what makes a failed backfill fixable.

revise.reason: The checksum is computed over unsorted ids, so the same rows in a different order produce a mismatch.
revise.directive: Sort the ids before hashing them in the checksum function.

notifications.title: Emit delivery latency metrics per provider
notifications.intent: Record the time from queue to provider acceptance as a histogram labelled by provider and channel, in src/notifications/observability/latency.ts. The metric uses the shared metrics client and no new dependency. Describe the metric name and labels in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A delivery accepted by a provider records one observation with the provider and channel labels. Labels stay within the closed provider and channel sets.
thinking: Latency is measured from the queue timestamp to the provider accept, which is the number the operator actually wants when a tenant asks why a message was slow.
I restrict the label values to the closed provider and channel unions. An open string label would let a typo create a new time series for every variant.
The metrics client is already a dependency of the catalog system, so I reuse it instead of wiring a second exporter.
The test stubs the clock and checks that the observed duration is exactly the difference, since a histogram that records the wrong unit would be silently wrong.
I wondered whether to include retries in the latency. I decided on the first accept only, and I wrote that choice into the contract so dashboards are read correctly.
notifications.approve: Closed label sets and a seconds unit make these metrics safe to put on a dashboard.

revise.reason: The histogram records milliseconds while the contract and the dashboard assume seconds.
revise.directive: Record the observation in seconds to match the metric name and contract.

notifications.title: Trace each dispatch through the outbox relay
notifications.intent: Propagate a trace id from the send command through the outbox row and into the relay in src/notifications/observability/trace.ts. The relay starts a child span per event so a single send is followed end to end. Note the trace attribute names in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A send and its relayed event share one trace id. The relay span is a child of the send span.
thinking: A trace that breaks at the outbox is useless, because the relay is where most of the delay happens. The trace id has to be stored on the outbox row itself.
I store the trace id as a column, not inside the payload, so the relay can read it without parsing the body and without exposing it to subscribers.
The relay creates a child span with the stored id as parent. I checked the tracing API to confirm the parent context can be built from a plain id.
The test runs a send and then the relay and asserts both spans report the same trace id. That is the thing a support engineer will search for.
I considered propagating the full span context, but a trace id and a parent span id are enough for this and keep the row small.
notifications.approve: Storing the trace id as a column keeps the trace intact across the outbox without touching payloads.

revise.reason: The relay starts a new root span, so the trace breaks at the outbox boundary.
revise.finding: Relay starts a new root span
revise.directive: Create the relay span as a child of the stored parent span context.

notifications.title: Log structured diagnostics for provider rejections
notifications.intent: Write a structured diagnostic line for every provider rejection, with the provider code, the classification and the delivery id, in src/notifications/observability/diagnostics.ts. Diagnostics never include the recipient value or the message body. List the diagnostic fields in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A provider rejection writes one JSON diagnostic line with the required fields. The line contains no recipient address or body text.
thinking: Diagnostics are read by people in a hurry, so each line has to be complete and parseable. I use one JSON object per line and no multi-line output.
The tricky rule is what not to log. The recipient and body are personal data, so I build the diagnostic from ids and codes only and never pass the message object in.
I considered logging the raw provider response for debugging. The response can echo the recipient back, so I log the code and a truncated reason instead.
The test scans the captured output for the recipient address and fails if it appears, which turns the privacy rule into an assertion.
I checked the logging wrapper and it already supports structured fields, so the diagnostic function is a thin call and not a new logger.
notifications.approve: The test that scans output for the recipient address turns the privacy rule into something enforced.

revise.reason: The diagnostic includes the provider raw reason text, which echoes the recipient address back into logs.
revise.directive: Replace the raw provider reason with its classification code in the diagnostic line.

notifications.title: Cap sends per recipient within a rolling window
notifications.intent: Limit how many messages one recipient receives within a rolling window, in src/notifications/quota/recipient-window.ts. The window and limit come from the tenant settings, and an over-limit send is rejected with a typed error. Document the limit and window fields in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: The sixth send within an hour to a recipient with a limit of five is rejected. The same send after the window passes is accepted.
thinking: A rolling window is easy to get wrong with fixed buckets, because a burst across a bucket boundary doubles the effective limit. I count sends in the trailing interval instead.
The count query needs an index on recipient and created time, and I checked the migrations to see if one exists. It does not, so I note it as a follow-up rather than adding it in this unit.
The rejection is a typed error with the next allowed time, so the caller can tell the user when to try again.
The test moves a fake clock across the window edge and checks the boundary send is accepted exactly when the oldest send falls out.
I am not sure whether suppressed sends should count toward the window. They never reach a provider, so I decided they do not count, and I wrote that into the contract.

edit.new: if (count >= limit) return reject('over_limit', { retryAt: oldestInWindow + windowMs });

notifications.approve: A rolling window with a retry time is fairer than buckets and tells the caller what to do next.

revise.reason: The window counts suppressed sends, so a recipient who opted out still uses up the limit for other channels.
revise.directive: Exclude suppressed sends from the window count query.

notifications.title: Throttle provider calls per tenant token bucket
notifications.intent: Throttle outbound provider calls per tenant with a token bucket in src/notifications/quota/provider-bucket.ts, so one busy tenant cannot starve the others. The bucket state is held in memory per worker and refilled on each call. Record the rate settings in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A tenant over its rate waits for a token instead of exceeding the provider limit. A second tenant's calls proceed while the first is throttled.
thinking: A token bucket per tenant is the fairness mechanism. Without it one large tenant's backlog would consume the shared provider quota and delay everyone else.
The bucket lives in memory per worker, which means the global rate is the per-worker rate times the worker count. I documented that so nobody assumes a global limit.
I was going to use a timer to refill the bucket, but computing the refill from elapsed time on each call is simpler and needs no background work.
The test uses two tenants and checks that the second one proceeds while the first waits. Without the per-tenant key the test would fail, which is what I wanted to see.
I considered a distributed limiter with a shared store, but that adds a dependency and a failure mode for a limit we can enforce locally, so I deferred it.
notifications.approve: Keying the bucket by tenant and provider is the fairness property, and the two-tenant test proves it.

revise.reason: The bucket is keyed by provider alone, so one tenant's burst throttles every other tenant on that provider.
revise.directive: Key the token bucket by tenant id and provider together.

notifications.title: Bound message body size at the command boundary
notifications.intent: Reject message bodies larger than the configured maximum before anything is written, in src/notifications/dispatch/body-limit.ts. The limit is checked on the rendered body, which is what the provider receives. Describe the size error in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A rendered body one byte over the limit returns body_too_large. A body exactly at the limit is accepted.
thinking: I measure the rendered body in bytes, not characters, because SMS segment and provider limits are byte based and a multibyte character would otherwise pass a character check and fail downstream.
The check runs after rendering, since a template with short placeholders can grow past the limit only once the values are inserted.
The test pins both the one-over and exact-limit cases. An off-by-one here would reject valid bodies or accept oversized ones, and both are visible to users.
I briefly considered also capping the template length at authoring time, but that is a catalog concern and is out of scope for this unit.
The error includes the limit and the actual size so the caller can show a useful message without guessing.

shell.description: Run message body size limit tests

notifications.approve: Measuring bytes rather than characters is the detail that stops a multibyte body slipping past the limit.

revise.reason: The check runs on the template source before rendering, so a short template with long values escapes the limit.
revise.directive: Move the body size check to run after the template has been rendered.

notifications.title: Gate the new dispatcher behind a tenant flag
notifications.intent: Route each send through the new dispatcher only when the tenant's flag is on, and through the legacy path otherwise, in src/notifications/rollout/flag.ts. The flag is read once per request and defaults to off. Record the flag name and default in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A tenant with the flag on takes the new dispatcher path. A tenant with the flag off or unset takes the legacy path, and both paths produce the same message row shape.
thinking: The flag is the rollout mechanism, so its default has to be off. An unset flag must never enable the new path by accident, and I test that case first.
I read the flag once per request and pass the decision down, so a flag flipped mid-request cannot send one message through two paths.
Both paths must produce the same message row shape, otherwise downstream readers would need to know which path wrote a row. I compared the two shapes in the test.
The flag helper is small on purpose. When the rollout completes I plan to delete it, and the file header says so.
I checked the flag service client and it caches for a short time, which is acceptable for a rollout flag, so I did not add a second cache.
notifications.approve: Defaulting the flag off and asserting identical row shapes on both paths makes the rollout safe.

revise.reason: The flag helper reads the flag once per message row instead of once per request, so one request can use both paths.
revise.finding: Flag read per row not per request
revise.directive: Read the rollout flag once at the start of the request and pass the decision down.

notifications.title: Document the rollback path for the dispatcher
notifications.intent: Write the rollback steps for the new dispatcher into contracts/notifications.md, covering the flag flip, the drain of in-flight attempts and the check that legacy sends resume. Add a rollback drill test in test/notifications/rollback-drill.test.ts that flips the flag and asserts sends continue. Keep the steps in the contract so on-call can follow them without reading code.
notifications.acceptance: The rollback drill test passes after flipping the flag off mid-run. The contract's rollback section lists the three steps in order.
thinking: Rollback is only real if someone has walked it, so the drill test is more important than the prose. The prose tells on-call what to do; the test tells me it works.
The drain step matters. In-flight attempts on the new path must finish before the flag flip is treated as complete, or a retry could land on the wrong path.
I wrote the rollback helper as a small function that waits for in-flight counts to reach zero with a deadline. Without a deadline a stuck attempt would hang the rollback forever.
The drill test flips the flag mid-run and checks that new sends take the legacy path. I also checked the in-flight drain returns within the deadline.
I was not sure the deadline value should live in the contract, but on-call needs to know how long to wait, so I wrote it there and read it from the same constant.
notifications.approve: A rollback drill that actually flips the flag is worth more than any amount of runbook prose.

revise.reason: The rollback drain has no deadline, so a stuck in-flight attempt would stall the rollback indefinitely.
revise.directive: Add a drain timeout to the rollback wait and fail loud when it is exceeded.

notifications.title: Purge delivery bodies after the retention period
notifications.intent: Delete rendered message bodies once they pass the tenant's retention period, in src/notifications/retention/purge.ts, keeping the message metadata rows. The purge runs in small batches and skips rows that are still pending. Describe the retention rule in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A body older than the retention period is cleared while its metadata row remains. A pending message is never purged regardless of age.
thinking: Purging is destructive, so I check the test database is the only target in the test run before anything else. The retention rule itself is simple: clear the body, keep the row.
I skip pending messages on purpose. A body still needed for a retry must not be cleared, and the test seeds one old pending row to prove it survives.
The purge clears the body column to null and keeps the row, which means the metadata queries stay valid. I considered deleting the row entirely and rejected it because the audit trail needs it.
Batches are sized by id range so the purge never holds a long lock. I tested the batch boundary with a row count that is not a multiple of the batch size.
I am still not sure whether the retention period should be measured from creation or from final status. I used creation for now and noted the question in the contract.
notifications.approve: Skipping pending rows and keeping metadata is the safe shape for a destructive purge.

revise.reason: The purge query has no status filter, so a pending message past retention loses the body its retry still needs.
revise.directive: Exclude pending messages from the purge predicate.

notifications.title: Record an audit entry for every manual resend
notifications.intent: Write an audit entry each time an operator resends a message from the operations console, in src/notifications/audit/resend-audit.ts. The entry records the actor, the original message id and the reason text. Describe the audit fields in contracts/notifications.md.
notifications.acceptance: A manual resend writes exactly one audit row in the same transaction as the new message. A resend without a reason is rejected.
thinking: An audit row written outside the transaction could record a resend that never happened, so I put it inside the same transaction as the new message.
Requiring a reason is a deliberate friction. An operator who resends without saying why is exactly the case the audit trail exists for, so the command rejects an empty reason.
The actor id comes from the authenticated session, not from the request body, which I confirmed in the handler before writing the test.
The migration adds a table with a foreign key to the original message, and I checked that deleting a message is restricted, so the audit reference cannot dangle.
The test checks that a failed message insert leaves no audit row, which is the atomicity property I care about most in this unit.

edit.new:
if (!reason.trim()) throw new AuditError('reason_required');
await tx.insert(auditLog).values({ actor, messageId, reason: reason.trim() });

notifications.approve: Writing the audit row in the same transaction and requiring a reason is exactly the trail operators need.

revise.reason: The audit actor is read from the request body rather than the authenticated session, so it can be forged.
revise.finding: Audit actor taken from request body
revise.directive: Read the audit actor from the authenticated session context instead of the request body.

search.title: Define the index document shape
search.intent: Define the TypeScript type for one indexed document, the record a catalog listing becomes before it is written to the index. The type lives in src/search/document.ts and must carry tenant id, entity id, version, the normalized text fields and the facet values. The contract in contracts/search.md lists which fields are required and which are optional so that the catalog and booking teams agree on the shape.
search.acceptance: The IndexDocument type compiles with no any and every field listed in contracts/search.md is present. A document missing its tenant id fails to construct.
thinking: The brief is only the shape for now, so I want the type to be boring. I will model IndexDocument as a plain readonly record with tenantId, entityId, version and fields, and leave the ranking logic for later.
I first wrote facets as an optional map, but the contract says every listing has at least an empty facet set. Making it required removes a branch from every consumer, so I am changing it.
Tenant id is a branded string rather than a plain string. If a raw string gets passed where a TenantId is expected, the compiler should catch it before a query ever runs against the wrong tenant.
The constructor helper will throw if tenantId is empty. That is a programmer error, not a runtime condition to recover from, so there is no fallback value.

I checked the contract file once more and found it still names the field 'listingId'. The catalog team renamed it to entityId last sprint, so I will follow the newer name and flag the stale contract line for them.

edit.old: export type IndexDocument = { tenantId: string; fields: Record<string, string> };
edit.new: export type IndexDocument = { readonly tenantId: TenantId; readonly entityId: EntityId; readonly version: number; readonly fields: Readonly<Record<string, string>>; readonly facets: Readonly<Record<string, string[]>> };

shell.description: Run the document shape unit tests

search.approve: The shape matches the contract exactly and the branded tenant id makes cross-tenant mixups a compile error.

revise.reason: The facets field is optional in the contract but required in the type, so consumers will disagree about it.
revise.directive: Make facets optional in the type or mark it required in contracts/search.md, then align both.

search.title: Create the tenant-scoped index registry
search.intent: Build the registry that maps a tenant id to its index name and current generation, so that no code path ever builds an index name by string concatenation. The registry lives in src/search/registry.ts and reads its mapping from a Postgres table created in the foundations migration. Other systems ask the registry for an index name and never construct one themselves.
search.acceptance: Two tenants never resolve to the same index name, and an unknown tenant id returns a typed not-found result instead of throwing.
thinking: The registry is the only place index names are born, so I want every caller to go through one function, indexNameFor. Anything else would scatter the naming rule across the codebase.

I started by hashing the tenant id into the index name to keep it short. Then I realized that makes the name unreadable when someone is debugging a live tenant, so I switched to the tenant slug plus generation.
The unknown-tenant case is a real situation, since a tenant can be created in identity before its index exists. A typed not-found result lets the caller decide, which a thrown error would not.
I need the lookup to be cached but the cache must not outlive a generation bump. I will key the cache on tenant and generation together, so a rebuild invalidates it without a separate signal.
The migration creates the registry table with a unique constraint on tenant id. I double checked that the constraint also covers the slug so two tenants cannot collide on the same index name.

edit.old: export function indexNameFor(slug: string) { return 'idx_' + slug; }
edit.new: export function indexNameFor(tenant: TenantRecord): IndexName { return `idx_${tenant.slug}_g${tenant.generation}` as IndexName; }

search.approve: Index naming now has exactly one owner and the generation suffix makes rebuilds safe to reason about.

revise.reason: The cache key ignores generation, so a rebuilt tenant can keep resolving to the old index name.
revise.directive: Include the generation in the cache key used by the registry lookup.

search.title: Configure the Postgres full-text dictionaries
search.intent: Configure the text search configuration used for indexed fields, with an English dictionary and a custom stopword list for venue and studio terms. The configuration is created in migrations/search_0002_dictionaries.sql and wrapped by src/search/dictionary.ts so the rest of the code asks for a named config. A short note in contracts/search.md records which dictionary each field uses.
search.acceptance: A stemmed query for 'studios' matches a document containing 'studio', and the custom stopword 'venue' is excluded from the tsvector.
thinking: The dictionary choice is easy to get wrong later, so I want it pinned in one migration and nowhere else. I will create a tidewater_text configuration that copies the english config and adds the custom stopwords.

Before writing the stopword file I checked how many venue words would be filtered. 'studio' and 'venue' are domain words users actually type, so stopping them would hide results, and I am removing 'studio' from the list.

The dictionary is referenced by name from the config module, and a typo there fails only at query time. I added a startup check that asks Postgres to resolve the configuration once and fails loudly if it is missing.
I considered per-tenant dictionaries and dropped the idea. Nothing in the brief needs them and they would multiply migrations, so the single configuration stays.
The test runs against a real local Postgres because the stemming output is the behaviour under test, and mocking it would prove nothing.

shell.description: Check the text configuration output directly

search.approve: Pinning the configuration in one migration with a startup check is the right amount of care for this.

revise.reason: The custom stopword list drops 'hire' too, which hides a common booking term from results.
revise.directive: Remove 'hire' from the custom stopword list and add a test that it still matches.

search.title: Set up index naming and tenancy keys
search.intent: Add the tenancy keys that every index document and query must carry, including the partition key used by the storage layer. The keys are defined in src/search/tenancy.ts and reuse the tenant id brand from the foundations work. The contract in contracts/search.md describes how a missing tenancy key is rejected at the boundary.
search.acceptance: A document or query without a tenancy key is rejected before it reaches storage, and the rejection carries the field name that was missing.
thinking: Tenancy keys are a cross-cutting rule, so I want them checked in one function rather than sprinkled across handlers. I will write requireTenancy and have every entry point call it first.
I was going to derive the partition key from the entity id to spread load. Then I remembered the brief wants per-tenant isolation first, so the partition key is the tenant id and nothing cleverer.
The error for a missing key needs to name the field. A generic 'invalid tenancy' message would send the next engineer hunting through the whole call chain.
I checked whether the outbox events also need the key. They do, since downstream consumers filter on it, so the same helper is reused on the event payload path.
The test covers the empty string, the whitespace-only string and an absent key separately, because each one fails for a different reason in the validator.

edit.old: export function requireTenancy(input: { tenantId?: string }) { return input.tenantId; }
edit.new: export function requireTenancy(input: { tenantId?: string }): TenantId { if (!input.tenantId?.trim()) throw new MissingTenancyKey('tenantId'); return input.tenantId as TenantId; }

search.approve: One helper that every path calls is exactly the kind of boring rule I want for tenancy.

revise.reason: The whitespace-only tenant id passes the trim check on the event path but not on the query path.
revise.directive: Route the event payload check through requireTenancy so both paths share one validator.

search.title: Map catalog listings into indexed documents
search.intent: Write the mapper that turns a catalog listing payload into an IndexDocument, pulling title, description, amenities and category into the fields map. The mapper lives in src/search/map-listing.ts and is pure, so it can be exercised without the database. Fields that the catalog marks as internal are dropped here and never copied into the index.
search.acceptance: A listing with an internal-only field produces a document without that field, and a listing missing a title fails with a typed mapping error.
thinking: The mapper should be a pure function from the catalog payload to an IndexDocument, so I start by writing the test with two fixture listings. Then I can see the mapping without spinning up anything.

The catalog payload has an internalNotes field that must never reach the index. I am filtering by an explicit allowlist rather than a denylist, so a new internal field added later stays out by default.
Amenities arrive as an array of objects with a label and an id. I flatten them to labels only, since the id is an internal catalog key that users never see.
A missing title should not be patched with an empty string. An empty title would index and then rank oddly, so the mapper returns a MappingError instead.

I noticed the category field is sometimes an object in older payloads. Rather than guessing at both shapes, I decided to reject the object form loudly and note it in the contract, since the catalog has already moved to the string form.

edit.old: const fields = { title: p.title, notes: p.internalNotes };
edit.new: const fields = { title: requireField(p, 'title'), description: p.description ?? '' };

search.approve: The allowlist keeps internal fields out by default, which is the safe failure direction.

revise.reason: The mapper still passes through the legacy category object without a test, so a regression would go unnoticed.
revise.directive: Add a test that asserts the object-form category is rejected with a MappingError.

search.title: Normalize resource names before indexing
search.intent: Normalize resource names so that 'Studio A', 'studio-a' and 'STUDIO  A' index to the same normalized form. The normalizer is in src/search/normalize.ts and runs before the dictionary step, so case, punctuation and repeated spaces are gone by the time the tsvector is built. Notes on the rules go into contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: Three spelling variants of one resource name normalize to an identical string, and the normalizer never changes digits.
thinking: Normalization has to be idempotent, otherwise re-indexing a document would keep changing its text. I will run the normalizer twice in the test and assert the second pass is a no-op.
I first wrote a regex that strips every non-letter character. That removed digits, so 'Room 12' and 'Room 21' would collapse into the same text, which is a real bug for venues.

Unicode case folding is subtle. I used toLowerCase rather than a locale-dependent call, because a studio in Istanbul should not index differently from one in London on a server with a different locale.

The normalizer is called from the mapper, so I need to make sure the mapper passes the raw title and not an already trimmed one. Trimming twice is harmless, but I want the normalizer to own that rule.
I added a small hyphen rule so 'studio-a' becomes 'studio a'. That keeps the dictionary tokenizer from splitting it oddly.
search.approve: Keeping digits and making the function idempotent fixes both the room-number bug and the re-index churn.

revise.reason: The hyphen rule runs after punctuation stripping, so the hyphen is removed without becoming a space.
revise.directive: Move the hyphen replacement ahead of the punctuation strip and cover it with a test.

search.title: Model facet values for availability filters
search.intent: Model the facet values that availability filters use, such as capacity band, accessibility and open-day, as a closed set of enums rather than free strings. The model lives in src/search/facets.ts and the allowed values are listed in contracts/search.md. Unknown facet names are rejected at the mapper, so a typo cannot silently create a new filter.
search.acceptance: A facet name outside the closed set is rejected with the offending name in the error, and every listed value round-trips through the parser.
thinking: Facets are a closed vocabulary that the booking team and the search team both depend on. A free-string model would let either side drift without anyone noticing, so I am using a discriminated union.
I want the parser to be strict but the error message to be specific. I will return the bad facet name and the list of allowed names together, which makes a typo obvious on sight.
Capacity band has numeric boundaries. I considered modelling it as a range type, then decided a three-value enum is enough until the product asks for finer bands.
I double checked the contract and found open-day listed twice with different spellings. I am keeping the hyphenated form because the catalog emits that one.
The parser is used in both the write path and the read path, so I put it in facets.ts rather than in either handler, to keep one canonical definition.

edit.old: export function parseFacet(name: string, value: string) { return { name, value }; }
edit.new: export function parseFacet(name: string, value: string): Facet { const kind = FACET_NAMES.find((n) => n === name); if (!kind) throw new UnknownFacet(name, FACET_NAMES); return { name: kind, value: parseValueFor(kind, value) }; }

search.approve: A closed facet vocabulary with a specific error is what keeps the filter surface honest.

revise.reason: The parser accepts a valid facet name with an out-of-range value and returns it unchanged.
revise.directive: Validate the value against the allowed set for that facet before returning.

search.title: Track document versions per tenant entity
search.intent: Track a monotonically increasing version for every indexed document, so that a late or replayed catalog event cannot overwrite a newer one. The version column and its helper live in src/search/versions.ts and the matching column is added in the foundations migration. The contract spells out that the version comes from the catalog event, not from the index.
search.acceptance: An update with a lower version than the stored one is ignored and reported as stale, and an equal version is treated as a no-op.
thinking: The version must come from the catalog, because the index cannot know the true order of changes made upstream. I will take the version as an input and never generate one here.
I was tempted to use the updated-at timestamp instead of a counter. Timestamps can tie or skew between hosts, so a counter from the source is the safer comparison.
Equal versions are a real case when an event is delivered twice. Treating them as a no-op rather than an error keeps the consumer quiet on normal redelivery.
The stale result needs to be visible in logs, not swallowed, so the helper returns a discriminated result and the caller decides how loudly to report it.
The migration adds the version column with a default of zero. Existing rows are all version zero, which is correct because the first real event will have a higher number.

edit.old: export function shouldApply(stored: number, incoming: number) { return incoming > stored; }
edit.new: export function decideVersion(stored: number, incoming: number): VersionDecision { if (incoming < stored) return { kind: 'stale', stored, incoming }; if (incoming === stored) return { kind: 'noop' }; return { kind: 'apply' }; }

search.approve: Using the source's counter and returning a typed decision keeps replays safe and visible.

revise.reason: The stale branch returns the same shape as apply, so callers cannot tell a dropped update from a written one.
revise.directive: Return a distinct discriminant for stale results and update the callers to handle it.

search.title: Accept index upsert commands from catalog events
search.intent: Accept an upsert command that carries one catalog listing change and writes the resulting IndexDocument. The command handler lives in src/search/commands/upsert.ts and calls the mapper, the version decision and the registry in that order. The contract in contracts/search.md lists the command fields so the catalog publisher can build them.
search.acceptance: A valid upsert writes exactly one document, and a command with a missing tenant id is rejected before any write happens.
thinking: The upsert is the first command that writes, so I want its order of checks fixed and obvious. Tenancy first, then mapping, then the version decision, and only then the write.
I considered letting the handler write and then check the version afterward. That would race with a concurrent update, so the version check must sit in front of the write.
The handler returns a result object instead of throwing on stale input. A stale event is expected traffic, not an error, so throwing would flood the logs.
I found the catalog publisher sends the listing as a nested envelope. The handler unwraps it once at the top and passes the plain payload downstream, so the mapper stays ignorant of the envelope.
The test asserts that a rejected command performs zero writes by counting calls on a fake store. That is the property that matters most here.

edit.old: export async function upsert(cmd: UpsertCommand) { return store.write(mapListing(cmd.payload)); }
edit.new: export async function upsert(cmd: UpsertCommand): Promise<UpsertResult> { const tenant = requireTenancy(cmd); const doc = mapListing(cmd.payload.listing); const decision = decideVersion(await store.version(tenant, doc.entityId), doc.version); if (decision.kind !== 'apply') return { kind: decision.kind }; await store.write(doc); return { kind: 'written' }; }

search.approve: Fixed check order and zero writes on rejection is exactly the contract I wanted to see here.

revise.reason: The version is read and the write happens in separate statements, so two concurrent upserts can both apply.
revise.directive: Move the version comparison into the same transaction as the write using a conditional update.

search.title: Validate query strings against length limits
search.intent: Validate incoming query strings for length, character class and emptiness before they reach the dictionary step. The validator is in src/search/validate-query.ts and returns a typed result that the read handler maps onto an error envelope. Limits come from the contract in contracts/search.md so they can change without touching code.
search.acceptance: A query longer than the configured maximum is rejected with a length error, and a whitespace-only query is treated as empty rather than matching everything.
thinking: Validation has to happen before tokenization, or a huge query string would reach Postgres and cost real time. The validator runs first in the read path, with no exceptions.

A whitespace-only query would normalize to an empty string, and an empty tsquery matches nothing in some configurations and everything in others. I am rejecting it explicitly so the behaviour does not depend on Postgres defaults.
The length limit is read from the contract constants rather than hard coded, so a product change does not need a code change. I still assert the constant exists at startup.
I thought about stripping control characters silently. I decided to reject them instead, since silent stripping would make a bug report look like the search returned wrong results.
The error includes the limit value in the message so a client developer can see the boundary without reading the contract.

edit.old: export function validateQuery(q: string) { return q.length > 0; }
edit.new: export function validateQuery(q: string): QueryCheck { const trimmed = q.trim(); if (trimmed.length === 0) return { ok: false, reason: 'empty' }; if (trimmed.length > QUERY_MAX_LENGTH) return { ok: false, reason: 'too-long', max: QUERY_MAX_LENGTH }; if (CONTROL_CHARS.test(trimmed)) return { ok: false, reason: 'control-characters' }; return { ok: true, query: trimmed }; }

search.approve: Rejecting rather than stripping keeps bad input visible, which is what a reviewer would want from a validator.

revise.reason: The length check runs on the untrimmed string, so padded queries are rejected even when their content is short.
revise.directive: Measure the length of the trimmed query, not the raw input, and test a padded short query.

search.title: Return a typed error for malformed filters
search.intent: Return a typed error when a request's filter object is malformed, such as a missing operator or a value of the wrong type. The error type and its mapping to the error envelope live in src/search/errors.ts, and the envelope shape is taken from the platform contract that the write path already uses. The filter parser reports which path inside the object failed.
search.acceptance: A filter with an unknown operator returns a 400 envelope naming the offending path, and no partial filter is ever applied.
thinking: The error type needs to say where the problem is, so I will carry a path array rather than a single string. A path like filters.venue.op is far more useful to a client than 'bad filter'.

I first wrote the parser to skip unknown operators and keep going. That would silently widen the result set, which is the worst kind of failure for a filter, so the parser now stops at the first error.
The envelope mapping has to match what the write path returns. I compared with the existing error envelope helper and reuse its status and code fields rather than inventing new ones.
I need to decide whether to report every bad path or only the first. Reporting only the first is simpler and keeps the envelope to one error, which is enough for a client to fix one thing at a time.
The test feeds a wrong-typed value into a range operator and checks that the returned path points at the value, not the whole filter.

edit.new: if (!OPS.includes(op)) throw new FilterError(['filters', key, 'op'], `unknown operator '${op}'`);

search.approve: Stopping at the first bad operator instead of skipping it is the correct failure direction for filters.

revise.reason: The thrown FilterError is not caught by the read handler, so the client receives a 500 rather than the typed 400.
revise.directive: Catch FilterError in the read handler and map it to the 400 envelope with its path.

search.title: Reject writes that target a closed index
search.intent: Reject any write whose target index generation is closed, which happens while a rebuild is cutting over. The check lives in src/search/commands/guard.ts and reads the generation state from the registry rather than caching it. Callers receive a retryable error so the catalog event is redelivered after the cutover completes.
search.acceptance: A write to a closed generation returns a retryable result and performs no database write.
thinking: A closed generation means a rebuild is swapping indexes, and writing into the old one would lose the update. The guard has to run before any write, so it is the first thing in the command chain.
