I want the guard to read fresh state rather than the cache, because a cached open state could be stale for the length of a cutover. The cost is one indexed lookup per write, which is acceptable here.
The error must be retryable, not fatal, so the outbox redelivers the event later. I checked the outbox contract and it treats a retryable result as a reschedule, not a dead letter.
I double checked that a read is not blocked by a closed generation. Reads can keep serving the old generation during cutover, so the guard only applies to writes.
The test simulates a cutover by flipping the registry state between two calls, which catches the case where the guard passes and the write is then made into a closed index.

edit.old: export function guardWrite(t: TenantRecord) { return true; }
edit.new: export async function guardWrite(t: TenantRecord, registry: Registry): Promise<GuardResult> { const gen = await registry.currentGeneration(t.id); if (gen.state === 'closed') return { kind: 'retry', after: CUTOVER_RETRY_MS }; return { kind: 'open', generation: gen.number }; }

search.approve: Reading fresh state for the guard is the right trade for correctness during a cutover.

revise.reason: The guard returns the generation number but the upsert still writes to the generation it read earlier.
revise.directive: Pass the generation returned by the guard through to the write so both use the same value.

search.title: Serve ranked results with a stable cursor
search.intent: Serve ranked results for a query, returning a page of documents and a cursor that resumes the same ordering. The read handler lives in src/search/queries/ranked.ts and the cursor encoding in src/search/cursor.ts. The contract in contracts/search.md fixes the ordering as rank, then version, then entity id, so ties never shuffle between pages.
search.acceptance: Paging through a result set twice returns the same ordering, and the cursor from one page resumes exactly after its last item.
thinking: The ordering needs a total tie-breaker, otherwise two documents with equal rank can swap between pages. I am using entity id as the last key, since it is unique per tenant.
I considered an offset-based cursor because it is the obvious first version. It breaks as soon as a document is inserted, so I am encoding the last seen tuple instead.
The cursor is opaque to clients but I still want it tamper-evident. I sign it with a tenant-scoped key so a cursor from one tenant cannot be replayed against another.
I was worried that ranking the whole table per page would be slow. The query uses an index on the tsvector and the version, and I checked the plan before going further.
The test pages through a fixture of seven documents with two equal ranks and checks that the concatenated pages equal one full fetch.

edit.new: export const encodeCursor = (last: RankKey, tenant: TenantId): Cursor => sign({ r: last.rank, v: last.version, e: last.entityId }, keyFor(tenant));

search.approve: A total order with a tuple cursor and a tenant-scoped signature gives stable paging I can trust.

revise.reason: The signing key is shared across tenants, so a cursor from one tenant validates against another.
revise.directive: Derive the signing key from the tenant id so a cursor only validates for its own tenant.

search.title: Filter results by venue category and region
search.intent: Apply venue category and region filters to the ranked query, combining them with AND across facets and OR within a facet. The filter composition lives in src/search/queries/filter-clause.ts and uses the facet model from earlier. Region values come from the closed set in contracts/search.md, so an unknown region cannot quietly match nothing.
search.acceptance: Two categories in one facet match documents in either category, and combining a category with a region returns only documents that satisfy both.
thinking: The AND-across, OR-within rule is the one most likely to be built backwards, so I write the test cases for it first. Two categories should widen, while category plus region should narrow.
The clause builder must use parameter placeholders for every value. Concatenating a region name into SQL would be a real injection risk, even though the value is from a closed set.
I was going to skip empty facets entirely. Then I realized an explicit empty array from the client should mean no filter, not match nothing, so I handle that case deliberately.
The composed clause is wrapped in a single parenthesized group, because a later OR in the query builder would otherwise bind to the wrong side.
I checked the closed region set and found one region name with a trailing space in the contract. I fixed it there and added a test so the trailing space cannot come back.

edit.new: return { sql: `(${values.map((_, i) => `${col} = $${base + i}`).join(' OR ')})`, params: values };

search.approve: Parameterized clauses with the boolean rule pinned by tests is what I wanted to see here.

revise.reason: The clause uses an interpolated column name derived from the request, which bypasses the facet allowlist.
revise.directive: Resolve the column name only through the facet allowlist and reject anything else.

search.title: Page results with keyset pagination
search.intent: Page results with keyset pagination on the ranked order, keeping page requests fast on large tenants. The page builder lives in src/search/queries/page.ts and reuses the cursor from the ranked read. The limit is capped by the contract value, and a request above the cap is clamped with a header that says so.
search.acceptance: A page of size twenty returns at most twenty items and a next cursor only when more results exist.
thinking: Keyset paging needs one extra row fetched to know whether a next page exists. I will request limit plus one and trim it, which avoids a second count query.
The clamp on the limit is a product rule, so I put it in the page builder and not the handler. A client asking for a thousand should get twenty, with a header that explains the clamp.
I thought about returning a total count. It is expensive on a large tenant and nobody asked for it, so I am leaving it out and noting that in the contract.
The test seeds exactly twenty and exactly twenty-one documents, because the boundary between a final page and a page with a next cursor is where off-by-one bugs live.
Paging with a cursor from a different query shape should be rejected. I added a check that the cursor's filter hash matches the current request.

edit.new: const cap = Math.min(limit, PAGE_MAX); const rows = await db.query(sql, [cap + 1]); const hasNext = rows.length > cap;

search.approve: Fetching one extra row for the next-page decision is a clean way to avoid the count query.

revise.reason: The clamp is applied after the query is built, so the query fetches the unclamped limit.
revise.directive: Clamp the limit before building the query so the database never reads more rows than the cap.

search.title: Expose a suggestion endpoint for partial names
search.intent: Expose a suggestion endpoint that returns up to five resource names for a partial input, used by the booking form autocomplete. The handler lives in src/search/queries/suggest.ts and uses a prefix match on the normalized name column. Suggestions never include documents from another tenant, and the response shape is listed in contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: A two-character prefix returns at most five suggestions, all of which start with the normalized prefix.
thinking: The suggestion input goes through the same normalizer as the index, otherwise an uppercase prefix would never match a lowercase stored name.
I considered fuzzy matching with trigrams. It is better quality but I do not have a real need for typo tolerance yet, so I am keeping the prefix match and noting trigrams as a later idea.
The limit of five is small on purpose. A long suggestion list is a usability problem for a form, and the cap also keeps the query cheap.
I verified the prefix query uses the normalized name index by checking the plan. A sequential scan here would be fine at current sizes but would be noticed later.
The test includes a document from a second tenant with a matching name to prove that the tenant filter is applied before the limit.

edit.new: const q = normalize(input); if (q.length < SUGGEST_MIN_PREFIX) return { suggestions: [] };

search.approve: Normalizing the prefix with the index normalizer prevents the silent empty-result bug.

revise.reason: The minimum prefix check returns an empty list silently, which hides a client bug from the endpoint's caller.
revise.directive: Return a typed validation error for prefixes below the minimum instead of an empty list.

search.title: Consume catalog change events into the index
search.intent: Consume catalog change events from the outbox and feed each one into the upsert command, acknowledging only after the write commits. The consumer lives in src/search/consumers/catalog.ts and reads its subscription name from the platform config. The event shape is fixed by the catalog section of contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: A catalog event is acknowledged only after its document is committed, and a handler failure leaves the event unacknowledged for redelivery.
thinking: The acknowledgement ordering is the whole point of this unit. If I ack before the write commits, a crash loses the change permanently, so the ack goes last.
I checked how the outbox reports a handler failure. It redelivers unacknowledged events, so a thrown error is the right signal and I do not need to build retry logic here.
The consumer must not swallow a mapping error into an ack, or a malformed listing would be dropped without a trace. A mapping error goes to the dead-letter path instead.
I noticed the subscription name was hard coded in the consumer. I moved it to the platform config so the staging environment can run its own subscription.
The test simulates a commit failure after the write and asserts that the event is not acknowledged, which is the case a naive implementation gets wrong.

edit.new: const result = await upsert(msg.data); if (result.kind === 'written' || result.kind === 'noop' || result.kind === 'stale') await msg.ack();

shell.description: Run catalog consumer ack ordering tests

search.approve: Acking after commit with a dead-letter path for malformed input is exactly the delivery guarantee I want.

revise.reason: The ack is sent on the retry result, so a retryable guard response acknowledges an event that was never written.
revise.directive: Leave retryable results unacknowledged so the outbox redelivers them.

search.title: Publish index-updated events to the outbox
search.intent: Publish an index-updated event to the outbox after each committed write, so that analytics and notifications can react without reading the index. The publisher lives in src/search/events/publish.ts and writes in the same transaction as the document, so the event and the change commit together or not at all.
search.acceptance: A committed write produces exactly one outbox event, and a rolled-back write produces none.
thinking: Publishing outside the transaction would let the event exist without its document, so the outbox row goes in the same transaction as the write. That is the whole reason outboxes exist.
The event payload should carry the version and entity id but not the full document. Consumers that need fields can read the document, and a smaller payload keeps the outbox table lean.
I thought about publishing on every stale result too, for observability. That would make analytics count noise, so I am only publishing on a real write.
I checked the upsert to confirm the publish call sits inside the transaction boundary and not after it. I had put it after the commit once, and I moved it back.
The test forces a rollback after the document write and asserts zero outbox rows, which proves the transactional coupling holds.

edit.new: await outbox.enqueue(tx, { type: 'index.updated', tenantId: doc.tenantId, entityId: doc.entityId, version: doc.version });

search.approve: Writing the outbox row in the same transaction with a slim payload is the right coupling.

revise.reason: The enqueue call is missing the transaction handle, so it commits on a separate connection.
revise.directive: Pass the open transaction into the enqueue call so the event commits with the document.

search.title: Honor the catalog contract version
search.intent: Honor the catalog contract version on incoming events, rejecting any event whose contract major version this consumer does not understand. The version check lives in src/search/consumers/contract-version.ts and the supported major is listed in contracts/search.md. Unknown versions go to the dead-letter path rather than being guessed at.
search.acceptance: An event with a supported major version is processed and an event with an unsupported major goes to the dead-letter path with its version recorded.
thinking: Contract versions are a promise between teams. If I guess at an unknown major version, I might index fields with different meanings, which is worse than refusing the event.
I only check the major number. Minor versions are additive by the catalog's own rule, so a higher minor should still be processed.
The dead-letter path needs the version in its record, otherwise the on-call engineer cannot tell a new catalog release from a corrupt message.
I double checked the version format in the contract. It is a plain string like '2.4', and I parse it with a strict pattern so '2' or 'v2' fail loudly.
The test covers a minor bump on a supported major, which should pass, since a naive equality check would have wrongly rejected it.

edit.new: const major = parseMajor(event.contractVersion); if (!SUPPORTED_MAJORS.includes(major)) return { kind: 'dead-letter', reason: 'unsupported-major', major };

search.approve: Matching on the major only with a strict parse is the right reading of the contract rule.

revise.reason: The strict parse accepts '2' with no minor part, which the contract says must be rejected.
revise.directive: Reject version strings that do not match the major.minor pattern.

search.title: Deliver index changes to webhook subscribers
search.intent: Deliver index changes to tenant webhook subscribers, signing each request and retrying on non-2xx responses. The delivery worker lives in src/search/webhooks/deliver.ts and reads subscriber URLs from the tenant's configuration. The payload and signature header are described in contracts/search.md so subscribers can verify them.
search.acceptance: Each delivery carries a valid HMAC signature over the body, and a 500 response causes a retry with the same event id.
thinking: The signature is computed over the exact bytes sent, so I serialize the body once and sign that buffer rather than signing an object and serializing again.
Retries must reuse the event id, so a subscriber can deduplicate. I generate the id at enqueue time and never in the delivery loop.
I considered an unbounded retry. A subscriber that is down for a week should not hold a worker forever, so retries are capped and the event is then dead-lettered.
The timeout on each request is short. I checked the platform default and it is longer than a sensible webhook timeout, so I set an explicit value.
The test returns a 500 once and then a 200, and checks that both attempts carry the identical event id header.

shell.description: Run webhook delivery and retry tests

search.approve: Signing the exact serialized bytes and reusing the event id gives subscribers what they need to verify and dedupe.

revise.reason: The body is serialized twice, so the signed bytes and the sent bytes can differ if key order ever changes.
revise.directive: Serialize the body once and use that buffer for both the signature and the request.

search.title: Guard index writes with optimistic version checks
search.intent: Guard index writes with an optimistic version check in the store, so that two workers racing on one document cannot both win. The conditional write lives in src/search/store/write.ts and compares the expected version in the WHERE clause. A lost race returns a conflict result that the command handler retries once before giving up.
search.acceptance: Two concurrent writes at the same expected version result in exactly one applied write and one conflict.
thinking: The version check has to live in the SQL, not in the application, because the application read is exactly the window the race needs. A conditional update closes it.
A conflict should be retried once, since the other writer may have applied an equal or newer version. After that I give up and let the outbox redeliver, rather than loop.
The retry must re-read the version before deciding. Retrying the same write blindly could overwrite a newer document with an older one.
I checked the isolation level of the connection pool. The conditional update is safe under read committed, so I do not need serializable and its cost.
The concurrency test starts two writers behind a barrier, so both read before either writes, which reproduces the race reliably.

edit.old: await db.query('update docs set fields = $1 where entity_id = $2', [f, id]);
edit.new: const res = await db.query('update docs set fields = $1, version = $2 where entity_id = $3 and version = $4', [f, next, id, expected]); if (res.rowCount === 0) return { kind: 'conflict' };

search.approve: Putting the version predicate in the UPDATE is the only place this race is actually closed.

revise.reason: The conflict path retries with the stale expected version from the first read, so every retry conflicts.
revise.directive: Re-read the stored version before the single retry and use the fresh value as the expected one.

search.title: Deduplicate replayed catalog events by key
search.intent: Deduplicate replayed catalog events by their idempotency key, so a redelivered event that already committed is recognized and skipped. The processed-key table is written in the same transaction as the document, and the check lives in src/search/consumers/dedupe.ts. The key format is described in contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: An event with an already-recorded key is acknowledged without a second write, and the processed-key row is written in the same transaction as the document.
thinking: The version check already makes most replays harmless, but a replay of an older event with a lower version is still a stale result. I want an explicit key so the replay is recognized rather than merely ignored.
The processed-key row has to commit with the document. If it committed separately, a crash between them would either double apply or drop the event.
I considered keeping keys forever. The migration sets a retention column so old keys can be pruned later, which I am deferring to the rollout unit.
I double checked the key includes the tenant id. Two tenants can produce the same entity key, and a global key would wrongly skip the second one.
The test replays the same event three times and asserts exactly one document write and one processed-key row.

edit.new: if (await seen(tenantId, key, tx)) return { kind: 'noop' };

search.approve: A tenant-scoped key checked inside the transaction is the right replay guard.

revise.reason: The seen check runs outside the transaction, so two replays arriving together can both pass it.
revise.directive: Run the seen lookup and the key insert inside the same transaction as the document write.

search.title: Retry failed index flushes with jittered backoff
search.intent: Retry failed index flushes with jittered exponential backoff, so a brief Postgres outage does not cause a thundering herd on recovery. The retry policy lives in src/search/flush/retry.ts and is applied by the flush loop in src/search/flush/loop.ts. The policy limits are in contracts/search.md so operations can tune them.
search.acceptance: Retry delays grow exponentially with jitter inside the configured bounds, and the flush gives up after the configured attempt count.
thinking: A flush that fails should back off, not spin. I am using full jitter so that a fleet of workers recovering together do not all retry on the same beat.
I checked the random source. I want it injectable for tests, so the policy takes a random function and the production code passes Math.random.
The cap on total attempts matters. Without it a long outage would keep a flush alive indefinitely, and the lag metric would look like a healthy but slow flush.
I was going to retry every error. Validation errors will never succeed on retry, so only transient connection and timeout errors are retried.
The test pins the random function to fixed values and asserts the exact sequence of delays, which catches an off-by-one in the exponent.

edit.new: const ceiling = Math.min(CAP_MS, base * 2 ** attempt); const delay = Math.floor(random() * ceiling);

search.approve: Full jitter with an injectable random source makes the backoff both correct and testable.

revise.reason: The ceiling is not applied before jitter, so a late attempt can exceed the configured maximum delay.
revise.directive: Apply the cap to the exponential ceiling before drawing the jittered delay.

search.title: Serialize concurrent reindex jobs per tenant
search.intent: Serialize concurrent reindex jobs per tenant with an advisory lock, so two reindex runs for the same tenant cannot interleave. The lock is taken in src/search/reindex/lock.ts using the tenant's numeric lock key, and a second job waits briefly and then exits with a clear message. The lock key derivation is noted in contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: A second reindex for a tenant with a running job exits with a locked result and does not write any documents.
thinking: An advisory lock is the lightest tool here and it releases on connection drop, which matters if a worker crashes mid-job. I do not want a table-based lock that could be left stuck.
The lock key is derived from the tenant id with a stable hash. I checked that the hash does not change between Node versions, because a changed key would let two runs lock different keys.
Waiting forever for the lock would hide a stuck job. I wait a bounded interval, then exit with a locked result that names the holder.
I thought about locking at the registry level instead. That would block reads too, so the lock is scoped to reindex jobs only.
The test starts two jobs concurrently and asserts that exactly one writes and the other returns locked.

edit.new: const got = await db.query('select pg_try_advisory_lock($1) as ok', [key]); if (!got.rows[0].ok) return { kind: 'locked', tenant };

search.approve: A try-lock with a clear locked result beats a blocking lock that can hang a worker forever.

revise.reason: The try-lock result is returned but the lock is never released on the locked path, which is fine but the release call is missing on success.
revise.directive: Release the advisory lock in a finally block on every path that acquired it.

search.title: Add the documents table migration
search.intent: Add the documents table migration that creates the storage for indexed documents with the tenant, entity, version and fields columns. The migration is migrations/search_0003_documents.sql and the table definition is mirrored in src/search/store/schema.ts for the typed query builder. The primary key is tenant plus entity, matching the contract.
search.acceptance: The migration applies cleanly on an empty database and rolls back to the prior schema with no leftover objects.
thinking: The primary key is tenant plus entity, not entity alone, because two tenants may legitimately share an entity key. Getting this wrong would make cross-tenant writes collide.
I wrote the down migration first, so I know the rollback is possible before I commit to the up. It drops the table and the two indexes and nothing else.
The fields column is jsonb rather than a set of columns. The contract allows arbitrary text fields, so a fixed column list would need a migration for every new field.
I checked the schema mirror against the migration by hand and found the version column typed as text in the mirror. I changed it to bigint to match.
The migration test applies up, down and up again to prove it is repeatable on the same database.
search.approve: Tenant-plus-entity as the key and a reversible down migration are both right for this table.

revise.reason: The down migration drops the table but not the index on the fields column, so a re-apply fails on the existing name.
revise.directive: Drop every index created by the up migration in the down migration and re-test the round trip.

search.title: Backfill existing listings into the index
search.intent: Backfill existing catalog listings into the index in batches, so that tenants onboarded before the consumer existed become searchable. The backfill job lives in src/search/backfill/run.ts and reads listings through the catalog read API in batches of five hundred. Progress is checkpointed so a restart resumes from the last committed batch.
search.acceptance: A backfill over a fixture of twelve hundred listings writes every listing exactly once and resumes correctly after a simulated crash.
thinking: A backfill and the live consumer can write the same entity at the same time. The version check makes that safe, so the backfill uses the same upsert path rather than a bulk insert that bypasses it.
The checkpoint is written after each committed batch. If I checkpointed before the batch, a crash mid-batch would skip listings silently.
I was going to read the whole catalog in one call. That would hold memory for a large tenant, so I page through the catalog read API in fixed batches.

I considered running the backfill while the consumer is paused. That is an operational step rather than a code guarantee, so I left the version check as the real protection and documented the operator step separately.
The test kills the job after the third batch and restarts it, then checks that the final count is exactly twelve hundred with no duplicates.

edit.new: for await (const batch of catalog.pages(tenant, { size: BACKFILL_BATCH })) { await upsertBatch(batch); await checkpoint.save(tenant, batch.cursor); }

shell.description: Run backfill resume and count tests

search.approve: Routing the backfill through the same versioned upsert with a post-batch checkpoint is the safe design.

revise.reason: The checkpoint is saved before the upsert batch completes, so a crash mid-batch loses those listings.
revise.directive: Save the checkpoint only after the batch upsert has committed.

search.title: Rebuild a tenant index without downtime
search.intent: Rebuild a tenant index into a new generation without downtime, then switch reads over once the new generation is populated. The rebuild lives in src/search/rebuild/generation.ts and uses the registry to create the next generation and flip the active pointer. The cutover order is written out in contracts/search.md so operators can follow it during an incident.
search.acceptance: Reads keep returning results throughout a rebuild, and after the pointer flips every read uses the new generation.
thinking: The old generation keeps serving reads until the flip, so the rebuild never takes the tenant offline. The only moment of downtime is a closed write window, which the guard already handles.
I need the flip to be a single pointer update in the registry. If reads resolved the generation in two steps, a read could mix old and new results.
I considered deleting the old generation right after the flip. Deletion is destructive and cannot be undone, so the old generation stays until the cleanup unit removes it under the retention rule.

The new generation is built while the consumer keeps writing to the old one, so the rebuild has to replay writes that arrive during the build. I am recording a high-water mark and replaying from it before the flip.
The test runs a read loop during the rebuild and asserts no read returns an error or an empty result for a populated tenant.

edit.new: await replayFrom(tenant, highWaterMark); await registry.flipGeneration(tenant, { from: current, to: next });

shell.description: Run zero-downtime rebuild read loop tests

search.approve: Replaying from a high-water mark before a single flip is what makes the rebuild genuinely non-disruptive.

revise.reason: The flip does not check that the replay finished, so a flip with pending replay could lose the last writes.
revise.directive: Assert the replay has reached the high-water mark before calling flipGeneration.

search.title: Drop stale index columns after cutover
search.intent: Drop the stale index columns left over from the pre-generation layout once every tenant has cut over. The removal is a separate migration, migrations/search_0005_drop_legacy.sql, that is only applied after the cutover check passes. The check is written in src/search/migrate/cutover-check.ts and refuses to run while any tenant still reads the legacy column.
search.acceptance: The cutover check fails while a single tenant still has a legacy pointer, and passes once all tenants are on a generation.
thinking: Dropping a column is irreversible in practice, so the migration is gated behind a check rather than run unconditionally. I want the check to be the thing that makes the drop safe.
The check counts tenants whose registry row still points at the legacy layout. Zero is the only passing answer, and I do not allow a threshold.
I was going to write the down migration as re-adding the column empty. That would silently lose the legacy data, so the down path is documented as a restore from backup rather than scripted.
I checked for any code still reading the legacy column. One old query in the read path still selects it, and I removed that reference before writing the drop.
The test seeds one legacy tenant and asserts the check fails, then flips it and asserts the check passes.

edit.old: export async function canDrop() { return true; }
edit.new: export async function canDrop(db: Db): Promise<boolean> { const { rows } = await db.query('select count(*)::int as n from search_registry where layout = $1', ['legacy']); return rows[0].n === 0; }

shell.description: Run legacy column cutover gate tests

search.approve: A gate with zero tolerance and a documented restore path is the correct level of care for a destructive drop.

revise.reason: The cutover check counts only active tenants, so suspended tenants still on legacy are not counted and the drop would strand them.
revise.directive: Count every tenant row regardless of status when checking for legacy layout.

search.title: Emit index lag metrics per tenant
search.intent: Emit an index lag metric per tenant, measuring the time between a catalog event being published and its document being committed. The metric is recorded in src/search/metrics/lag.ts with a tenant label and exported through the platform metrics client. The metric name and buckets are listed in contracts/search.md so dashboards can be built against them.
search.acceptance: Each committed write records one lag observation labelled with its tenant, and a redelivered event records no extra observation.
thinking: Lag is measured from the event's publish time, not the consume time, because the consume time would hide a backlog that built up in the outbox.
The tenant label is a real cardinality concern. Tenants are bounded in this system, so a tenant label is acceptable, but I am not adding entity ids as labels under any circumstance.
A redelivered event should not record a second observation, since that would double count the same change and skew the histogram. I record only on the apply branch.
I checked that the clock comes from the event's publish timestamp and the local clock, which can skew across hosts. I clamp negative lag to zero and count those in a separate counter.
The test feeds an event published two seconds ago and asserts the histogram observation falls in the two-second bucket.

edit.new: export const recordLag = (tenant: TenantId, publishedAt: number, now: number) => { const raw = now - publishedAt; if (raw < 0) skewCounter.inc({ tenant }); lagHistogram.observe({ tenant }, Math.max(0, raw)); };

shell.description: Run index lag metric observation tests

search.approve: Measuring from publish time with a separate skew counter keeps the lag honest across hosts.

revise.reason: The skew counter is incremented but the negative raw value is still observed unclamped in the histogram elsewhere.
revise.directive: Record only the clamped value in every lag histogram observation path.

search.title: Trace query latency across the ranker stages
search.intent: Trace query latency across the ranker stages, with one span each for validation, filter composition, the ranked fetch and the page build. The spans are opened in src/search/queries/trace.ts and attach the tenant and result count as attributes. The span names are listed in contracts/search.md so trace queries stay stable.
search.acceptance: A single read request produces four child spans under one root with the tenant attribute set on each.
thinking: Four spans make the cost visible without drowning the trace. I resisted per-document spans, since they would dominate the trace on a page of twenty.
The span helper takes a name from a closed union, so a typo in a span name becomes a compile error and the names in the contract stay authoritative.
The tenant attribute goes on every span, not only the root, so a dashboard can filter a stage by tenant without joining through the root.

I was unsure whether the result count belongs on the page span or the ranked span. The page span is where the count is final, so I attach it there and leave the ranked span with the raw candidate count.
The test uses an in-memory span exporter and asserts the parent id of each child points at the root.

edit.new: export const span = (name: SpanName, tenant: TenantId) => tracer.startSpan(name, { attributes: { tenant } });

shell.description: Run read path span hierarchy tests

search.approve: A closed union of span names with the tenant on every span gives a stable and filterable trace.

revise.reason: The root span is not ended when the ranked stage throws, so the trace is left open and never exported.
revise.directive: End the root span in a finally block so an error still exports the trace.

search.title: Log structured diagnostics for rejected queries
search.intent: Log structured diagnostics for every rejected query, carrying the reason, the tenant and a truncated query hash rather than the raw text. The logger call is in src/search/diagnostics/rejected.ts and uses the platform structured logger. The field names are listed in contracts/search.md so log queries work across the platform.
search.acceptance: A rejected query produces one log line with a reason and a hash, and the raw query text never appears in the log output.
thinking: Raw query text can contain personal information, such as a customer's name typed into a search box, so I log a hash rather than the text. The hash is enough to group repeated bad queries.
I truncate the hash to twelve characters. That is long enough to avoid useful collisions for diagnostics and short enough to read in a log line.
The reason comes from the closed union in the validator, so the log never invents a free-text reason that someone would then have to parse.
I checked whether the logger already redacts known fields. It does not, so the redaction is my responsibility here and I keep the raw text out of the log object entirely.
The test captures the log output and asserts the raw query string does not appear anywhere in the serialized line.

edit.new: log.warn({ tenant, reason, queryHash: hashQuery(q).slice(0, 12) }, 'query rejected');

shell.description: Run rejected query log redaction tests

search.approve: Logging a truncated hash and never the raw text is the right privacy default for diagnostics.

revise.reason: The hash function is applied to the untrimmed query, so the same logical query produces two different hashes.
revise.directive: Hash the normalized and trimmed query so equivalent rejections group together.

search.title: Cache hot query results with a short TTL
search.intent: Cache hot query results with a short TTL, keyed on tenant, generation, filter hash and cursor, so repeated first-page queries skip the database. The cache lives in src/search/cache/results.ts and uses the platform cache client. The TTL and key format are fixed in contracts/search.md, and writes invalidate by generation rather than by key.
search.acceptance: A repeated first-page query is served from cache within the TTL, and a write to the tenant makes the next read miss.
thinking: A short TTL keeps the staleness bound small, but writes should invalidate too. Keying on generation alone would not catch a write within a generation, so I need a per-tenant write counter in the key as well.
Caching the cursor-bearing pages is a waste, since they are rarely repeated. I cache only the first page, which is where the repeated traffic from the booking form lands.
The cache key includes the filter hash so two filter combinations never share an entry. I checked that the filter hash is canonical, so a reordered filter object produces the same key.
I considered caching the parsed query. The parse is cheap, so caching the final result is where the saving is, and I left the parse uncached.
The test writes to the tenant between two identical reads and asserts the second read misses.

shell.description: Run first-page cache hit and invalidation tests

search.approve: Putting the write epoch in the key makes invalidation exact without any explicit purge.

revise.reason: The key omits the cursor condition for first pages, so a page request with a cursor can hit the first-page entry.
revise.finding: Cache key collides with cursor pages
revise.directive: Only read and write the cache when the request has no cursor, and keep the first-page marker in the key.

search.title: Cap query fan-out per tenant per minute
search.intent: Cap query fan-out per tenant per minute, so one busy tenant cannot starve the others of database connections. The limiter lives in src/search/quotas/rate.ts and uses a token bucket keyed by tenant. Limits and the response for an exceeded bucket are in contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: A tenant exceeding its bucket receives a 429 with a retry-after header, and a second tenant is unaffected during that time.
thinking: A token bucket handles bursts better than a fixed window, which is what a booking form produces when someone types quickly. The bucket refills continuously.
The limiter is keyed by tenant and not by client, because the isolation goal is between tenants. A client-level limit would not protect the other tenants from a noisy one.
I considered an in-memory bucket. Multiple workers would each get their own budget, so the cap would be multiplied by the worker count, and I am noting a shared store as the later step.
The retry-after value is computed from the refill rate, not hard coded. I verified the arithmetic with a case where the bucket is exactly empty.
The test drains a tenant's bucket and asserts a second tenant still gets a result in the same instant.

edit.new: if (bucket.tokens < 1) return { ok: false, retryAfterMs: Math.ceil((1 - bucket.tokens) / bucket.refillPerMs) };

search.approve: A per-tenant token bucket with a computed retry-after is a clean isolation boundary.

revise.reason: The bucket is keyed by the raw tenant string, so a tenant id with different casing gets a separate budget.
revise.directive: Key the bucket by the canonical branded tenant id so casing cannot split a budget.

search.title: Limit index document size and field count
search.intent: Limit index document size and field count, rejecting any document over the configured byte or field ceiling before it reaches the store. The check is in src/search/store/limits.ts and runs in the mapper's output path. The ceilings are set in contracts/search.md so an oversized catalog entry fails visibly rather than bloating the table.
search.acceptance: A document with one field over the byte ceiling is rejected with the field name in the error, and a document at exactly the ceiling is accepted.
thinking: Limits are cheaper to enforce before the write than to clean up after. An oversized document would bloat the table and slow every index scan that touches it.
The byte count has to be measured in UTF-8 bytes, not characters, or a field full of multi-byte characters would sneak past a character limit.
The boundary test is the one that matters most, so I assert that exactly the ceiling passes and one byte over fails, since the off-by-one here would be easy to miss.
I was going to cap the total document size only. A single huge field could still dominate, so the per-field check is also needed and names the field.
The limit values are read from the contract constants, and the test asserts they are positive integers so a bad config fails at startup.

edit.new: for (const [name, value] of Object.entries(doc.fields)) { if (Buffer.byteLength(value, 'utf8') > FIELD_MAX_BYTES) throw new DocumentTooLarge(name); }

search.approve: Measuring UTF-8 bytes per field with an exact boundary test is the careful version of this check.

revise.reason: The total size check still uses character length, so multi-byte content passes the total check while exceeding the byte ceiling.
revise.directive: Measure the total document size in UTF-8 bytes as well as each field.

search.title: Gate the ranking rollout behind a feature flag
search.intent: Gate the new ranking profile behind a feature flag, so it can be enabled per tenant and turned off without a deploy. The flag check lives in src/search/rollout/flag.ts and is read once per request through the platform flag client. The flag name and default are recorded in contracts/search.md.
search.acceptance: A tenant with the flag off gets the legacy ranking, and enabling the flag for that tenant switches its next request to the new ranking.
thinking: The flag gates only the ranking choice, not the cursor or the filters. Those must behave the same under both rankings or a client paging across a flip would break.
I read the flag once per request and pass the answer down, rather than checking it in several places. Two checks in one request could disagree if the flag flips between them.
The default is off. A new ranking that accidentally turns on for everyone would be the kind of rollout surprise the brief warns about.
I checked whether the flag client has a timeout. It does, and a timeout falls back to the default off value, which is the safe direction here.
The test flips the flag between two requests on the same tenant and asserts that each request uses the ranking that was active when it started.

edit.new: export const useNewRanking = (t: TenantId, flags: FlagClient): Promise<boolean> => flags.enabled('search.ranking.v2', { tenant: t, default: false });

shell.description: Run ranking flag default and per-tenant tests

search.approve: Reading the flag once per request with a safe-off default is the right rollout shape.

revise.reason: The flag is read separately for the cursor and the ranking, so a flip mid-request can mix rankings within one page.
revise.directive: Read the flag once at the start of the request and pass the value to both the cursor and the ranking.

search.title: Add a rollback path for the ranking profile
search.intent: Add a rollback path that restores the previous ranking profile for a tenant in one operation, without a migration. The rollback is a registry call in src/search/rollout/rollback.ts that points the tenant back at the stored prior profile. The procedure and its limits are written in contracts/search.md for the on-call engineer.
search.acceptance: Rolling back a tenant restores the prior profile within one request, and rolling back a tenant with no prior profile fails with a typed error.
thinking: The rollback should be a pointer change to a stored profile, not a recomputation. Recomputing would take time exactly when someone needs the fix quickly.
A tenant with no prior profile has nothing to roll back to. I fail with a typed error instead of silently applying the default, since the default might not be what the operator expects.
I checked whether the rollback needs to bump the generation. It does not, because the documents are unchanged and only the ranking profile pointer moves.
The rollback itself must not be behind the new flag, or a broken flag client would block the fix. I kept it on its own path.
The test rolls a tenant forward to the new profile, then back, and asserts the ranked order matches the pre-rollout order.

edit.old: export async function rollback(t: TenantId) { return registry.setProfile(t, 'default'); }
edit.new: export async function rollback(t: TenantId, registry: Registry): Promise<RollbackResult> { const prior = await registry.priorProfile(t); if (!prior) throw new NoPriorProfile(t); await registry.setProfile(t, prior); return { kind: 'rolled-back', profile: prior }; }

search.approve: A pointer rollback that fails loudly on a missing prior profile is exactly what on-call needs.

revise.reason: The rollback writes the default profile name, not the stored prior one, so it does not restore what the tenant had.
revise.directive: Restore the stored prior profile for the tenant instead of the default name.

search.title: Set retention for deleted document tombstones
search.intent: Set a retention window for deleted document tombstones, so deletes can be replayed to lagging consumers before the tombstone is removed. The retention rule lives in src/search/store/tombstones.ts and the window length is in contracts/search.md. A prune job deletes only tombstones older than the window.
search.acceptance: A tombstone younger than the window is kept, and one older than the window is removed by the prune job.
thinking: A tombstone is the only record that a document was deleted, so removing it too early would let a lagging consumer resurrect the document. The window has to exceed the worst expected consumer lag.
I considered keeping tombstones forever. That is safe but grows the table without bound, so a finite window with a documented length is the middle path.
The prune query uses the deleted-at column with an index, so it does not scan the live documents table. I checked the plan to be sure.
The window is measured against the time the consumer last acknowledged, not the wall clock, when a consumer is lagging. I decided that belongs in a later unit and noted it.
The test seeds one tombstone at the window minus a second and one at the window plus a second, then asserts only the older one is pruned.

edit.new: await db.query('delete from tombstones where deleted_at < now() - make_interval(secs => $1)', [TOMBSTONE_RETENTION_SECS]);

search.approve: A bounded tombstone window stated in the contract is the honest trade between replay safety and table size.

revise.reason: The prune statement has no where clause on the window in the shipped SQL, so it removes every tombstone regardless of age.
revise.directive: Restore the age predicate so only tombstones older than the retention window are deleted.

search.title: Record an audit entry for every reindex run
search.intent: Record an audit entry for every reindex run, capturing who started it, the tenant, the generation pair and the outcome. The audit writer lives in src/search/audit/reindex.ts and writes to the platform audit log through the outbox so it commits with the run's result. The entry fields are listed in contracts/search.md for the compliance review.
search.acceptance: Every completed or failed reindex run produces exactly one audit entry carrying the generation pair, and a locked run produces none.
thinking: An audit entry is only useful if it reflects what actually happened, so I write it at the end of the run in the same transaction as the outcome, not at the start.
A locked run did not do any work, so it should not appear in the audit log as a run. Recording it would make the audit look busier than the system really was.
The actor is the operator or service identity from the request, not a model or a worker id. The contract requires a person or service name here, so I checked that the job carries one before writing.

I considered logging the document contents for traceability. That is not needed for an audit of runs and would leak customer data into the audit store, so I record only the generation pair and counts.
The test runs a successful job, a failing job and a locked job, then asserts exactly two audit rows with the correct outcomes.

edit.new: await audit.write(tx, { tenant, outcome, actor: job.actor, from: job.fromGeneration, to: job.toGeneration, documents: job.count });

search.approve: Writing the audit row with the outcome in one transaction and skipping locked runs keeps the trail accurate.

revise.reason: The audit write happens outside the transaction that records the outcome, so a crash can leave an outcome with no audit entry.
revise.directive: Write the audit entry inside the same transaction that records the run outcome.

analytics.title: Scaffold the event ingestion module and public exports
analytics.intent: Create the src/analytics/ module skeleton with an index.ts that is the only public surface for other Tidewater systems. Add the ingest, rollup and query folders as empty modules so later units have a fixed place to land. The contracts/analytics.md file gets its first heading so reviewers can see what is exported.
analytics.acceptance: The package compiles with tsc --noEmit and importing the index exposes no internal modules.
thinking: Starting with the empty module layout. The index file is the contract with the other seven systems, so I want it to be small and deliberate.
I considered generating the folders with a script, but three empty files are easier to read in review than a generator nobody will rerun.
Checked the existing booking module: it exports a single factory and nothing else. I will do the same here so the rule is consistent across systems.
Wrote an exports test that asserts the index keys. If someone later leaks an internal helper, that test fails loudly rather than silently widening the surface.

shell.description: Run the module export surface test

analytics.approve: Clean skeleton, and the index is the only thing other systems can reach, which is exactly what we want.

revise.reason: The index re-exports an internal helper that other systems should not depend on.
revise.finding: Internal helper leaks through the public index
revise.directive: Remove the re-export of the ingest helper from src/analytics/index.ts and keep only the factory.

analytics.title: Define the tenant-scoped event envelope type
analytics.intent: Introduce the EventEnvelope type in src/analytics/ingest/envelope.ts with tenantId, occurredAt, kind and a typed payload. Every event must carry a tenant identifier so rollups can be partitioned without a join. The envelope shape is written into contracts/analytics.md so the booking and catalog teams can emit against it.
analytics.acceptance: A type-level test rejects an envelope with no tenantId, and the contract file lists every envelope field.
thinking: The envelope is the one shape every producer will depend on, so I want the tenant field to be non-optional at the type level.
I first sketched a generic payload parameter, then dropped it. A discriminated union on kind is simpler for the switch statements in the rollup code.
Went back and forth on whether occurredAt should be a Date or an ISO string. I picked a branded string because JSON round trips through the outbox would lose Date precision otherwise.
The contract doc needs the same field names as the type, so I will generate the table from the type file rather than retyping it.
analytics.approve: The envelope is tight and the tenant key cannot be forgotten, which is the right default.

revise.reason: The tenant identifier was declared optional, so an unscoped event could reach the rollup writer.
revise.finding: Tenant identifier is optional on the envelope
revise.directive: Make tenantId required and typed as TenantId in src/analytics/ingest/envelope.ts.

analytics.title: Load metric retention settings from typed config
analytics.intent: Read the retention window for raw events and for each rollup grain from the typed config loader in src/analytics/config.ts. Defaults live beside the loader so a missing key fails at startup instead of at the first expiry run. The retention table is documented in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: Startup fails with a named error when a retention key is missing, and the defaults match the documented table.
thinking: Retention is the first config that matters for cost, so I want the loader to be strict rather than forgiving.
The existing config helper returns undefined for missing keys. I will wrap it so the analytics loader throws with the key name in the message.
Checked whether the defaults should be per tenant. They should not, not yet; per tenant overrides are a later unit and I will note it instead of building it.
Ran the config test against a deliberately empty environment to confirm the error text names the missing key.
analytics.approve: Fails fast with a useful message, and the defaults are written down where the next person will look.

revise.reason: A missing retention key falls back to zero, which would expire every raw event on the first sweep.
revise.finding: Missing retention key silently defaults to zero
revise.directive: Make requireInt throw a named error when ANALYTICS_RAW_RETENTION_DAYS is absent in src/analytics/config.ts.

analytics.title: Wire tenant keys into the rollup partition scheme
analytics.intent: Derive the partition key for rollup rows from tenantId and grain in src/analytics/rollup/partition.ts. Keeping tenant in the leading column lets the per-tenant query use a range scan. The chosen scheme is recorded in contracts/analytics.md under partitioning.
analytics.acceptance: Two different tenants never produce the same partition key for the same grain and day.
thinking: The partition key is hard to change later, so this unit deserves more care than its size suggests.
I looked at hashing the tenant identifier, but a readable prefix makes operator queries far easier. Readability wins here.
Noticed that a day boundary in UTC versus the tenant's local zone would split a day in two. I kept UTC and wrote that decision into the contract.
The partition test enumerates a small grid of tenants and grains to catch collisions, which is cheap and catches the obvious mistakes.

shell.description: Check partition keys do not collide

analytics.approve: Readable keys, collision test in place, and the UTC choice is written down.

revise.reason: The partition key omits the tenant, so two tenants share one rollup row for the same day.
revise.directive: Include tenantId as the leading segment of the key built in src/analytics/rollup/partition.ts.

analytics.title: Model the page-view and booking-funnel event kinds
analytics.intent: Add the closed list of event kinds the analytics system accepts, starting with page views and the booking funnel steps. The kinds are a string union in src/analytics/ingest/kinds.ts so the rollup switch can be exhaustive. Booking funnel steps mirror the names the booking system emits, and contracts/analytics.md lists each one.
analytics.acceptance: An unknown kind string fails type checking in the rollup switch and at runtime in the ingest validator.
thinking: A closed union is what makes the rollup switch exhaustive, so I am starting with the kinds rather than the handlers.
Booking names its funnel steps in snake case. I will match them exactly, because renaming at the boundary is where events get lost.
The first draft had a generic 'custom' kind as an escape hatch. I removed it: an open escape hatch is how we end up with twenty unowned event types.
Compiled the rollup switch against the new union to confirm the never-check fires when a kind is missing.

analytics.approve: Good closed set, and the exhaustive check is working as intended.

revise.finding: Funnel completion kind has no rollup branch
revise.directive: Add a case for funnel_step_completed to the switch in src/analytics/rollup/switch.ts.

analytics.title: Enforce a closed set of metric dimension names
analytics.intent: Restrict the dimension names a metric may group by to a fixed list in src/analytics/metrics/dimensions.ts. Free-form dimension strings would make the rollup table unbounded, so new dimensions need a code change and a contract update. The allowed list is copied into contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: Grouping by an unlisted dimension returns a validation error naming the dimension.
thinking: Dimension names are a cardinality decision as much as a naming one, so I am treating the list as a budget.
I started with a Set built at runtime. A frozen const array with a derived type gives the compiler the same information and is easier to read.
Checked whether any existing caller passes a dimension we have not listed. The booking dashboard does, for 'venue_region', so I added it and noted it.
The validation error includes the closest allowed name, which is a small thing that saves a support round trip.
analytics.approve: A bounded dimension list is the right constraint, and the error message is useful.

revise.reason: The dimension check accepts any string prefixed with a listed name, so partial names slip through.
revise.directive: Compare dimension names with strict equality against the DIMENSIONS constant in src/analytics/metrics/dimensions.ts.

analytics.title: Compute session boundaries from ordered event times
analytics.intent: Group a tenant's page views into sessions using a thirty-minute inactivity gap, implemented in src/analytics/sessions/boundaries.ts. The function takes events already sorted by occurredAt and returns session start markers. The gap length and its rationale go in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A gap of exactly thirty minutes starts a new session, and a gap of twenty-nine minutes does not.
thinking: Session boundaries look trivial until you hit the exact-threshold case, so the tests matter more than the loop.
I initially compared with greater-than-or-equal and then realised the contract says a gap of exactly thirty minutes starts a new session. The comparison has to match the words in the contract.
There is a temptation to sort inside the function. I decided against it; the caller already sorts for the rollup, and sorting twice would hide a bug upstream.
Ran the boundary tests with a fixture that has a gap of exactly thirty minutes to pin the edge.
analytics.approve: The edge is pinned by a test and matches the contract wording.

revise.reason: The boundary uses a strict greater-than, so an event exactly thirty minutes later merges into the prior session.
revise.finding: Exact-gap event merges into the previous session
revise.directive: Change the gap comparison in src/analytics/sessions/boundaries.ts to treat a gap equal to the threshold as a new session.

analytics.title: Reject events stamped outside the accepted clock skew
analytics.intent: Refuse events whose occurredAt is more than ten minutes in the future or more than seven days in the past, in src/analytics/ingest/skew.ts. Producers with drifting clocks would otherwise write rows into rollup windows that are already closed. The window is stated in contracts/analytics.md so producers know what to expect.
analytics.acceptance: An event ten minutes and one second ahead of the server clock is rejected with a skew error code.
thinking: Clock skew bugs look like data corruption weeks later, so I want the rejection to be explicit and early.
I considered clamping the timestamp instead of rejecting. Clamping hides a producer bug, so rejecting is the honest choice even though it is less forgiving.
Checked how the test harness fakes the clock. It uses a fixed now, which makes the boundary deterministic; I will pass now in as an argument rather than read Date.now inside the check.
The seven day past window is generous on purpose because the outbox can replay for days after an outage.
analytics.approve: Explicit rejection with a deterministic clock, which is exactly how this should behave.

revise.reason: The future check uses a strict comparison, so an event at exactly the limit passes when the contract says it must be rejected.
revise.finding: Future limit comparison is off by one
revise.directive: Use an inclusive comparison for the future skew limit in src/analytics/ingest/skew.ts to match the contract.

analytics.title: Accept event batches through the ingest command
analytics.intent: Expose an ingestBatch command in src/analytics/ingest/ingest.ts that takes up to five hundred envelopes and validates each one before anything is written. The command returns per-item accept or reject results so producers can retry only the failures. The request and response shapes are fixed in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A batch of five hundred valid envelopes returns five hundred accepted results in input order.
thinking: The batch command is the first place where many things can go wrong at once, so I want the result type to describe every item.
I thought about a transaction around the whole batch and decided on per item results instead. A single poisoned event should not block four hundred and ninety nine good ones.
Input order matters to producers that match results back to their own ids. I wrote a test that shuffles input and asserts the output follows the input index.
Limit of five hundred comes from the outbox payload budget, which I checked in the outbox config before setting it.

edit.new: if (batch.length === 0 || batch.length > MAX_BATCH) throw new BatchSizeError(batch.length);

analytics.approve: Per item results and ordered output are what producers need, and the size guard is in the right place.

revise.reason: The batch command accepts more than five hundred envelopes, which overflows the outbox payload budget.
revise.finding: Batch size limit is not enforced
revise.directive: Reject batches longer than MAX_BATCH with BatchSizeError in src/analytics/ingest/ingest.ts.

analytics.title: Validate event payload size before enqueueing
analytics.intent: Measure each serialised envelope in src/analytics/ingest/size.ts and refuse any single event above sixty-four kilobytes. Oversized payloads are caught before they reach the outbox so they cannot poison a whole batch write. The limit is listed in contracts/analytics.md next to the batch limit.
analytics.acceptance: A payload of sixty-four kilobytes plus one byte is rejected with a size code and the batch continues.
thinking: Measuring bytes rather than characters matters here, since multi byte page titles would otherwise slip under the limit.
I first measured after JSON.stringify and then realised the outbox adds its own framing, so I budget a small margin below the hard limit.
The check runs per item, so one oversized event produces one rejection rather than failing the batch. That keeps the batch semantics from the previous unit intact.
Ran the size test with a string of exactly the limit and one more byte to confirm the boundary.
analytics.approve: Byte counting with a per item rejection is correct and the boundary is tested.

revise.reason: The size check counts JavaScript string length, so multi byte characters are undercounted against the byte limit.
revise.finding: Size measured in characters not bytes
revise.directive: Measure the serialised envelope with Buffer.byteLength in src/analytics/ingest/size.ts.

analytics.title: Return structured errors for malformed batch items
analytics.intent: Map each validation failure in src/analytics/ingest/errors.ts to a stable error code, a JSON pointer to the bad field, and a human message. Producers match on the code, so codes are a closed union and are listed in contracts/analytics.md. Malformed items never abort the batch they arrived in.
analytics.acceptance: Each validation rule yields exactly one code and a pointer that names the offending field.
thinking: Error codes are a public contract once a producer matches on them, so I am making the union closed from the start.
The pointer format is the part producers actually use to find their bug, so I checked it resolves against the envelope shape in a test.
Some validators throw while others return a result. I normalised everything to a result value here so the batch loop has one path.
Found a case where a missing kind produced two codes. I kept only the first failing rule, which matches how the other systems report.

shell.description: Verify each rule yields one error code

analytics.approve: One code per rule with a resolving pointer is what producers can actually act on.

revise.reason: The error result omits the JSON pointer, so producers cannot tell which field failed.
revise.finding: Validation error has no field pointer
revise.directive: Add the JSON pointer to every error object returned from src/analytics/ingest/errors.ts.

analytics.title: Deduplicate repeated client event identifiers on write
analytics.intent: Use the client-supplied eventId as a natural key so a retried producer does not double count events, implemented in src/analytics/ingest/dedupe.ts. The dedupe window and key rules are written into contracts/analytics.md. Duplicates are reported as accepted with a duplicate flag rather than as errors.
analytics.acceptance: Sending the same event twice within the window stores one row and reports the second as a duplicate.
thinking: Deduplication is where a producer retry storm becomes a double count, so I want the key rules to be explicit before any code.
I was tempted to dedupe by content hash. Client event ids are cheaper and the producers already generate them, so I used those.
Duplicates returning an error would make producers retry forever. Reporting them as accepted with a flag gives an idempotent result.
The test replays a batch twice and asserts the row count, which is the number that would be wrong in production.

shell.description: Confirm replayed batches store single rows

analytics.approve: Duplicates are accepted idempotently and the row-count test is the one that matters.

revise.reason: Duplicate events are rejected as errors, so producers retry them indefinitely.
revise.directive: Return a duplicate result instead of an error for a repeated eventId in src/analytics/ingest/dedupe.ts.

analytics.title: Expose a paginated query over raw event rows
analytics.intent: Add a listEvents query in src/analytics/query/events.ts that pages through raw events for one tenant using a keyset cursor on occurredAt and eventId. Offset pagination would scan more rows the deeper a caller goes, so the cursor is opaque and encodes both keys. The cursor format is written into contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: Paging through ten thousand raw events returns each event exactly once across all pages.
thinking: Keyset pagination needs a total order, which is why the cursor carries eventId as a tiebreak as well as occurredAt.
I checked whether two events can share both keys. They can when a producer batches duplicates, so the tiebreak is necessary and not just tidy.
The cursor is base64 of a small JSON object. It is opaque to callers, which lets me change the encoding later without a breaking change.
Paged through a fixture of ten thousand rows in the test and compared the union of pages against the full sorted list.

edit.old: where tenant_id = $1 order by occurred_at limit $2
edit.new: where tenant_id = $1 and (occurred_at, event_id) > ($2, $3) order by occurred_at, event_id limit $4

shell.description: Page through raw events and compare

analytics.approve: Keyset pagination with a real tiebreak, and the ten thousand row check proves the union.

revise.reason: The keyset query orders by occurredAt alone, so paging skips events that share a timestamp.
revise.finding: Keyset cursor lacks a unique tiebreak
revise.directive: Order the events query by occurredAt and eventId in src/analytics/query/events.ts and carry both in the cursor.

analytics.title: Filter rollups by tenant, metric and time window
analytics.intent: Support a rollupQuery filter in src/analytics/query/rollups.ts that takes a tenant, one or more metrics and an inclusive time window. The filter is validated before it reaches SQL, and the parameter names mirror the public query contract in contracts/analytics.md. Callers outside the tenant scope are rejected before the query runs.
analytics.acceptance: A filter with a window that ends before it starts returns a validation error and issues no SQL.
thinking: Filters are where a tenant leak usually happens, so I want the tenant check to run before any other branch.
The window validation is cheap but easy to skip. I added a test that asserts no SQL was issued for an inverted window, because that is the property worth guarding.
I considered accepting a free-form metric string list. I restricted it to the dimension allowlist so the query planner sees a finite set of metrics.
Compared my parameter names with the contract. One name had drifted, so I renamed the code to match the document rather than the other way round.

edit.new: if (filter.from > filter.to) throw new InvertedWindowError(filter.from, filter.to);

analytics.approve: Tenant first, validation before SQL, and the tests assert the no-query property directly.

revise.reason: An inverted time window returns an empty result silently, which hides a caller bug.
revise.directive: Throw InvertedWindowError for filters whose end precedes their start in src/analytics/query/rollups.ts.

analytics.title: Sort daily rollup results with a stable cursor
analytics.intent: Return daily rollup rows in ascending grain order with a stable cursor in src/analytics/query/sort.ts, so repeated reads of an unchanged window return the same sequence. The sort key is day then metric name, and the cursor shape is documented in contracts/analytics.md. Consumers can page through a month of days without gaps.
analytics.acceptance: Two reads of the same window return identical row order, and the cursor resumes after the last row returned.
thinking: A stable sort is only stable if every key is included, so I am sorting by day and then metric name explicitly.
The tricky part is the cursor across a day boundary. I tested a page that ends exactly on the last metric of a day to make sure the next page does not repeat it.
I thought about sorting in SQL versus in memory. SQL is correct here because the index already matches the key, and in memory sorting would load the whole window.
Ran the sort test twice in a row to confirm the output is deterministic without relying on insertion order.

shell.description: Confirm sort order and cursor resume

analytics.approve: Every sort key is explicit and the cursor boundary test covers the awkward case.

revise.reason: Rows with the same day come back in arbitrary order, so pages overlap when the cursor resumes.
revise.directive: Add metric name as a secondary sort key in src/analytics/query/sort.ts and test the boundary case.

analytics.title: Return zero-filled buckets for empty time ranges
analytics.intent: Fill missing buckets with zero values in src/analytics/query/fill.ts so charts do not show gaps as missing data. The fill runs after the query and before the response is serialised, using the grain of the request. The fill rule is recorded in contracts/analytics.md because consumers must know zeros are synthetic.
analytics.acceptance: A seven-day window with two stored days returns seven buckets with five zeros in order.
thinking: Zero filling is a product decision as much as a code one, so the contract has to say that zeros are synthetic and not measured.
I iterated by day with a plain Date and got a timezone bug on a daylight saving boundary. Switching to UTC arithmetic removed it.
The fill should not invent buckets outside the requested window, so I clamp the start and end before generating the sequence.
The test covers a window with no data at all, which returns a full run of zeros and nothing else.

edit.old: for (let d = start; d <= end; d = nextDay(d)) {
edit.new: for (let d = start; d.getTime() <= end.getTime(); d = nextDayUtc(d)) {

shell.description: Check zero fill across a window

analytics.approve: UTC arithmetic and a clear synthetic-zero contract are exactly right.

revise.reason: The fill loop uses local calendar days, so a daylight saving week returns eight buckets instead of seven.
revise.finding: Daily fill uses local time arithmetic
revise.directive: Generate bucket dates with UTC day arithmetic in src/analytics/query/fill.ts.

analytics.title: Publish a rollup-updated event to the outbox
analytics.intent: Write a rollup-updated event to the outbox in src/analytics/rollup/publish.ts whenever a flush changes a stored row. Downstream systems such as search and notifications use it to refresh cached totals. The event payload and topic name are recorded in contracts/analytics.md so consumers subscribe to the same name.
analytics.acceptance: A flush that changes one row emits exactly one outbox event carrying the tenant and grain.
thinking: The event must be written in the same transaction as the rollup row, otherwise a crash leaves a changed total with no notification.
I checked the outbox client signature and it takes a transaction handle, which makes the atomic write straightforward.
I was unsure whether an unchanged flush should emit at all. It should not, and I added a check that compares the old and new totals before publishing.
The publish test forces a crash after the row write and asserts that no event was recorded, which proves the atomicity.

shell.description: Verify atomic outbox publish on flush

analytics.approve: Atomic enqueue with a no-change guard and a crash test is solid.

revise.reason: The event is enqueued outside the rollup transaction, so a crash can leave the total changed without any notification.
revise.directive: Enqueue the rollup-updated event with the same transaction handle that writes the rollup row in src/analytics/rollup/publish.ts.

analytics.title: Consume booking events into funnel counters
analytics.intent: Subscribe to the booking funnel events in src/analytics/ingest/booking-consumer.ts and increment the matching funnel counters. The consumer is idempotent on the outbox message id so a redelivery does not double count. The subscribed topic names are listed in contracts/analytics.md under inbound contracts.
analytics.acceptance: Delivering the same booking funnel message twice increments the counter once.
thinking: Inbound messages from booking are the first cross system edge in this module, so I want the idempotency keyed on the message id.
I considered keying on the booking entity id, but one booking emits several funnel steps and that key would collapse them.
The consumer reads a message, increments, and records the message id in one transaction. I checked that the counter table and the seen table live in the same database.
The redelivery test fires the same message twice and asserts the counter, which is the only check that really proves the guard works.

shell.description: Test redelivery does not double count

analytics.approve: Keyed on the message id with a redelivery test, which is the guard that matters.

revise.reason: The consumer increments the counter before claiming the message id, so a failed claim still leaves the count bumped.
revise.directive: Claim the message id before incrementing in src/analytics/ingest/booking-consumer.ts, inside the same transaction.

analytics.title: Document the metric contract for the catalog system
analytics.intent: Write the outbound metric contract that the catalog system reads, covering which catalog views are counted and under which dimensions. The contract is authored in contracts/analytics.md and the matching read helper lives in src/analytics/metrics/catalog-view.ts. Catalog must be able to read counts without knowing rollup internals.
analytics.acceptance: The contract lists every catalog metric with its dimensions, and the helper returns the same counts as the rollup query.
thinking: Catalog should not know how rollups are partitioned, so the helper hides the partition key behind a plain count call.
Writing the contract forced me to decide whether a catalog view counts once per session or once per page load. Per session is what the product team asked for, so I encoded that.
Compared the helper output with a direct rollup query on a seeded fixture to make sure the two cannot silently diverge.
The contract needs a version line so catalog can detect a breaking change, and I added that at the top.

shell.description: Compare catalog helper with rollup counts

analytics.approve: The contract is explicit about session counting and the helper matches the rollup exactly.

revise.reason: The catalog helper counts page loads while the contract says sessions, so the two disagree.
revise.finding: Helper counts disagree with contract wording
revise.directive: Count distinct sessions in src/analytics/metrics/catalog-view.ts to match the contract in contracts/analytics.md.

analytics.title: Reconcile webhook delivery receipts against rollups
analytics.intent: Compare webhook delivery receipts from the notifications system against rollup totals in src/analytics/reconcile/receipts.ts and report any drift above a small tolerance. Drift is written to a reconcile table rather than logged, so it can be queried later. The reconciliation schedule and tolerance are documented in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A seeded drift of two events on a window of one hundred produces one reconcile row with the correct delta.
thinking: Reconciliation is only useful if the tolerance is written down, so the number goes in the contract before the code uses it.
I considered comparing exact totals. Receipts arrive late, so an exact comparison would flag every window that closed a minute early.
The reconcile row records both the expected and actual totals, which is the detail someone will need when they investigate a drift.
The seeded test drift is deliberately small and sits inside the tolerance on the first run, so I also check it fires once the window exceeds the limit.

shell.description: Check drift tolerance and reconcile rows

analytics.approve: Tolerance is documented, drift is queryable, and the test covers both sides of the threshold.

revise.reason: Any nonzero delta is recorded as drift, so late receipts create noisy reconcile rows every window.
revise.directive: Compare the drift against the documented tolerance constant rather than zero in src/analytics/reconcile/receipts.ts.

analytics.title: Make rollup writes idempotent under retried deliveries
analytics.intent: Change the rollup writer in src/analytics/rollup/writer.ts so a retried flush of the same window produces the same stored totals. Each flush carries a flush id and the writer records which ids it has applied. The idempotency rule is stated in contracts/analytics.md so operators know a retry is always safe.
analytics.acceptance: Applying the same flush id twice leaves the stored total unchanged after the second call.
thinking: A retried flush is the normal path after a timeout, so idempotency is the default here rather than a special case.
I considered using the outbox message id as the flush id. That couples the writer to the publish path, so I added a separate flush id instead.
The applied ids table can grow forever. I noted that as a retention question for later instead of solving it now.
Ran the writer test with a forced retry after a simulated timeout to confirm the total is not doubled.
