shell.description: Confirm retried flush leaves total unchanged

analytics.approve: Flush ids make retries safe and the retention question is noted rather than hidden.

revise.reason: The writer adds the delta on every call, so a retried flush doubles the stored total.
revise.finding: Retried flush double counts the delta
revise.directive: Check the applied flush id before adding the delta in src/analytics/rollup/writer.ts.

analytics.title: Guard counter increments with optimistic version checks
analytics.intent: Add a version column to the counter rows and check it on every increment in src/analytics/rollup/counter.ts. Two workers flushing the same counter must not silently overwrite each other, so a stale version is rejected and retried. The versioning rule goes in contracts/analytics.md under concurrency.
analytics.acceptance: Two concurrent increments on one counter both land, with the final value equal to the sum of both deltas.
thinking: Two workers hitting one counter is the realistic race here, and I want the test to reproduce it rather than reason about it.
I weighed a row lock against a version column. A lock would serialise every flush for a hot tenant, which is the wrong trade for counters.
The migration adds the version column with a default, so existing rows keep working without a backfill step.
First run of the concurrency test failed with a lost update, which confirmed the race; the version check is what fixes it.

edit.old: update counters set total = $2 where id = $1
edit.new: update counters set total = $2, version = version + 1 where id = $1 and version = $3

analytics.approve: Optimistic versioning with a real concurrency test is the right fix for counter races.

revise.reason: The counter update has no version predicate, so concurrent flushes overwrite each other.
revise.directive: Add the version equality predicate to the counter update in src/analytics/rollup/counter.ts and retry on zero rows.

analytics.title: Retry failed rollup flushes with bounded backoff
analytics.intent: Wrap the flush call in src/analytics/rollup/retry.ts with bounded exponential backoff: four attempts, starting at two hundred milliseconds. Only transient database errors are retried, and the final failure is surfaced rather than swallowed. The retry policy is listed in contracts/analytics.md under failure handling.
analytics.acceptance: A flush failing with a transient error succeeds on the third attempt, and a permanent error fails after one attempt.
thinking: Retries hide problems if they are unbounded, so the cap and the final error both matter as much as the backoff itself.
I classified errors by SQLSTATE class. Connection and serialisation failures are transient; constraint violations are not, and retrying them would only repeat the bug.
The backoff sleep is injected as a dependency, which lets the test run in milliseconds instead of waiting on real timers.
Checked that the final error keeps its original cause, since a bare retry exhausted message would hide the database error from the on call.

shell.description: Check transient and permanent retry behaviour

analytics.approve: Bounded, classified retries that surface the final cause are the behaviour we want.

revise.reason: The retry loop returns silently after the last attempt, so a failed flush looks like a successful one.
revise.directive: Throw FlushExhaustedError with the last cause when attempts run out in src/analytics/rollup/retry.ts.

analytics.title: Recover in-flight rollup windows after a worker crash
analytics.intent: On startup, scan for rollup windows left in the flushing state in src/analytics/rollup/recover.ts and resume or reset them. A window is only marked complete after its totals and its outbox event commit together. The recovery rule is written into contracts/analytics.md so on call knows what a restart does.
analytics.acceptance: A window killed mid flush is reset to pending on restart and flushes exactly once more.
thinking: Crash recovery is where the flush id from the earlier unit earns its keep, because a resumed window can be recognised as already applied.
I considered resuming from the last written row. That needs per row progress tracking I do not have, so resetting to pending and relying on idempotency is simpler and correct.
Found a gap where a window marked flushing with no live owner would wait forever. The recovery scan compares a heartbeat timestamp to decide it is abandoned.
The crash test kills the worker between the total write and the outbox enqueue, which is the window I am most worried about.

shell.description: Test recovery after mid flush crash

analytics.approve: Idempotency makes reset the simple answer, and the mid flush crash test is the one that proves it.

revise.reason: Windows stuck in the flushing state are skipped forever, so a crashed flush is never retried.
revise.directive: Reset flushing windows with a stale heartbeat to pending during recovery in src/analytics/rollup/recover.ts.

analytics.title: Backfill historical page views into daily rollups
analytics.intent: Read the legacy page view log and fold it into daily rollups in src/analytics/backfill/historical.ts, using the same writer as live traffic. The backfill runs per tenant so one failing tenant cannot stall the others. The source table and cutover day are recorded in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: Backfilling one tenant's legacy page views produces rollup totals equal to the legacy row count for that tenant.
thinking: The backfill has to feed the same writer as live traffic, otherwise two code paths would drift and we would be debugging the difference for months.
I considered one giant transaction for the whole history and rejected it, since a single tenant with a huge log would hold locks for hours.
The migration adds a marker row per tenant so a rerun skips tenants already finished, which keeps the backfill safe to restart.
Ran the historical test against a small legacy fixture and compared the totals to a plain count, which is the number that proves correctness.

edit.new: await writer.apply(tenant, day, rows, { flushId: backfillFlushId(tenant, day) });

shell.description: Compare backfilled totals with legacy counts

analytics.approve: Same writer for both paths and a per tenant marker is a safe, restartable shape.

revise.reason: The backfill writes each day without a flush id, so restarting the job double counts every finished day.
revise.directive: Pass a deterministic flush id per tenant and day into the writer in src/analytics/backfill/historical.ts.

analytics.title: Add a migration for the rollup partition table
analytics.intent: Create the partitioned rollup table in migrations/analytics/0025_rollup_partitions.sql with a range partition per month and a tenant leading key. The migration is additive and creates the table alongside the old one so the switch can be rolled back. The table layout is recorded in contracts/analytics.md under storage.
analytics.acceptance: The migration applies cleanly to an empty database and the partition for the current month exists afterwards.
thinking: The rollup table is the largest thing this system stores, so the partition layout deserves a dry run before anything is applied.
I wrote the table with a tenant leading key to match the partition scheme from earlier, then checked that the monthly range bounds cover month end correctly.
I considered replacing the old table in place. Keeping it alongside makes rollback a config flip rather than a restore from backup.
Ran the migration against a scratch database and listed partitions to confirm the current month exists.

shell.description: Apply partition migration to scratch database

analytics.approve: Additive partitioned table with the old one kept for rollback is a safe cutover.

revise.reason: The monthly range bounds exclude the last day of each month, so those rows fail to insert.
revise.directive: Use an exclusive upper bound at the first day of the next month in migrations/analytics/0025_rollup_partitions.sql.

analytics.title: Rebuild rollups from raw events in resumable chunks
analytics.intent: Recompute rollup rows from raw events in fixed chunks in src/analytics/backfill/rebuild.ts, persisting the last chunk key so a stopped rebuild resumes. Chunks are sized by tenant and day so each one commits independently. The rebuild procedure and its resume behaviour are written into contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A rebuild stopped halfway and restarted produces the same final rows as an uninterrupted rebuild.
thinking: A rebuild that cannot resume is a rebuild nobody starts on a Friday, so resumability is the main requirement here.
I chose chunks keyed by tenant and day because they map onto the partition scheme and keep each transaction small.
The resume key is written in the same transaction as the chunk rows. If it were written separately, a crash between them would replay a chunk and rely on idempotency alone.
Interrupted the test rebuild after the third chunk and compared final rows with a clean run, which is the equivalence the contract promises.

shell.description: Compare interrupted and clean rebuild results

analytics.approve: Cursor and rows commit together, and the interrupted run matches the clean one.

revise.reason: The resume cursor is saved in a separate step from the chunk rows, so a crash can replay chunks inconsistently.
revise.directive: Commit the chunk rows and the resume key in a single transaction in src/analytics/backfill/rebuild.ts.

analytics.title: Verify backfill totals against the source of truth
analytics.intent: Compare backfilled rollup totals with a direct count over the source events in src/analytics/backfill/verify.ts and record any mismatch per tenant and day. The verifier is read only and can run while traffic continues. Mismatch handling and the report shape are documented in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A seeded mismatch on one tenant and day is reported with both counts and no other rows are flagged.
thinking: Verification is the only thing that proves a backfill is correct, so I am giving it its own unit rather than trusting the rebuild test.
The verifier counts source events with the same filter the rollup uses. If the filters differ, the verifier will flag correct data, which I want to prevent by sharing one predicate.
Considered running the verifier inside the rebuild. Keeping it separate means it can run against production read replicas without touching the writer.
Seeded one mismatched day on purpose and confirmed the report names that tenant and day and nothing else.

edit.new: const expected = await source.countFor(tenant, day, ROLLUP_PREDICATE);

shell.description: Check verifier flags only the seeded mismatch

analytics.approve: Shared predicate and a read only verifier with a precise mismatch report is well judged.

revise.reason: The verifier counts source events without the rollup predicate, so it flags rows the rollup correctly excludes.
revise.directive: Use the shared ROLLUP_PREDICATE when counting source events in src/analytics/backfill/verify.ts.

analytics.title: Emit counters for ingest latency and drop rate
analytics.intent: Record ingest latency histograms and accepted and dropped counts in src/analytics/ops/ingest-metrics.ts, labelled by outcome only. Tenant identifiers are deliberately kept out of metric labels to protect cardinality. The metric names are listed in contracts/analytics.md under observability.
analytics.acceptance: A batch with two rejected items increments the dropped counter by two and records one latency sample.
thinking: Tenant labels would explode the metric cardinality, so I am keeping them off the metrics and leaving tenant detail to the structured logs.
The latency histogram is recorded once per batch rather than per item, because per item timing overstates the cost of a batch.
Checked the metrics client to see whether it supports exemplars. It does not yet, so I noted that as a later improvement.
The test asserts the dropped counter increments by item rejections, not batch failures, which is the distinction operators need.

shell.description: Verify drop counter and latency sample

analytics.approve: Labels stay bounded and the per batch histogram is the honest measure.

revise.reason: The dropped counter is labelled with tenant identifiers, which creates unbounded metric cardinality.
revise.directive: Remove the tenant label and label dropped events by outcome only in src/analytics/ops/ingest-metrics.ts.

analytics.title: Trace each rollup flush across the outbox boundary
analytics.intent: Attach a trace span to each rollup flush in src/analytics/ops/flush-trace.ts and carry the trace context into the rollup-updated outbox payload. A consumer can then link its work back to the flush that caused it. The trace header name is documented in contracts/analytics.md under observability.
analytics.acceptance: A flush and its downstream consumer share one trace id in the captured spans.
thinking: Traces that stop at the outbox are the most common gap in this kind of system, so I want the context to cross that boundary deliberately.
I put the trace context in the payload rather than in headers, because the outbox does not forward headers and I would have had to change it.
Checked the span attributes and kept them to flush id and grain, leaving out tenant to match the metrics decision.
The test captures spans from both sides and asserts the parent id chain, which is the only thing a trace viewer needs to link them.

edit.new: const span = tracer.startSpan('rollup.flush', { attributes: { flushId, grain } });

shell.description: Confirm trace id shared across outbox

analytics.approve: Context in the payload is the honest choice given the outbox, and the span chain test proves the link.

revise.reason: The flush span starts a new trace instead of continuing the one that triggered it, so the link is lost.
revise.finding: Flush span starts a new trace
revise.directive: Pass the upstream trace context as the parent when starting the span in src/analytics/ops/flush-trace.ts.

analytics.title: Log structured diagnostics for rejected event batches
analytics.intent: Emit one structured log line per rejected batch from src/analytics/ops/diagnostics.ts, with the batch id, reject counts by code and the producer name. The log shape is fixed so log queries can rely on it, and it is documented in contracts/analytics.md. Full envelopes are never logged, only pointers and codes.
analytics.acceptance: A batch with three rejected items produces one log line whose counts sum to three.
thinking: A log line per batch keeps the volume sane; a line per item would bury the one problem an operator is looking for.
I considered logging the envelopes for debugging. Envelopes can carry user data, so I log pointers and codes only, and wrote a test that a payload value never appears in the output.
The counts are built from the error results of the previous unit, so the logger takes no new inputs and does not re-validate anything.
Checked the log level: a fully rejected batch is a warning and a partially rejected one is info, which I encoded in the test.

shell.description: Check diagnostic line counts and content

analytics.approve: Counts by code, no payload values, and a level that matches severity.

revise.reason: The diagnostic line includes the raw envelope values, which can carry user data into logs.
revise.directive: Log only pointers and error codes for rejected items in src/analytics/ops/diagnostics.ts.

analytics.title: Benchmark rollup query latency at week-long volumes
analytics.intent: Add a benchmark in src/analytics/query/bench.ts that runs the main rollup query against a seeded week of traffic and records p50 and p95 latency. The benchmark is the gate for the query index decision and its thresholds are written into contracts/analytics.md. It runs as a separate suite so the fast unit tests stay fast.
analytics.acceptance: The benchmark reports p95 under the documented threshold on the seeded week and fails loudly if it is exceeded.
thinking: A benchmark that runs in the normal suite would make every change slower, so this one lives in the serial tier.
I seeded a full week of volume rather than a day, because the partition pruning only shows up across several partitions.
The threshold is written into the contract first. Choosing it after seeing the number would make the benchmark a rubber stamp.
Ran the benchmark twice to check the variance, and the second run was within ten percent of the first, which is stable enough to gate on.

edit.new: if (p95 > P95_BUDGET_MS) throw new LatencyBudgetError(p95, P95_BUDGET_MS);

analytics.approve: Serial tier, a written threshold, and a loud failure rather than a warning.

revise.reason: The latency check logs a warning when the budget is exceeded, so a slow query passes the gate.
revise.directive: Throw when p95 exceeds the budget instead of warning in src/analytics/query/bench.ts.

analytics.title: Cap per-tenant event ingest with a token bucket
analytics.intent: Limit each tenant's accepted event rate with a token bucket in src/analytics/ingest/rate-limit.ts, so one noisy producer cannot starve other tenants of ingest capacity. Limits are read from typed config and the defaults are in contracts/analytics.md. Throttled items return a retry hint rather than being dropped silently.
analytics.acceptance: A tenant exceeding its bucket receives throttled results with a retry-after value while other tenants are unaffected.
thinking: A token bucket per tenant is the simplest fairness mechanism that works across instances, so I am not reaching for anything fancier yet.
I checked how the clock is injected. The bucket takes now as an argument so the refill maths is testable without sleeping.
The retry-after value is computed from the deficit and the refill rate, which is more useful to producers than a fixed backoff.
Found that a burst at the exact refill boundary double counted one token. The test caught it and I changed the refill to use the elapsed time from the last update.

shell.description: Test per tenant bucket refill and throttling

analytics.approve: Per tenant isolation with a retry hint and a refill test that caught a real boundary bug.

revise.reason: The bucket refills without a capacity cap, so a long idle tenant can burst far beyond its limit.
revise.finding: Token bucket has no capacity cap
revise.directive: Clamp refilled tokens to the bucket capacity in src/analytics/ingest/rate-limit.ts.

analytics.title: Enforce a maximum query window for raw event reads
analytics.intent: Reject raw event queries that span more than thirty-one days in src/analytics/query/window-limit.ts, since unbounded scans against the raw table are the main cost risk. Callers needing a longer span must use rollups instead, which the contract states directly. The limit and the error code are recorded in contracts/analytics.md.
analytics.acceptance: A raw event query spanning thirty-two days returns a window limit error and runs no SQL.
thinking: Raw reads are the expensive path, so the cap belongs next to the query rather than in each caller.
I thought about silently truncating to thirty-one days. That would return a partial answer the caller does not know is partial, so I reject instead.
The limit is computed in whole days, which means a window of exactly thirty-one days is allowed and thirty-two is not. The test pins both sides.
Confirmed the check runs before the tenant scope lookup, which keeps the rejection cheap for abusive callers.

edit.new: if (spanDays > RAW_WINDOW_DAYS) throw new WindowTooLargeError(spanDays, RAW_WINDOW_DAYS);

shell.description: Check raw query window boundary behaviour

analytics.approve: A hard rejection instead of silent truncation is the right call, and both boundaries are pinned.

revise.reason: Oversized raw queries are truncated silently, so callers receive partial data with no signal.
revise.directive: Reject raw queries over the window limit with WindowTooLargeError in src/analytics/query/window-limit.ts.

analytics.title: Gate the new rollup engine behind a tenant flag
analytics.intent: Route a tenant to the partitioned rollup engine only when its flag is on, implemented in src/analytics/rollup/engine-select.ts. The flag is read per request so a tenant can be moved back without a deploy. The flag name and default are documented in contracts/analytics.md under rollout.
analytics.acceptance: A tenant with the flag off writes to the legacy table and a tenant with it on writes to the partitioned table.
thinking: The cutover is the riskiest step in this system, so the flag decides which engine a tenant uses and nothing else.
I considered a global flag for the switch. Per tenant gating lets us move one small tenant first and watch it before the rest.
Reading the flag per request means a rollback takes effect on the next write, which is the property the rollback unit depends on.
The test checks both engines receive the expected writes and that neither receives the other tenant's traffic.

shell.description: Verify tenant flag routes to correct engine

analytics.approve: Per tenant routing with a per request read is a clean, reversible rollout.

revise.reason: The engine selector ignores the tenant, so a global flag switches every tenant at once.
revise.directive: Pass the tenant identifier to the flag check in src/analytics/rollup/engine-select.ts.

analytics.title: Add a rollback path that replays from raw events
analytics.intent: Provide a rollback in src/analytics/rollup/rollback.ts that flips a tenant back to the legacy engine and rebuilds its recent rollups from raw events. Raw events are retained for the full retention window, so the replay is always possible. The rollback procedure and its limits are recorded in contracts/analytics.md under rollout.
analytics.acceptance: After a rollback the legacy rows for the last seven days equal a fresh rebuild from raw events.
thinking: Rollback is only trustworthy if it can be verified, so the test compares the rebuilt rows against the raw events rather than against the old engine.
I flip the flag first and then rebuild, because writes during the rebuild must go to the engine that will stay active.
Thought about whether the rebuild needs its own lock. The per tenant flag already serialises the flip, so I did not add a second lock.
Checked the retention assumption against the config, since a rollback beyond the retention window would silently fail to replay.

edit.new:
await flags.set(ROLLUP_ENGINE_FLAG, tenantId, false);
  await rebuild.recentDays(tenantId, ROLLBACK_REPLAY_DAYS);

shell.description: Compare rolled back rows with raw rebuild

analytics.approve: Rebuild from raw as the verifier of rollback is the right way to prove it.

revise.reason: The rollback flips the flag but does not rebuild, so legacy rows miss writes made during the partitioned period.
revise.directive: Rebuild the recent days from raw events after the flag flip in src/analytics/rollup/rollback.ts.

analytics.title: Set retention on raw events and expire old partitions
analytics.intent: Drop raw event partitions older than the configured retention window in src/analytics/retention/expire.ts, one whole partition at a time. Dropping whole partitions avoids a long delete and its vacuum cost on the raw table. The expiry schedule and the partition naming rule are written into contracts/analytics.md under retention.
analytics.acceptance: A partition older than the retention window is dropped and a partition inside the window is left untouched.
thinking: Expiry deletes data for good, so the scheduler, the dry run and the partition name rule all need to be right before the drop is enabled.
I considered deleting rows in batches. Dropping whole monthly partitions is far cheaper, and the retention window is already aligned to months.
Added a dry run mode that lists the partitions it would drop. It is the first thing I run on the scratch database, not the last.
Checked the partition name parser against the migration naming, because a mismatch would mean dropping nothing or the wrong month.

shell.command: psql -d analytics_scratch -c 'select relname from pg_class where relname like $$rollups_p%$$'
shell.description: List partitions before a dry run expiry

analytics.approve: Dry run first and whole partition drops are a safe, cheap way to expire data.

revise.reason: The expiry compares partition months without respecting the dry run flag, so a dry run still drops partitions.
revise.directive: Honour the dry run flag before dropping any partition in src/analytics/retention/expire.ts.

analytics.title: Write an audit trail for metric configuration changes
analytics.intent: Record every change to metric definitions and dimension allowlists in an append only audit table, written from src/analytics/audit/log.ts. Each entry holds the actor role, the before and after values, and a timestamp. The audit shape is documented in contracts/analytics.md so the operations system can query it.
analytics.acceptance: Changing a metric definition writes exactly one audit row with both the before and after values.
thinking: An audit trail is only useful if it is written in the same transaction as the change, so I am not leaving it to a later step.
The table is append only at the grant level, so the application role cannot update or delete an audit row even by accident.
I recorded the actor as a role rather than a user id, to match the convention that actors are roles everywhere in this system.
The audit test changes a metric definition and then reads the audit table, asserting exactly one new row with the expected before and after.

edit.new: await audit.insert(tx, { actorRole: actor.role, before, after, changedAt: clock.now() });

shell.description: Check one audit row per definition change

analytics.approve: Same transaction, append only grants, and role based actors make a clear audit trail.

revise.reason: The audit insert runs outside the metric change transaction, so a failed change can leave a misleading audit row.
revise.finding: Audit row written outside change transaction
revise.directive: Insert the audit row with the same transaction handle as the metric definition change in src/analytics/audit/log.ts.

operations.title: Scaffold the runbook module and its entry point
operations.intent: Create the operations module skeleton so later units have a place to land. Add src/operations/index.ts as the public entry point and src/operations/runbook.ts for the step runner, and record the module boundary in contracts/operations.md. Keep the scaffold empty of behaviour so the first real logic arrives in a reviewable diff.
operations.acceptance: Importing the entry point from a test file succeeds with no side effects. The contract file lists every exported name and marks the rest as internal.
thinking: The brief says this system is operations, so the module lives under src/operations and the contract file is contracts/operations.md. I want the entry point to be the only thing other systems import.
I was about to add a placeholder runner class, then decided against it. An empty class would invite callers to start using it before the contract says what it does.
Checking the existing scaffolds in src/booking and src/billing, they export everything from index.ts. That is the pattern I will follow, but I will only re-export the two names that exist today.
Import side effects are the failure I most want to avoid here. I will keep top-level code to type declarations and a single frozen default config object.
Writing the contract stub last so it reflects what the code actually exports rather than what I planned.

shell.description: Run the module scaffold import test

operations.approve: The scaffold is minimal, imports cleanly, and the contract names every export.

revise.reason: The contract lists an export that the entry point does not re-export.
revise.directive: Re-export every name the contract lists from src/operations/index.ts or remove it from the contract.

operations.title: Load paging and alert thresholds from validated config
operations.intent: Read paging and alert threshold settings from the environment in src/operations/config.ts and validate them once at startup. Thresholds such as the escalation delay and the error budget burn rate must be positive numbers within documented bounds. The accepted keys are listed in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Starting with a non-numeric escalation delay throws a named error that names the variable. Valid settings produce a frozen config object.
thinking: Settings come from the environment, so every value is a string until I parse it. I want the parsing to happen in one function that returns the frozen config.
I considered falling back to a default when the escalation delay is missing. The house rule is to fail loudly, so a missing required value will throw instead of guessing a number.
The burn rate has a documented upper bound. Checking the contract, I found I had written the bound as inclusive in one place and exclusive in another, so I fixed the contract first.
Tests will feed a fixed env object rather than process.env, which keeps them independent of the shell that runs them.
The error message names the variable and the rule it broke, nothing more, because the operator reads it straight from a failed startup log.
operations.approve: Config fails loudly on bad input and the bounds match the contract.

revise.reason: A zero burn rate is accepted but the contract says it must be positive.
revise.finding: Zero accepted for a positive-only setting
revise.directive: Reject zero in parsePositive and add a test that asserts the rejection.

operations.title: Derive tenant-scoped keys for health check records
operations.intent: Build the composite key for health check records so every row is addressed by tenant, service and check name. Put the key helper in src/operations/keys.ts and use it from the health check repository. The key format is documented in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Two tenants with the same service and check name produce different keys. The key string round-trips through parseHealthKey without loss.
thinking: The tenancy key is the first thing every query filters on, so getting the format right here saves me from a cross-tenant leak later.
I initially joined the parts with a colon. Then I realised a service name can contain a colon in our naming scheme, which would make the key ambiguous when parsed back.
I switched to a length-prefixed encoding for each segment. It is uglier to read in logs but unambiguous, and the logs are not where humans key off it anyway.
The round-trip test is the real guard here, so I wrote it before the helper and watched it fail on the colon case first.
Updating the contract so the format is spelled out for the analytics team, who parse these keys from the outbox.
operations.approve: Keys are unambiguous and the round-trip property is covered by a test.

revise.reason: The parser splits on the separator and breaks when a service name contains it.
revise.directive: Replace the separator split with the length-prefixed segment decoder.

operations.title: Register the service heartbeat table with a migration
operations.intent: Add the migration that creates the heartbeat table holding the last seen time for each service instance. The migration file lives in migrations/ and the repository module src/operations/heartbeat-repo.ts reads and writes the table. The schema is recorded in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: The migration applies cleanly on an empty database and rolls back to the prior schema. The table has a unique index on tenant, service and instance.
thinking: A heartbeat table is written every few seconds, so I want its primary key to match the write pattern and not require a secondary lookup.
I checked whether instance identity should be a generated id or the hostname. Hostnames get reused on autoscaled nodes, so I will key on an instance id that the worker generates at boot.
Before writing the down migration I ran a psql dry run against a scratch database to confirm the index name does not collide with the one in the booking schema.
The repository only needs upsert and a range read, so I am not adding an update path that could drift from the upsert semantics.
I documented the retention expectation in the contract because the table will grow without bound unless a later unit prunes it.

edit.new: ON CONFLICT (tenant, service, instance) DO UPDATE SET seen_at = EXCLUDED.seen_at

shell.description: Apply heartbeat migration to scratch database

operations.approve: The migration is idempotent on a fresh database and the upsert key matches the unique index.

revise.reason: The upsert conflict target omits instance, so a second instance overwrites the first.
revise.directive: Add instance to the ON CONFLICT target so it matches the unique index.

operations.title: Model a maintenance window as a bounded interval
operations.intent: Represent a maintenance window as a value with a start, an end and a service scope in src/operations/maintenance.ts. Construction rejects windows whose end is not after their start. The shape is fixed in contracts/operations.md so the booking system can read it.
operations.acceptance: Constructing a window with end equal to start throws. A window reports whether an instant falls inside it, with the end exclusive.
thinking: A maintenance window is a plain value, so I will model it as an immutable object with a constructor that validates, and nothing else.
The boundary semantics matter for booking. If the end were inclusive, a booking that starts exactly when maintenance ends would be wrongly blocked, so I am making the end exclusive.
I wrote the containment test with the boundary instants first, because those are the cases a reviewer would question.
Time zones: I store UTC instants only. The contract says so explicitly so nobody passes a local wall time by accident.
The class has no persistence and no clock access, which keeps it trivially testable.

edit.new: if (end.getTime() <= start.getTime()) throw new RangeError('window end must be after start');

operations.approve: The interval semantics are explicit and the boundary behaviour is tested.

revise.reason: The containment check treats the end instant as inside the window.
revise.directive: Change the containment comparison so the end instant is excluded and add a test for it.

operations.title: Reject maintenance windows that overlap for one service
operations.intent: Add an overlap check in src/operations/maintenance-schedule.ts that refuses a new window when it overlaps an existing one for the same service. Windows for different services may overlap freely. The rule is written into contracts/operations.md under scheduling.
operations.acceptance: Adding a window that starts inside an existing window for the same service is rejected with the conflicting window id. The same window for another service is accepted.
thinking: The overlap test is the heart of scheduling, so I am writing the table of cases first: fully inside, partially overlapping, touching at the boundary, and a different service.
Touching at the boundary should be allowed because the end is exclusive. I confirmed that against the maintenance value before trusting my own table.
I considered loading every window and checking in memory. For now the per-service list is small, so I will query by service and check in the repository layer.
The error carries the conflicting window id so the operator can find the clash without guessing.
This is the first place two windows interact, so I flagged it in the contract for the reviewer who reads the scheduling section.

edit.new: if (w.start < candidate.end && candidate.start < w.end) return conflict(w.id);

operations.approve: Overlap is rejected per service with the right boundary semantics and a clear conflict id.

revise.reason: The check only tests whether the new window starts before an existing one ends.
revise.directive: Compare both start and end bounds so windows that fully contain an existing one are also rejected.

operations.title: Represent incident severity as a closed enum
operations.intent: Define the incident severity values as a closed union in src/operations/severity.ts with a parser that rejects anything else. Severity drives paging policy, so unknown values must never reach the escalation code. The allowed values and their meaning are listed in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Parsing an unknown severity string throws. Each allowed value parses to itself, and the list of values matches the contract exactly.
thinking: I want severity to be a discriminated union, not a free string, so the escalation switch can be checked for exhaustiveness by the compiler.
The house style forbids enums because they do not erase cleanly under Node type stripping, so I am using a const array and a derived union type.
I wrote a test that compares the array against the contract table. If someone adds a value in one place and not the other, the test breaks.
Parsing is strict. A lowercase 'sev1' is rejected rather than normalised, because normalising here would hide a caller bug.
The parser is the only way in from the outside, so the rest of the module can trust the type.

edit.new:
export const SEVERITIES = ['sev1', 'sev2', 'sev3', 'sev4'] as const;
export type Severity = (typeof SEVERITIES)[number];

shell.description: Run severity parser and contract match test

operations.approve: The severity set is closed, strict to parse, and pinned to the contract by a test.

revise.reason: The parser lowercases its input, which silently accepts SEV1 from a caller.
revise.directive: Remove the lowercase step and reject any input that is not exactly one of the allowed values.

operations.title: Track incident state transitions in a guarded state machine
operations.intent: Encode the incident lifecycle as a transition table in src/operations/incident-state.ts so that only legal moves such as open to acknowledged to resolved succeed. Illegal moves return a typed rejection rather than mutating state. The table is copied into contracts/operations.md for the console team.
operations.acceptance: Attempting to resolve an incident that is still open is rejected. Every legal transition in the table succeeds and returns the new state.
thinking: The state machine is the spine of incident handling, so I am putting the legal moves in one table and deriving the guard from it rather than writing if-chains.
I was tempted to allow resolve from any state for convenience during incident response. I decided against it: a resolve that skips acknowledgement would erase the on-call audit trail.
The test iterates the full cross product of states and events, and asserts that exactly the table entries succeed. That catches a new state added without a rule.
Rejection returns a discriminated result with the from state and the attempted event, which the command layer will turn into an error envelope later.
Checking the contract, I found the diagram and the table disagreed about reopening. The table is the source, so I corrected the diagram text.

edit.new:
const next = TRANSITIONS[state][event];
  if (next === undefined) return { kind: 'rejected', from: state, event };

shell.description: Run incident state transition matrix tests

operations.approve: Illegal transitions are rejected by construction and the table is the single source of truth.

revise.reason: The transition table allows resolving directly from open without an acknowledgement.
revise.directive: Remove the open-to-resolved entry from the transition table and update the matrix test expectation.

operations.title: Accept a command to open an incident with validated fields
operations.intent: Implement the open-incident command in src/operations/commands/open-incident.ts. It validates title, severity and affected service, then returns the new incident record. The command shape and the required fields are fixed in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Opening an incident with an empty title is rejected with a field error. A valid command returns a record in the open state with a generated id.
thinking: The command is the first write path, so I want validation to happen before anything touches the repository. The handler is pure until the final persist call.
I am reusing the severity parser from the previous unit rather than writing a second check. Two parsers for the same enum would drift.
The title limit is 120 characters. I checked the contract and the console truncates at 80, so I am keeping the stored limit wider and noting the display cut.
The id is generated by the caller and passed in, which makes the command deterministic under test.
I noticed the handler returns the record before the persist call resolves. I moved the return after the await so a failed write cannot look like success.

edit.new:
await repo.insert(record);
  return { ok: true, record };

operations.approve: The command validates first, persists before reporting success, and reuses the shared severity parser.

revise.reason: The command returns success before the repository write completes.
revise.directive: Await the repository insert before returning the success result.

operations.title: Return a structured error envelope for rejected incident commands
operations.intent: Build the error envelope used by every operations command in src/operations/errors.ts. Each envelope carries a stable code, a field path when relevant, and a human message. The codes are enumerated in contracts/operations.md so clients can branch on them.
operations.acceptance: Every rejection from the open-incident command maps to a code in the enumerated list. The envelope serialises to JSON with no extra keys.
thinking: Clients should branch on codes, never on message text, so I am making the code a closed union and keeping the message purely for humans.
I considered a single generic error class with a free-form details bag. That would let every command invent its own shape, so I rejected it in favour of one envelope type.
The field path is optional. Only validation errors have one, and forcing it on all errors would produce fake paths for conditions like a missing tenant.
I checked the serialised output in the test to confirm there is no leaked stack or internal class name in the JSON.
The mapping function from internal rejection to envelope is in one place so the commands cannot each build their own error shape.

edit.new: return { code: toCode(err), field: err.field, message: err.message };

operations.approve: The envelope is one closed shape, leaks nothing internal, and maps every rejection.

revise.reason: An internal error class name leaks into the serialised envelope.
revise.finding: Internal class name leaked to clients
revise.directive: Serialise only the code, optional field and message keys and drop any other properties.

operations.title: Validate on-call rotation handoff requests before persisting
operations.intent: Check handoff requests in src/operations/rotation.ts so an outgoing responder can only hand off to someone who is on the roster for that tenant. Handoffs that would leave a shift uncovered are refused. The roster and coverage rule are described in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A handoff to a responder not on the tenant roster is rejected. A handoff that leaves no responder for a time slot is rejected with the uncovered slot.
thinking: The coverage rule is the part that can page someone at 3am if it is wrong, so I am testing gaps explicitly rather than trusting the happy path.

Shift boundaries are half-open, the same convention as maintenance windows. I am reusing that intuition but I wrote a separate test because the rotation code does not depend on the maintenance module.
For coverage I walk the timeline in sorted order and track the furthest covered instant. A single pass is enough and easy to read.
I briefly wondered whether handoffs should be allowed to create a gap if the new responder is about to be added. The answer is no, the roster must already contain them.
The rejection names the first uncovered slot, not every slot, so the message stays short for a busy rotation.
operations.approve: Handoffs are checked against the roster and coverage, and the gap report names the first uncovered slot.

revise.reason: A handoff to an unlisted responder returns without a rejection.
revise.directive: Return the not_on_roster rejection in that branch instead of falling through silently.

operations.title: Enforce a single acknowledgement per page for each responder
operations.intent: Make acknowledgement idempotent per responder and page in src/operations/acknowledge.ts. A second acknowledgement from the same responder is a no-op that returns the original timestamp, and a different responder is still allowed. The rule is written under acknowledgement in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Acknowledging the same page twice from one responder returns the first timestamp both times. Two different responders each get their own acknowledgement recorded.
thinking: Pagers get double-tapped constantly, so the acknowledge endpoint has to tolerate repeats without changing history.
I am keying the acknowledgement on the pair of page id and responder id, and letting the database enforce uniqueness rather than checking in code first.
The second acknowledgement returns the original timestamp. Returning the new time would make the audit trail look like the responder acknowledged twice.
Testing the race needs two concurrent calls, so I wrote the test with Promise.all against the in-memory repo and confirmed one insert happens.
This unit is small but the audit consequence is large, so I flagged the no-op behaviour in the contract for the reviewer.

edit.new:
const existing = await repo.insertIfAbsent(ack);
  return existing ?? ack;

operations.approve: Repeated acknowledgements are idempotent and keep the original timestamp.

revise.reason: A repeated acknowledgement overwrites the first timestamp.
revise.directive: Switch the write to insert-if-absent and return the existing acknowledgement on conflict.

operations.title: Expose a paginated list of open incidents by severity
operations.intent: Add the list query for open incidents in src/operations/queries/list-incidents.ts, sorted by severity then age. Results are paginated with an opaque cursor. The response shape and page size limit are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Requesting pages with the returned cursor yields every open incident exactly once in severity order. A page size above 100 is rejected.
thinking: Sorting by severity then age means the cursor has to encode two values. I am encoding both into an opaque string so clients never build their own.
I first wrote offset pagination and then realised incidents open and close during a page walk, which would skip or repeat rows. Keyset pagination is the right tool here.
The page limit is capped at 100. The contract says so, and the test asserts the rejection rather than silently clamping.
I wrote a test that closes an incident between pages and checks that it is simply absent from later pages, not duplicated.
The query file stays free of SQL concatenation. Parameters go through the repository's prepared statement helper.
operations.approve: Keyset pagination is stable across concurrent closes and the page cap is enforced.

revise.reason: Ordering uses creation time, so pages do not follow the documented severity order.
revise.directive: Order by severity rank first, then opened time, then id as the tiebreaker.

operations.title: Filter deployment history by service, environment and time range
operations.intent: Implement the deployment history filter in src/operations/queries/deploy-history.ts. Callers can narrow by service, environment and a half-open time range. The filter keys and their defaults are documented in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Each filter narrows the result, and combining them is an AND. A range with start after end is rejected before the query runs.
thinking: Filters are optional, so I am building the WHERE clause from only the supplied keys and making sure no empty clause is emitted.
The time range is half-open to match the rest of the module. I checked the contract because the analytics team reads these ranges and would be surprised by an inclusive end.
A start after end should fail fast in validation. Letting the query run would return an empty set and look like a real answer.
The environment filter takes only known values. I reused the closed environment list so a typo cannot silently match nothing.
I wrote a test that combines all three filters, because the AND behaviour is what most callers depend on.
operations.approve: Filters compose as an AND, the range is validated up front, and the environment set is closed.

revise.reason: A service filter with an empty string produces a clause that matches nothing without warning.
revise.finding: Empty filter value matches nothing silently
revise.directive: Reject empty string filter values during validation with a field error.

operations.title: Query the runbook step list with cursor pagination
operations.intent: Expose the runbook step listing in src/operations/queries/list-steps.ts with cursor pagination over ordered steps. Steps are returned in their defined sequence, and the cursor is the last step ordinal. The listing shape is recorded in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Paging through a runbook returns every step once in order. A runbook with no steps returns an empty page with no cursor.
thinking: Runbook steps are ordered by an explicit ordinal, so the cursor can simply be the last ordinal returned.
An empty runbook should return a page with no cursor, not a null cursor that clients might loop on. I am making that an explicit test.
I considered loading the whole runbook and slicing in memory. Runbooks can be long, so I am pushing the limit into the query.
The step type is shared with the runner, so I import it rather than redefining the fields here.
Checked that the ordinal index exists in the migration, otherwise this query would scan the table on every page.

edit.new: WHERE runbook_id = $1 AND ordinal > $2 ORDER BY ordinal LIMIT $3

testOutput: migrations/0302_runbook.sql:14: CREATE INDEX runbook_steps_ordinal ON runbook_steps (runbook_id, ordinal)
operations.approve: Paging is in order, terminates cleanly on empty runbooks, and uses the ordinal index.

revise.reason: The step query lacks an ORDER BY, so pages can return steps out of sequence.
revise.directive: Add ORDER BY ordinal to the step listing query and extend the test to assert order across pages.

operations.title: Return alert rule summaries with stable sort ordering
operations.intent: Build the alert rule summary view in src/operations/queries/alert-summary.ts, which lists each rule with its last evaluation result. The sort is by rule name with the rule id as a tiebreaker so output is deterministic. The summary fields are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Two rules with the same name always appear in the same order across calls. The summary includes the last evaluation status and time.
thinking: Dashboards flicker when rows reorder between refreshes, so deterministic sorting is worth a test of its own.
Rule names are not unique across tenants, so the id tiebreaker is necessary and not just defensive.
The last evaluation comes from a left join. If a rule has never been evaluated, the status is a literal not-evaluated value rather than null.
I checked the join cardinality by hand: one evaluation row per rule is the invariant, and the test asserts it through a duplicate row fixture.
The summary is read-only, so there is no transaction concern here.
operations.approve: Output is deterministic and the never-evaluated case is explicit.

revise.reason: The left join can duplicate a rule when two evaluations share a timestamp.
revise.finding: Join duplicates rules on tied timestamps
revise.directive: Select only the latest evaluation per rule using a lateral subquery ordered by evaluated time and id.

operations.title: Publish incident opened events through the outbox
operations.intent: Write an incident-opened event into the outbox in the same transaction as the incident insert, from src/operations/events/incident-opened.ts. Downstream systems consume it from the outbox relay. The event envelope and version are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A failed incident insert leaves no outbox row. A successful open produces exactly one incident-opened event with the incident id.
thinking: The outbox is only useful if the event and the state change commit together, so the event insert goes inside the same transaction as the incident insert.

I wrote the failure test first: force the incident insert to throw and assert the outbox is empty. That test would have passed for a wrong design only if I had also skipped the transaction, so I checked both.
The event envelope carries a version number. I am not adding a payload schema registry, just the integer and a contract entry.
The relay is out of scope here. This unit only writes the row, and the relay unit will consume it.
I reconsidered including the full incident in the payload. A slim payload with the id and severity keeps consumers from depending on fields that change often.
operations.approve: The event is written atomically with the state change and the failure path leaves nothing behind.

revise.reason: The outbox insert runs on a separate connection, outside the incident transaction.
revise.directive: Pass the incident transaction handle into the outbox insert so both commit together.

operations.title: Send page-acknowledged webhooks with signed payloads
operations.intent: Deliver page-acknowledged webhooks from src/operations/webhooks/ack-webhook.ts, signing each body with the tenant's HMAC secret. Retries are handled by the caller, and this unit covers signing and the request shape. The header names and signature scheme are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: The signature header verifies against the body with the tenant secret. A body modified after signing fails verification in the test.
thinking: The signature is computed over the exact serialised bytes that go on the wire, so I serialise once and sign that buffer rather than signing an object and re-stringifying.
I considered a timestamp in the signed material to prevent replay. I added it to the header and the signed string, and wrote the verification helper the consumer will use.
Secrets come from the tenant record and are never logged. I checked the log call in the send path to confirm it prints only the delivery id.
The test mutates one byte of the body and expects verification to fail, which is the property the consumer relies on.
The HTTP client is injected, so the test does not hit the network.

edit.new:
const body = Buffer.from(JSON.stringify(payload), 'utf8');
  const sig = hmacSha256(secret, `${ts}.${body.toString('utf8')}`);

operations.approve: Signing covers the exact wire bytes and a tampered body is caught by the test.

revise.reason: The signed string omits the timestamp, so a captured request can be replayed.
revise.directive: Include the timestamp in the signed string and reject signatures older than the documented tolerance.

operations.title: Define the deploy-status contract consumed by booking
operations.intent: Specify the deploy-status record that the booking system reads to decide whether to pause bookings during a rollout. Write the schema and its validator in src/operations/contracts/deploy-status.ts and document the fields in contracts/operations.md. The booking team reads only the documented fields.
operations.acceptance: A status record with an unknown rollout phase fails validation. The documented example in the contract validates successfully.
thinking: This is a cross-system contract, so the fields and their meanings matter more than the implementation. I am writing the contract text before the validator.
Rollout phase is a closed set. I considered a free string so that new phases could be added without a release, and rejected that because booking would silently treat an unknown phase as safe.
The example in the contract is validated by the test. If the example drifts from the schema, the test fails, which is what I want.
I added a version field so booking can detect a shape change and refuse rather than misread the record.
I noted in the contract that booking must treat an unrecognised version as a pause, not a pass, which is a decision for their side that I want on record.
operations.approve: The contract is closed, versioned, and the documented example is pinned by a test.

revise.reason: The phase field accepts any string, so booking cannot rely on its meaning.
revise.directive: Restrict the phase field to the closed set of documented phases.

operations.title: Replay missed alert events from the outbox on restart
operations.intent: On worker start, re-read unpublished alert events from the outbox and republish them in order, in src/operations/events/replay.ts. Replay must not duplicate events that were already published. The replay cursor semantics are described in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: After a simulated crash between publish and mark, restart republishes that event once and no others. Events are replayed in their committed order.
thinking: Replay is where at-least-once delivery turns into a real question, so I am being explicit that consumers must dedupe on event id.
I need a crash point between publish and mark-published to test this. The project's single test seam is crashPoint, so I am using that rather than adding another hook.
Ordering is by outbox sequence, not by timestamp, because two events in the same millisecond would otherwise swap.
I briefly considered a separate replay table. It is not needed while the outbox row carries a published flag, and one canonical place for state is better.
The test asserts exactly one duplicate in the crash case, which documents the at-least-once guarantee instead of hiding it.
operations.approve: Replay is ordered by sequence and the at-least-once duplicate is bounded and documented.

revise.reason: Replay orders by commit timestamp, which can reorder events written in the same millisecond.
revise.directive: Order replay by the monotonic outbox sequence column instead.

operations.title: Make page creation idempotent under client retries
operations.intent: Accept an idempotency key on page creation in src/operations/commands/create-page.ts so a retried request returns the original page rather than creating a second one. Keys are scoped per tenant and expire after a documented window. The header and expiry are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Two requests with the same key and body return the same page id. The same key with a different body is rejected with a conflict error.
thinking: Pagers are created from automation that retries on timeouts, so duplicate pages are a real and noisy failure mode.
The key has to be scoped to the tenant, or two tenants sending the same key would collide. I am reusing the tenancy key helper from the foundations unit.
Same key with a different body is a client bug, not a retry. I am returning a conflict rather than quietly returning the first page.
I checked the expiry window against the outbox retention to make sure a retry inside the window always finds its record.
The idempotency record and the page insert share a transaction, so a crash cannot leave a key without a page.
operations.approve: Retries return the original page, mismatched bodies conflict, and keys are tenant-scoped.

revise.reason: The idempotency lookup is hardcoded to null, so retries always create a new page.
revise.directive: Replace the hardcoded null with the keyed lookup and add a test that fails without it.

operations.title: Retry failed pager delivery with bounded exponential backoff
operations.intent: Retry pager delivery failures in src/operations/delivery/retry.ts with exponential backoff and a hard cap on attempts. After the final attempt the delivery is marked failed and surfaces to the escalation path. The retry policy is recorded in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A transient failure is retried with increasing delays up to the cap. After the last attempt the delivery is marked failed and no further attempts run.
thinking: Backoff needs an injected clock or the test has to sleep. I am passing a sleep function so the test runs instantly and checks the delay sequence.
The delay doubles with a cap. I wrote out the exact sequence for the documented settings and asserted it, because a subtle off-by-one would be easy to miss.
I considered retrying forever on rate limit responses. The attempt cap applies to all failures, because an unbounded retry on a pager is worse than a missed page that the escalation path can catch.
Jitter would spread load, but this is a low-volume path, so I am leaving it out and noting it as a deferred idea in the contract.
The final failure is an explicit result, not an exception, so the escalation path can branch on it.
operations.approve: The delay sequence is exact, the cap is enforced, and exhaustion is an explicit result.

revise.reason: The delay grows without a cap, so a long outage pushes retries out for hours.
revise.directive: Clamp the computed delay to the documented maximum before sleeping.

operations.title: Guard concurrent escalation runs with a row-level lock
operations.intent: Serialise escalation runs for the same incident using a row lock taken in src/operations/escalation/run-escalation.ts. Two workers picking up the same incident must not both advance its escalation step. The locking rule is documented in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: With two concurrent runs on one incident, exactly one advances the step. The other observes the step already advanced and exits without writing.
thinking: Two workers racing on the same escalation step would page the next responder twice, which is exactly the noise we are trying to remove.
I am using SELECT FOR UPDATE on the incident row inside the transaction rather than an advisory lock, so the lock is released with the transaction and cannot leak.
The test runs two real transactions against the test database, because a mocked lock would prove nothing about the interleaving.
I checked whether the lock could be held across the outbound page call. It cannot; the call would hold a database connection for a network round trip, so the page is sent after commit.
The losing worker re-reads the step and returns a no-op result, which keeps its logs honest.

edit.old: SELECT step FROM incidents WHERE id = $1
edit.new: SELECT step FROM incidents WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE

operations.approve: The row lock serialises the step advance and the page is sent only after commit.

revise.reason: The step is read without a lock, so both workers see the same step and both advance it.
revise.directive: Take the row lock with FOR UPDATE in the same query that reads the current step.

operations.title: Recover stuck runbook executions after a worker crash
operations.intent: Detect runbook executions whose worker heartbeat has gone stale and return them to a runnable state in src/operations/runbook-recovery.ts. Recovery is a sweep that runs on an interval and never touches executions that are live. The stale threshold is set in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: An execution with a stale heartbeat is requeued by the sweep. A live execution with a recent heartbeat is left untouched.
thinking: A crashed worker leaves an execution marked running forever, so the sweep is the only thing that can free it. It needs to be conservative.
The stale threshold has to be well above the heartbeat interval, or a slow worker would have its work stolen. I am using three intervals and documenting the reason.
I checked that requeue does not reset the step counter. Resetting it would replay side effects that already happened, so the step is kept and only the lease is cleared.
The sweep runs with a bounded batch size so one bad night does not lock the whole table.
Doubt: a worker that is merely paused might resume after requeue and double-run a step. I could not fully close that here, so I am recording it as a known gap for the lease fencing unit.
operations.approve: The sweep only touches stale executions, keeps the step counter, and the paused-worker gap is recorded.

revise.reason: The sweep requeues executions regardless of heartbeat age.
revise.directive: Add the stale-heartbeat predicate to the sweep query so only expired leases are requeued.

operations.title: Backfill incident timelines from legacy ticket exports
operations.intent: Import historical timeline entries from the legacy ticket export into incident_timeline rows using src/operations/backfill/timeline-import.ts. The import is keyed on the legacy ticket id so it can be rerun safely. The mapping from legacy fields is written in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Running the import twice leaves the same row count. Every legacy entry maps to one timeline row with a non-null actor.
thinking: The legacy export is untrusted input with inconsistent actor fields. I am mapping each known variant explicitly and rejecting unknown ones rather than guessing.
Rerunnability is the requirement that matters. I keyed each row on the legacy ticket id and entry index, and the insert is an upsert on that key.
I ran the import against a copy of a small export sample to see the shape before writing the mapping. Two fields were nested that I had assumed were flat.
Rows with no actor were the hard case. I am failing the import for that ticket and listing it, instead of inventing a placeholder actor that would appear in audit results.
The import never reads the live tickets system, only the frozen export file, so it cannot disturb production data.

edit.old: INSERT INTO incident_timeline (legacy_id, seq, actor, body)
edit.new: INSERT INTO incident_timeline (legacy_id, seq, actor, body) VALUES ($1, $2, $3, $4) ON CONFLICT (legacy_id, seq) DO NOTHING

operations.approve: The import is rerunnable on its key and fails loudly instead of inventing actors.

revise.reason: The import inserts without a conflict clause, so a rerun doubles every timeline row.
revise.directive: Add the ON CONFLICT clause on the legacy id and sequence key and assert the row count after two runs.

operations.title: Add a migration that splits alert rules into rule versions
operations.intent: Create the migration that moves alert rule definitions into a versioned table so an edit no longer rewrites history. The migration lives in migrations/0325_rule_versions.sql and its backing code is in src/operations/rules/versioning.ts. The new shape and the rollback path are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: The migration backfills one version per existing rule and the current pointer matches the old definition. The down migration restores the original table.
thinking: This changes a table that alert evaluation reads, so the backfill has to produce exactly one current version per rule or evaluation silently changes.
The system is still pre-release, so I am not building a dual-read compatibility layer. A hard cutover with a verified backfill is simpler to reason about.
I ran the backfill on a scratch database with a few hundred rules and compared a checksum of the definitions before and after.
Doubt: the current pointer column defaults to null for rules created after the cutover. I checked and the creation path sets it, so the default is only a guard I will remove in the cleanup unit.
The down migration is written but I have not run it against the scratch database yet, so I am noting that in the commit body.

edit.old: UPDATE alert_rules SET definition = $2 WHERE id = $1
edit.new: INSERT INTO alert_rule_versions (rule_id, version, definition) VALUES ($1, $2, $3)

shell.command: psql -d tidewater_scratch -c 'SELECT count(*) FROM alert_rule_versions WHERE is_current'
shell.description: Count current rule versions after backfill

operations.approve: The backfill is verified by checksum and the cutover is hard, as the design intends.

revise.reason: The backfill creates two current versions for rules that were edited twice.
revise.directive: Mark only the highest version as current in the backfill and add a uniqueness constraint on current rows.

operations.title: Migrate on-call schedules to timezone-aware start times
operations.intent: Convert on-call schedule start times from naive local times into UTC instants with an explicit zone in migrations/0326_schedule_tz.sql and the converter in src/operations/schedules/tz-convert.ts. Shift boundaries must not move across a daylight saving change. The conversion rule is written in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A weekly shift starting at 09:00 local keeps its local start across the spring change. Converted rows store UTC and the zone name.
thinking: Naive local times are a classic source of a shift moving by an hour, so I am storing the zone name next to every converted instant.
I wrote the test on the day of the spring change because that is where a naive conversion breaks. Using a fixed offset would pass most of the year and fail exactly then.
The converter uses the zone database through the standard Intl API. I checked that the runtime ships the zone data the test needs.
I considered rewriting the schedule as recurrence rules. That is a bigger change than this unit needs, so I am deferring it and noting the idea in the contract.
Rows with an ambiguous local time during the autumn overlap get the earlier offset, and the contract states that choice explicitly.

shell.description: Run daylight saving schedule conversion tests

operations.approve: Shifts keep their local start across daylight saving and the ambiguous hour rule is recorded.

revise.reason: The converter appends Z to the local time, which treats every shift as UTC.
revise.directive: Convert using the schedule's zone name so the offset is applied before storing the instant.

operations.title: Verify backfill counts against the source export nightly
operations.intent: Compare row counts and a content checksum between each backfill target and its source export in src/operations/backfill/verify.ts. A mismatch raises an alert and stops the next import stage. The verification rule and alert name are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A deliberately dropped row makes the verifier report a mismatch and exit non-zero. Matching counts and checksums report success.
thinking: Counts alone can hide a swapped row, so I am pairing the count with an order-independent checksum over the key and a content hash.
The verifier must fail the pipeline rather than log a warning. A mismatch that only logs is one nobody reads.
I wrote the test that drops a row from a copy of the fixture, because a verifier that never fails is worse than none.
The checksum uses sorted keys so that a different row order from the database does not produce a false mismatch. I confirmed that with a shuffled fixture.
The nightly schedule is configured elsewhere, so this unit only provides the command and its exit code.

edit.new: if (a.count !== b.count || a.checksum !== b.checksum) return fail(a, b);

operations.approve: The verifier fails loudly on a dropped row and the checksum ignores row order.

revise.reason: The verifier compares counts only and passes a swapped-row backfill.
revise.directive: Also compare the order-independent content checksum and fail when either differs.

operations.title: Emit a latency histogram for each runbook step
operations.intent: Record how long each runbook step takes as a histogram labelled by step kind in src/operations/metrics/step-latency.ts. Buckets are fixed in code and listed in contracts/operations.md. Labels must stay low cardinality, so no tenant or incident id.
operations.acceptance: Each completed step records one observation under its kind label. The label set contains only the documented step kinds.
thinking: The metric is useful only if the labels stay bounded, so I am allowing exactly the step kinds the runner knows and nothing derived from tenant data.
I chose histogram buckets from the observed step durations in the scale fixture rather than guessing round numbers.
The observation is recorded in a finally block so a failed step still shows up in latency. Skipping failures would make the slowest steps look fast.
The metrics client is injected. The test asserts the label set, which is the thing that breaks dashboards when it drifts.
I noted the cardinality rule in the contract so the next person adding a label reads it first.

edit.old: try { await run(step); } catch (e) { throw e; }
edit.new:
const t0 = performance.now();
  try { await run(step); } finally { hist.observe({ kind: step.kind }, performance.now() - t0); }

shell.description: Run step latency histogram label tests

operations.approve: The histogram records failures too and its labels stay within the documented set.

revise.reason: The observation is skipped when the step throws, so failing steps vanish from latency.
revise.directive: Record the observation in a finally block so every step contributes a sample.

operations.title: Attach trace identifiers to every escalation log line
operations.intent: Thread the trace id from the inbound request into each escalation log line in src/operations/logging/trace-context.ts. The logger reads the id from async context rather than from arguments. The log field name is fixed in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Every log line emitted during an escalation run carries the same trace id as the request. A log call outside any request carries no trace field rather than a fake one.
thinking: Passing the trace id through every function signature would touch dozens of call sites, so I am using AsyncLocalStorage and reading it in the logger.
A log line outside a request should omit the field entirely. Writing a placeholder would make a real missing trace look like a valid one.
I checked that the escalation worker's timers keep the context. The test schedules a timer inside a run and asserts the id is still present when it fires.
The log field is trace_id, matching the rest of the platform. I did not invent a new name.
Doubt: context propagation through the outbox relay does not happen automatically, so events published later will lose the trace. I am leaving that to the relay unit and noting it in the contract.
operations.approve: Trace ids flow through async boundaries and absent traces are omitted, not faked.

revise.reason: The logger reads the trace id from a parameter that most call sites never pass.
revise.finding: Trace id missing from most lines
revise.directive: Read the trace id from async context in the logger so every line inherits it without arguments.

operations.title: Surface structured diagnostics for failed deploy health checks
operations.intent: When a post-deploy health check fails, emit a structured diagnostic record with the failing check, its observed value and the threshold in src/operations/diagnostics/health-diagnostic.ts. The record shape is fixed in contracts/operations.md so the console can render it without parsing text.
operations.acceptance: A failed check produces one diagnostic with the check name, observed value and threshold populated. A passing check produces no diagnostic.
thinking: A diagnostic that is a sentence of prose is useless to the console, so the record is a typed object with the three numbers and names an operator needs.
I want the observed value kept as the raw measurement, not a rounded display string, so the console can format it per locale.
A passing check must produce nothing, because diagnostics on green deploys would train operators to ignore the channel.
I checked the threshold comparison direction for latency versus error rate. Latency fails above the threshold and availability fails below, so the check carries its own direction.
The diagnostic is written through the same logger as the rest, so it inherits the trace id from the deploy.
operations.approve: Diagnostics are typed, carry raw values, and only appear on real breaches.

revise.reason: The breach check always compares greater-than, so availability failures never produce a diagnostic.
revise.directive: Use the check's own breach predicate so availability checks fail when the value falls below the threshold.

operations.title: Throttle alert evaluation per tenant under heavy load
operations.intent: Cap how many alert rules a single tenant can evaluate per minute in src/operations/throttle/tenant-throttle.ts, so one noisy tenant cannot starve the others. Excess evaluations are deferred to the next window, not dropped. The limits are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A tenant over its limit has the extra evaluations deferred and none are lost. Other tenants keep their full budget during that minute.
thinking: Dropping an evaluation would silently miss an alert, so the throttle defers and I am writing the deferral as a queue, not a counter that discards.
I used a sliding window per tenant. A fixed window would let a tenant burst at the boundary, which is exactly the spike I want to shave.
The test runs one tenant over its limit while a second stays under, and asserts the second is never delayed.
I considered a global limit with a fair scheduler. Per-tenant isolation is simpler to explain and to debug, so I am keeping it.
The deferred queue is in memory for now. A worker restart could lose it, which the outbox replay unit does not cover, so I am recording that as a known gap.
operations.approve: Excess work is deferred per tenant with no drops, and the in-memory gap is recorded.

revise.reason: Over-limit evaluations are discarded rather than deferred to the next window.
revise.directive: Replace the drop with a deferral onto the next window and assert no evaluation is lost in the test.

operations.title: Cap concurrent runbook executions per tenant quota
operations.intent: Enforce a per-tenant ceiling on concurrently running runbook executions in src/operations/quota/execution-quota.ts. Starting an execution over the ceiling returns a quota error with the current count. The ceiling and error code are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: Starting the execution beyond the ceiling returns the quota error and creates no record. Finishing one execution frees a slot for the next start.
thinking: The quota check and the insert must agree, or two starts can both pass a check that only one slot allows, so I am doing the count inside the same transaction.
I considered counting with a cached value for speed. A stale count would let the ceiling be exceeded under load, so I am counting live rows.
The error includes the current count so the caller can show a useful message instead of a bare refusal.
The quota is read from tenant config, which is validated at startup elsewhere, so this unit does not revalidate it.
I checked that finishing an execution releases its slot in the same transaction that marks it finished, so a crash cannot leak a slot.
operations.approve: The count and the insert share a transaction and the error reports the live count.

revise.reason: The ceiling check runs outside the insert transaction, so two concurrent starts can both pass it.
revise.directive: Move the running count and the insert into one transaction so the ceiling is checked against the same snapshot.
