operations.title: Bound the size of incident attachment uploads
operations.intent: Reject incident attachments above the documented size limit in src/operations/attachments/size-guard.ts before any bytes are stored. The limit and the content types allowed are in contracts/operations.md. The check reads the declared length and then counts the streamed bytes, so a lying header cannot bypass it.
operations.acceptance: An upload one byte over the limit is rejected before storage. An upload exactly at the limit is accepted.
thinking: The declared content length can be wrong or missing, so trusting it alone is not enough. I am counting bytes as they stream and aborting at the limit.
I wrote the boundary tests at exactly the limit and one over, because an off-by-one here is the kind of bug that lets a large file through.
The guard sits in front of the storage call, so a rejected upload never writes a partial object.
I checked the content type allowlist against the contract. The contract lists three types and the code had four, so I removed the extra one.
The limit is a constant in the contract, not an environment setting, because changing it is a product decision.

edit.new:
if (declared > MAX_BYTES) reject();
    if (counted > MAX_BYTES) abort();

operations.approve: The guard counts real bytes, the boundary is exact, and it runs before storage.

revise.reason: The guard trusts the declared length and never counts the streamed bytes.
revise.directive: Count bytes as they stream and abort once the total passes the limit.

operations.title: Gate the new escalation policy behind a tenant feature flag
operations.intent: Route escalation through the new policy only for tenants whose flag is on, in src/operations/flags/escalation-flag.ts. Tenants off the flag keep the existing path unchanged. The flag key and default are documented in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A tenant with the flag off uses the legacy escalation path in the test. Turning the flag on switches that tenant to the new path without a restart.
thinking: The flag is read per evaluation rather than cached at startup, so flipping it for one tenant takes effect on the next escalation without a deploy.
The default is off. A missing flag row must not turn on a new policy for everyone, and I am testing that the absence path is the legacy one.
I considered removing the legacy path once the flag is proven. That is the next cleanup unit, not this one, so both paths stay in code for now.
The flag client is injected, and the test checks both branches with the same incident to show the only difference is the policy.
Doubt: a flag read failing could be treated as off, which is the safe default, but I want it logged rather than swallowed, so I am throwing and letting the caller decide.

shell.description: Run escalation feature flag branch tests

operations.approve: The new policy is off by default and each tenant switches independently without a restart.

revise.reason: A missing flag row enables the new policy for every tenant.
revise.directive: Default the flag to off when no row exists and add a test for the absent-row case.

operations.title: Roll back a deployment when the post-deploy check fails
operations.intent: When the post-deploy verification reports a breach, trigger rollback to the previous release in src/operations/deploy/rollback.ts. Rollback is idempotent and records who or what initiated it. The trigger conditions are in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A breached check starts exactly one rollback to the prior release. Running the trigger twice does not start a second rollback.
thinking: Rollback is the most consequential automatic action here, so I am keeping the trigger narrow: only a documented breach starts it, and a warning never does.
Idempotency matters because the health check can report the same breach on several polls. The rollback record is keyed on the deploy id, so the second trigger finds it and returns.
I checked that rollback targets the previous release from the release record, not from the current config, because config may already point at the bad build.
The test simulates two breach reports for one deploy and asserts a single rollback command was issued.
I left the actual deploy tool invocation behind an interface. This unit owns the decision and the record, not the tool.
operations.approve: Rollback targets the release record, runs once per deploy, and only on documented breaches.

revise.reason: The rollback target is read from current config, which may already point at the failing build.
revise.directive: Resolve the previous release from the deploy's release record and not from current configuration.

operations.title: Apply the retention policy to closed incident records
operations.intent: Purge closed incident records and their attachments after the retention period in src/operations/retention/purge-closed.ts. Records under legal hold are never purged. The periods and hold rule are documented in contracts/operations.md.
operations.acceptance: A closed record past its retention period is purged along with its attachments. A record under hold is untouched even when past the period.
thinking: Purging is destructive and cannot be undone, so the selection query is the thing I am most careful about. I am testing the hold exclusion before the age check.
The purge deletes attachments first and then the record, inside one transaction, so a crash cannot leave an orphaned attachment pointing at nothing.
I considered a soft delete with a tombstone. The retention policy says purge, and a tombstone would keep the data we are supposed to remove, so I am doing a hard delete.
I ran a dry-run count against the scratch database before writing the delete to confirm the hold filter matches the expected rows.
The purge is idempotent: rerunning it finds nothing new to delete and reports zero.

shell.description: Run retention purge hold exclusion tests

operations.approve: Holds are excluded before age, the purge is transactional, and rerunning is a no-op.

revise.reason: The purge query ignores the legal hold flag, so held records are deleted.
revise.directive: Add the legal hold exclusion to the selection query and assert a held record survives the purge.

operations.title: Write an audit entry for every manual override of a page
operations.intent: Record an audit entry each time an operator manually overrides a page's routing in src/operations/audit/override-audit.ts. The entry captures the operator, the reason and the before and after routing. The audit schema is documented in contracts/operations.md and is append-only.
operations.acceptance: An override writes exactly one audit entry in the same transaction as the routing change. An override without a reason is rejected before anything is written.
thinking: The audit trail is what makes an override defensible later, so the entry has to commit with the change or not at all. I am using the same transaction as the routing update.
I require a non-empty reason. A blank reason is the most common way audit trails end up useless, so validation rejects it before the write.
The audit table is append-only by convention and by a database permission. I checked the migration grants and the application role has insert and select only.
The before and after routing are stored as full snapshots rather than a diff, because a diff is harder to read during an incident review.
I verified that a failed routing update leaves no audit row, by forcing the update to throw in the test.

edit.new:
if (!reason.trim()) return reject('reason_required');
  await tx.insert(audit, entry);

shell.description: Run override audit transactional write tests

operations.approve: The audit entry commits atomically with the override and a blank reason is refused up front.

revise.reason: The audit insert runs after the routing update commits, so a failed audit leaves an unrecorded override.
revise.finding: Audit written outside the override transaction
revise.directive: Move the audit insert into the routing update's transaction so both commit or neither does.
